Then \[ b_\epsilon(y)=c_\epsilon\chi_+(y)y^{-p}\ (y\in\R),\qquad c_\epsilon=c_\alpha\int_0^1\bigl[(1+\epsilon t^2)^{-\alpha/2}-1\bigr](1-t)^{p-1}dt, \] and $|c_\epsilon|\le\frac{c_\alpha\alpha}{2p}\epsilon$. (In particular $c_0=0$.)
nodes.proof_html: Step 1 (formula for $\partial_1\Gamma_\epsilon$). Differentiating eq:G_epsilon in $u$: \begin{equation} \partial_1\Gamma_\epsilon(u,v)=c_\alpha\Bigl(\frac{A_\epsilon(v)}{A_\epsilon(u)}-1\Bigr)+c_\alpha\frac{A'_\epsilon(u)}{A_\epsilon(u)^2}\Bigl[p\int_u^vA_\epsilon(s)ds+(v-u)A_\epsilon(v)\Bigr]. \end{equation} Since $A_\epsilon(0)=1$, $A_\epsilon'(0)=0$: $\partial_1\Gamma_\epsilon(0,v)=c_\alpha(A_\epsilon(v)-1)$; in particular $\partial_1\Gamma_\epsilon(0,0)=0$. Step 2. Let $y>1$; then $W'(y)=0$. For $z\ge0$, $W(z)=W(y)=0$ so $S_W(y,z)=0$ and the integrand vanishes. For $z<0$, $S_W(y,z)=\frac{0-(-z)}{y-z}=\frac{z}{y-z}\in(-1,0)$. The integrand is bounded by $c_\alpha\frac\alpha2\epsilon|y-z|^{-\alpha}$ (lem:c03_A_eps_bounds) and $|y-z|\ge y>1$, so absolutely convergent. Step 3. Substitute $t=-z/(y-z)\in(0,1)$, i.e.\ $z=-yt/(1-t)$, $y-z=y/(1-t)$, $dz=-y(1-t)^{-2}dt$; using that $A_\epsilon$ is even, \[ \int_{-\infty}^0\frac{c_\alpha(A_\epsilon(\frac z{y-z})-1)}{|y-z|^\alpha}dz=c_\alpha\int_0^1(A_\epsilon(t)-1)\frac{(1-t)^\alpha}{y^\alpha}\frac{y}{(1-t)^2}dt=c_\epsilon y^{-p}. \] Step 4. $|A_\epsilon(t)-1|\le\frac\alpha2\epsilon t^2\le\frac\alpha2\epsilon$ and $\int_0^1(1-t)^{p-1}dt=1/p$.

nodes.title: Product estimate at a fractional order below one
nodes.statement_html: Let $0<\theta<1$, $I=[a,b]$ with $a\le b$, and $u,v\in C^\theta(I;\C)$. Then $uv\in C^\theta(I)$ and \[ \|uv\|_{C^\theta(I)}\le \|u\|_{L^\infty(I)}\|v\|_{C^\theta(I)}+ \|v\|_{L^\infty(I)}\|u\|_{C^\theta(I)}. \]
nodes.proof_html:
Write $u(x)v(x)-u(x')v(x')=u(x)(v(x)-v(x'))+v(x')(u(x)-u(x'))$,
  divide by $|x-x'|^\theta$, and take suprema. The value norm is bounded by either
  of the two value-norm products on the right, so their sum also bounds it.

nodes.title: Derivative recovery from a one-sided Taylor stencil
nodes.statement_html: For every integer $k\ge1$ and $0<\theta<1$, put $s=k+\theta$. There is $C=C(k,\theta)>0$ such that for every interval $I=[a,b]$ of length at least $1$, $g\in C^s(I;E)$ with values in a real normed space $E$ that is complete (a Banach space, e.g.\ $\C$), $x\in I$, $0<h\le1/(2(k+1))$, and $0\le i\le k$, \[ |g^{(i)}(x)|\le C\left(h^{-i}\|g\|_{L^\infty(I)} +h^{s-i}[g^{(k)}]_{C^\theta(I)}\right). \] Endpoint derivatives are derivatives within $I$.
nodes.proof_html:
At least one of $[x,x+1/2]$ and $[x-1/2,x]$ lies in $I$. Choose its sign $\sigma$.
  Taylor's integral formula at $x$ gives, for $j=0,\ldots,k$,
  $g(x+\sigma jh)=\sum_{i=0}^k (\sigma j)^ih^ig^{(i)}(x)/i!+E_j$ with
  $|E_j|\le C(k,\theta)h^s[g^{(k)}]_{C^\theta}$; for $j=0$ the remainder is zero.
  Invert the fixed Vandermonde matrix $((\sigma j)^i/i!)_{0\le i,j\le k}$.
  Its inverse norm depends only on $k$, and the two signs are conjugate by a diagonal sign matrix.
  This is the explicit finite-dimensional interpolation task required by the next lemma.

nodes.title: Interpolation between the value norm and a noninteger Holder norm
nodes.statement_html: For $s=k+\theta>0$, $k\in\N$, $0<\theta<1$, there is $C=C(s)>0$ such that for every compact interval $I$ of length at least $1$ and $g\in C^s(I;E)$, $E$ a real normed space that is complete (e.g.\ $\C$), writing $U=\|g\|_\infty$ and $V=\|g\|_{C^s(I)}$, for $0\le i\le k$, \[ \|g^{(i)}\|_\infty\le C U^{1-i/s}V^{i/s},\qquad [g^{(i)}]_{C^\theta(I)}\le C U^{1-(i+\theta)/s}V^{(i+\theta)/s}. \] If $U=0$, all the derivatives and seminorms in these inequalities vanish.
nodes.proof_html: If $U>0$, then $V\ge U$. Optimize the stencil bound at $h=\min\{1/(2(k+1)),(U/V)^{1/s}\}$; the cutoff case is absorbed using $V\ge U$. For $i<k$, split pairs of points at distance $(U/V)^{1/s}$: use the mean value theorem and the bound for $g^{(i+1)}$ at shorter distances, and $2\|g^{(i)}\|_\infty$ at longer distances. For $i=k$ use $[g^{(k)}]_{C^\theta}\le V$. The case $k=0$ uses only this last observation.

nodes.title: Tame product estimate at every noninteger order
nodes.statement_html: For every $s>0$, $s\notin\N$, there is $C=C(s)>0$ such that for every compact interval $I$ of length at least $1$ and $a,b\in C^s(I;\C)$, $ab\in C^s(I)$ and \[ \|ab\|_{C^s(I)}\le C\bigl(\|a\|_\infty\|b\|_{C^s(I)}+ \|b\|_\infty\|a\|_{C^s(I)}\bigr). \]
nodes.proof_html: Write $s=k+\theta$. Apply Leibniz to each derivative up to $k$ and the fractional-order product estimate to each summand of $(ab)^{(k)}$. Interpolation bounds each top-order term by $C X^tY^{1-t}$, where $X=\|a\|_{C^s}\|b\|_\infty$, $Y=\|a\|_\infty\|b\|_{C^s}$, and $0\le t\le1$. Use $X^tY^{1-t}\le tX+(1-t)Y$; lower derivative terms are bounded the same way, using $\|a\|_\infty\le\|a\|_{C^s}$ and its analogue for $b$.

nodes.title: Composition at a fractional order below one
nodes.statement_html: Let $0<\theta<1$, $K>0$, $M\ge0$, and let $G:\R^2\to\C$ be $C^1$ with $|G(q)|+\|DG(q)\|\le M$ for $q\in[-K,K]^2$ (Euclidean operator norm). If $u,v\in C^\theta(I;\R)$ and $|u|,|v|\le K$ on a compact interval $I$, then $G(u,v)\in C^\theta(I)$ and \[ \|G(u,v)\|_{C^\theta(I)}\le M\bigl(1+\|u\|_{C^\theta(I)}+ \|v\|_{C^\theta(I)}\bigr). \]
nodes.proof_html:
Integrate $DG$ along the segment between $(u(x),v(x))$ and $(u(x'),v(x'))$,
  which remains in the convex square. Divide the resulting difference bound by
  $|x-x'|^\theta$ and add the value bound.

nodes.title: Composition by induction on the integer part of the Holder order
nodes.statement_html: Fix $s=k+\theta$, $k\in\N$, $0<\theta<1$, $K>0$, and $M\ge0$. There is $C=C(s,K,M)>0$, independent of the interval $I$ of length at least $1$, such that if $G\in C^\infty(\R^2;\C)$, $\|D^jG\|\le M$ on $[-K,K]^2$ for $0\le j\le k+2$, and $u,v\in C^s(I;\R)$ with $|u|,|v|\le K$, then \[ G(u,v)\in C^s(I),\qquad \|G(u,v)\|_{C^s(I)}\le C(1+\|u\|_{C^s(I)}+\|v\|_{C^s(I)})^{k+1}. \]
nodes.proof_html: Induct on $k$. For $k\ge1$, use $(G(u,v))'=\partial_1G(u,v)u'+\partial_2G(u,v)v'$ and the induction hypothesis for each partial derivative of $G$ at order $s-1$. Apply the tame product bound at order $s-1$, and $\|u'\|_{C^{s-1}}\le\|u\|_{C^s}$, similarly for $v$. The value part of $G(u,v)$ is at most $M$; the derivative part has degree at most $k+1$ in $1+\|u\|_{C^s}+\|v\|_{C^s}$. The norm identity $\|f\|_{C^s}=\|f\|_\infty+\|f'\|_{C^{s-1}}$ supplies the induction step. This route requires the interval derivative/norm API but no multivariate Fa\`a di Bruno theorem.

nodes.title: H\"older product and composition estimates
nodes.statement_html:
Let $s>0$, $s\notin\N$, and $I$ a compact interval of length $|I|\ge1$. There is $C=C(s)$ such that for $a,b\in C^s(I)$:
  • $\|ab\|_{C^s(I)}\le C(\|a\|_{L^\infty(I)}\|b\|_{C^s(I)}+\|a\|_{C^s(I)}\|b\|_{L^\infty(I)})$;
  • if $G\in C^\infty(\R^2)$, $K>0$, and $u,v\in C^s(I;\R)$ with $|u|,|v|\le K$ on $I$, then $\|G(u,v)\|_{C^s(I)}\le C'(1+\|u\|_{C^s(I)}+\|v\|_{C^s(I)})^{\lceil s\rceil}$ with $C'=C'(s,K,\|G\|_{C^{\lceil s\rceil+1}([-K,K]^2)})$.
nodes.proof_html: (1) Write $s=k+\theta$. Interpolation (Gagliardo--Nirenberg on intervals of length $\ge1$): $\|g^{(i)}\|_{L^\infty(I)}\le C\|g\|_{L^\infty}^{1-i/s}\|g\|_{C^s}^{i/s}$ for $0\le i\le k$, and the analogous bound for the $\theta$-seminorm of $g^{(i)}$ with exponent $(i+\theta)/s$. Expand $(ab)^{(k)}$ by Leibniz; each term $a^{(i)}b^{(k-i)}$ and its $\theta$-H\"older quotient is bounded by products $\|a\|_\infty^{1-\sigma}\|a\|_{C^s}^{\sigma}\|b\|_\infty^{\sigma}\|b\|_{C^s}^{1-\sigma}$, $\sigma\in[0,1]$, and $X^{\sigma}Y^{1-\sigma}\le X+Y$ with $X=\|a\|_{C^s}\|b\|_\infty$, $Y=\|a\|_\infty\|b\|_{C^s}$. Lower derivatives are handled the same way. (2) Fa\`a di Bruno for $\partial^i[G(u,v)]$, $i\le k$, and the mean value theorem for the H\"older quotient of the top derivative; all derivatives of $G$ are evaluated in $[-K,K]^2$.

nodes.title: Integrals of H\"older families
nodes.statement_html: Let $s=k+ heta otin\N$, $I$ a compact interval, $(T, u)$ a $\sigma$-finite measure space and $H:I imes T o\C$ such that for $ u$-a.e.\ $ au$, $H(\cdot, au)\in C^s(I)$, the maps $(x, au)\mapsto\partial_x^iH(x, au)$, $i\le k$, are measurable, and $\int_T\|H(\cdot, au)\|_{C^s(I)}d u( au)<\infty$. Then $F(x)=\int_TH(x, au)d u( au)$ lies in $C^s(I)$ with $\|F\|_{C^s(I)}\le\int_T\|H(\cdot, au)\|_{C^s(I)}d u$.
nodes.proof_html: Differentiation under the integral sign $k$ times (dominated by $\|H(\cdot,\tau)\|_{C^s}$, integrable), then the triangle inequality for the H\"older quotient of $F^{(k)}$.

nodes.title: H\"older calculus on intervals of length at least $\ell$
nodes.statement_html: Fix $\ell\in(0,1]$. The statements of lem:c03_holder_stencil, lem:c03_holder_interpolation, lem:c03_holder_product_tame and lem:c03_holder_composition_higher hold verbatim for all compact intervals $I=[a,b]$ of length $b-a\ge\ell$ (instead of $\ge1$), with constants depending additionally on $\ell$ (and not on $I$), where in the stencil lemma the step range is $0<h\le\ell/(2(k+1))$ and in the composition lemma the exponent is $\lfloor s\rfloor+1$ and $\|D^jG\|\le M$ on $[-K,K]^2$ for $j\le\lfloor s\rfloor+2$. The four lemmas are the case $\ell=1$ (in Lean they are derived from these variants).
nodes.proof_html: Repeat the proofs of the four lemmas with $1$ replaced by $\ell$: in the stencil one of $[x,x+\ell/2]$, $[x-\ell/2,x]$ lies in $I$; the interpolation cutoff becomes $h=\min\{\ell/(2(k+1)),(U/V)^{1/s}\}$, which only changes the constants by powers of $\ell$; the product and composition estimates are then derived exactly as before. (These variants are what the near/far regularity lemmas below need on $[-R,R]$ with $R<1/2$.)

nodes.title: Regularity of the near part of $\mc I_\epsilon$
nodes.statement_html: Let $\epsilon\ge0$, $f\in W^{2,\infty}_{\textup{loc}}$, $f'\in L^\infty$, $s\notin\N$, $s>0$, and suppose $f'\in C^s_{\textup{loc}}$. Let $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\R)$ with $\chi=1$ on $[-1,1]$, $\operatorname{supp}\chi\subset[-2,2]$, $0\le\chi\le1$. Then \[ \mc I^{\textup{near}}_\epsilon(f)(y):=\int_\R\frac{\chi(t)\Gamma_\epsilon(f'(y),S_f(y,y-t))}{|t|^\alpha}dt \] lies in $C^s_{\textup{loc}}$, with $\|\mc I^{\textup{near}}_\epsilon(f)\|_{C^s([-R,R])}\le C$ where $C$ depends on $s,R,\epsilon,\alpha,\|f'\|_{L^\infty}$, $\|f''\|_{L^\infty(-R-2,R+2)}$ and $\|f'\|_{C^s([-R-2,R+2])}$.
nodes.proof_html: Fix $R\ge1$, $I=[-R,R]$, $J=[-R-2,R+2]$, $0<|t|\le2$. Put $v_t(y)=S_f(y,y-t)=\int_0^1f'(y-\tau t)d\tau$ and $d_t=f'-v_t$. Step 1. $\|v_t\|_{C^s(I)}\le\|f'\|_{C^s(J)}$ (differentiate under the $\tau$-integral; translation invariance of the H\"older quotient) and $|v_t|\le\|f'\|_\infty$. Step 2. $\|d_t\|_{L^\infty(I)}\le\frac12\|f''\|_{L^\infty(J)}|t|$ and $\|d_t\|_{C^s(I)}\le2\|f'\|_{C^s(J)}$. Step 3. By lem:c03_Gamma_quadratic_factor, $\Gamma_\epsilon(f',v_t)=d_t^2\,\sq\Gamma_\epsilon(f',v_t)$. By lem:c03_holder_calculus(2) with $K=\|f'\|_\infty$, $\|\sq\Gamma_\epsilon(f',v_t)\|_{C^s(I)}\le C$ uniformly in $t$; by (1) twice, $\|d_t^2\|_{C^s}\le 2C\|d_t\|_\infty\|d_t\|_{C^s}\le C|t|$ and $\|\Gamma_\epsilon(f',v_t)\|_{C^s(I)}\le C(\|d_t\|_\infty^2\|\sq\Gamma_\epsilon\|_{C^s}+\|d_t^2\|_{C^s}\|\sq\Gamma_\epsilon\|_\infty)\le C|t|$. Step 4. Apply lem:c03_parametric_holder with $T=[-2,2]\setminus\{0\}$, $d\nu=\chi(t)|t|^{-\alpha}dt$: $\int_{|t|\le2}|t|^{1-\alpha}dt=\int|t|^{-p}<\infty$. Measurability: $(y,t)\mapsto\partial_y^iH$ is continuous for $t\ne0$.

nodes.title: Regularity of the far part of $\mc I_\epsilon$
nodes.statement_html: Under the hypotheses of lem:c03_I_near, $\mc I^{\textup{far}}_\epsilon(f):=\mc I_\epsilon(f)-\mc I^{\textup{near}}_\epsilon(f)$, i.e. $\mc I^{\textup{far}}_\epsilon(f)(y)=\int(1-\chi(y-z))\Gamma_\epsilon(f'(y),S_f(y,z))|y-z|^{-\alpha}dz$, lies in $C^s_{\textup{loc}}$ with $\|\mc I^{\textup{far}}_\epsilon(f)\|_{C^s([-R,R])}\le C(s,R,\epsilon,\alpha,\|f'\|_{L^\infty},\|f'\|_{C^s([-R,R])})$.
nodes.proof_html: Let $\sq\chi\in C_c^\infty$, $\sq\chi=1$ on $[-\frac12,\frac12]$, $\operatorname{supp}\sq\chi\subset[-1,1]$, and $\psi(t)=(1-\sq\chi(t))/t$, which is smooth with $|\psi^{(i)}(t)|\le C_i\ang t^{-1-i}$. Step 1. $V_z(y):=(f(y)-f(z))\psi(y-z)$ equals $S_f(y,z)$ when $|y-z|\ge1$, satisfies $|V_z|\le\|f'\|_\infty$, and $\|V_z\|_{C^s(I)}\le C(\|f'\|_\infty+\|f'\|_{C^s(I)})$ uniformly in $z\in\R$: by Leibniz, $\partial_y^iV_z=\sum_{l<i}\binom il f^{(i-l)}(y)\psi^{(l)}(y-z)+(f(y)-f(z))\psi^{(i)}(y-z)$ and $|f(y)-f(z)||\psi^{(i)}(y-z)|\le C\|f'\|_\infty$; the H\"older quotient is treated likewise with the mean value theorem. Step 2. $\omega(t):=(1-\chi(t))|t|^{-\alpha}$ is smooth with $|\omega^{(i)}(t)|\le C_i\ang t^{-\alpha-i}$, and $\ang{y-z}^{-\alpha}\le 2^{\alpha}\ang R^{\alpha}\ang z^{-\alpha}$ for $|y|\le R$ (Peetre). Step 3. $H(y,z)=\Gamma_\epsilon(f'(y),V_z(y))\,\omega(y-z)$ equals the far integrand. By lem:c03_holder_calculus, $\|H(\cdot,z)\|_{C^s(I)}\le C\ang z^{-\alpha}$, integrable in $z$ as $\alpha>1$. Conclude with lem:c03_parametric_holder.

nodes.title: Regularity of the nonlinear term
nodes.statement_html: Let $\epsilon\ge0$, $f\in W^{2,\infty}_{\textup{loc}}$ with $f'\in L^\infty$, and $s>0$, $s\notin\N$. If $f'\in C^s_{\textup{loc}}$ then $\mc I_\epsilon(f)\in C^s_{\textup{loc}}$ and $B_\epsilon(f')(f-yf')\in C^s_{\textup{loc}}$.
nodes.proof_html: $\mc I_\epsilon=\mc I^{\textup{near}}_\epsilon+\mc I^{\textup{far}}_\epsilon$ (lem:c03_I_well_defined gives absolute convergence so the split is legitimate). For the local term: $f\in C^{s+1}_{\textup{loc}}\subset C^s_{\textup{loc}}$, $y\mapsto y$ smooth, $B_\epsilon$ smooth; use lem:c03_holder_calculus on each $[-R,R]$.

nodes.title: Singular-kernel formula for $|D|^p$
nodes.statement_html: Let $0<p<1$ and $c_p:=\bigl(\int_\R\frac{1-\cos z}{|z|^{1+p}}dz\bigr)^{-1}\in(0,\infty)$. Then $c_p\int_\R\frac{1-e^{i\lambda z}}{|z|^{1+p}}dz=|\lambda|^p$ for all $\lambda\in\R$ (absolutely convergent), and for every $g\in\mc S(\R)$ (or $g\in C^1(\R)$ with $g,g'$ bounded and $\hat g$ defined as a tempered distribution, as in def:frac_multiplier) \[ |D|^pg(y)=c_p\int_\R\frac{g(y)-g(y+z)}{|z|^{1+p}}dz . \]
nodes.proof_html: The odd part $\sin(\lambda z)|z|^{-1-p}$ integrates to $0$; scaling $z\mapsto z/|\lambda|$ gives $|\lambda|^p/c_p$ for the even part. For $g\in\mc S$: $g(y)-g(y+z)=\frac1{2\pi}\int\hat g(\xi)e^{iy\xi}(1-e^{iz\xi})d\xi$; Fubini is justified by $\int|1-e^{iz\xi}||z|^{-1-p}dz=C|\xi|^p$ and $\hat g\in\mc S$. For bounded $C^1$ functions this is the definition/characterisation in def:frac_multiplier.

nodes.title: Interior Schauder estimate for $|D|^p$
nodes.statement_html: Let $0<p<1$, $\beta>0$ with $\beta\notin\N$ and $\beta+p\notin\N$. There is $C=C(p,\beta)$ such that for every $w\in C^\infty(\R)$ with $w\in C^\beta(\R)$ (global H\"older norm finite), \[ \|w\|_{C^{\beta+p}([-\frac12,\frac12])}\le C\bigl(\|w\|_{C^\beta(\R)}+\||D|^pw\|_{C^\beta([-1,1])}\bigr). \]
nodes.proof_html: Use the fixed cutoff and the construction of sec:c12_schauder. The localized right-hand side is globally $C^\beta$ with the required quantitative bound; apply the compact-input estimate and restrict to $[-1/2,1/2]$. The target is Proposition 2.2 of the arXiv version of \cite{RosOton-Serra:dirichlet-fractional-laplacian}, with $n=1$, $s=p/2$. Corollary 2.4 in that version is the related weighted-tail estimate.

nodes.title: Localization of the fractional operator
nodes.statement_html: Fix $0<p<1$, $s>0$, $s\notin\N$, and $\eta\in C_c^\infty(\R;[0,1])$, $\eta=1$ on $[-2,2]$, $\operatorname{supp}\eta\subset[-3,3]$. Suppose $g$ is bounded and locally Lipschitz, $g\in C^s_{\rm loc}(\R)$, and $h=|D|^pg\in C^s_{\rm loc}(\R)$, with the defining singular integral absolutely convergent. Then $v=\eta g$ is compactly supported and globally Lipschitz, $v\in C^s(\R)$, and on $[-1,1]$ \[ |D|^pv=h-T,\qquad T(y)=-c_p\int_\R(1-\eta(z))g(z)|z-y|^{-1-p}\,dz. \] The displayed integral and all its $y$ derivatives converge absolutely on $[-1,1]$; $T$ is smooth on $(-2,2)$ and $\sup_{|y|\le1}|T^{(j)}(y)|\le C(p,j,\eta)\|g\|_\infty$. In particular $|D|^pv\in C^s([-1,1])$.
nodes.proof_html: The cutoffs are constant on a neighbourhood of the evaluation interval. Split $g=\eta g+(1-\eta)g$ in the absolutely convergent kernel formula. For the tail, differentiate only $|z-y|^{-1-p}$; on $|y|\le1$ its $j$-th derivative is bounded by $C(p,j)\mathbf1_{|z|\ge2}|z|^{-1-p-j}$, an integrable majorant. Product estimates on $[-4,4]$, and zero extension across the region where $\eta=0$, give the global Holder bound for $v$.

nodes.title: Mollification commutes with the fractional operator
nodes.statement_html: Fix $0<p<1$, $s>0$, $s\notin\N$, and a nonnegative $\rho\in C_c^\infty((-1,1))$ with $\int\rho=1$. Let $v:\R\to\R$ be compactly supported, globally Lipschitz, and in $C^s(\R)$, with $|D|^pv\in C^s([-1,1])$. For $0<\delta<1/2$, set $\rho_\delta(x)=\delta^{-1}\rho(x/\delta)$ and $w_\delta=v*\rho_\delta$. Then $w_\delta\in C_c^\infty(\R)$, $w_\delta\to v$ uniformly as $\delta\downarrow0$, and \[ |D|^pw_\delta=(|D|^pv)*\rho_\delta,\quad \|w_\delta\|_{C^s(\R)}\le\|v\|_{C^s(\R)},\quad \||D|^pw_\delta\|_{C^s([-1/2,1/2])}\le\||D|^pv\|_{C^s([-1,1])}. \] All convolutions and singular integrals in the identity converge absolutely.
nodes.proof_html: In the double integral, dominate $|v(x-z)-v(x)|$ by $\min\{\operatorname{Lip}(v)|z|,2\|v\|_\infty\}$ and integrate against $|z|^{-1-p}\rho_\delta$. Tonelli and Fubini justify commutation. Differentiation of the smooth compactly supported mollifier gives smoothness; averaging translates of $v$ and of $|D|^pv$ gives the norm bounds. Uniform continuity of $v$ gives uniform convergence, including outside its support.

nodes.title: Closedness of a bounded Holder ball under uniform convergence
nodes.statement_html: Let $s=k+\theta>0$, $k\in\N$, $0<\theta<1$, $I=[a,b]$ with $a<b$, $M\ge0$, and let $E$ be a real normed space that is complete (e.g.\ $\R$ or $\C$). If $f_n\in C^s(I;E)$, $\|f_n\|_{C^s(I)}\le M$ for every $n$, and $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $I$, then $f\in C^s(I)$ and $\|f\|_{C^s(I)}\le M$.
nodes.proof_html:
The top derivatives are equicontinuous by their common $\theta$-Holder bound;
  lower derivatives are equicontinuous by the next derivative bound. Arzel\`a--Ascoli,
  applied finitely many times, gives a subsequence with uniform convergence of derivatives
  through order $k$. Pass to the limit in
  $f_n^{(i)}(x)-f_n^{(i)}(a)=\int_a^x f_n^{(i+1)}$ to identify the limits as the derivatives of $f$.
  For every finite collection of evaluation points and one Holder quotient, pass to the limit
  in their sum bounded by $M$; taking independent suprema gives the bound for the full norm,
  without multiplying $M$ by the number of derivatives.

nodes.title: Translation invariance of $|D|^p$
nodes.statement_html: For every $p\in\R$, every $g:\R\to\R$ and all $x_0,y\in\R$, $|D|^p[g(\cdot+x_0)](y)=(|D|^pg)(y+x_0)$, where $|D|^p$ is the singular-integral expression $c_\alpha\int_\R\frac{g(y)-g(z)}{|y-z|^{1+p}}\,dz$ of def:frac_multiplier (Lean fracD; both sides are the Bochner integral, so the identity holds also when the integral diverges).
nodes.proof_html: Substitute $z\mapsto z+x_0$ (translation invariance of Lebesgue measure) in the defining integral.

nodes.title: Gluing local H\"older bounds
nodes.statement_html: Let $s'>0$, $s'\notin\N$, and $g:\R\to\R$. If $g\in C^{s'}([x_0-\frac12,x_0+\frac12])$ for every $x_0\in\R$, then $g\in C^{s'}_{\textup{loc}}(\R)$.
nodes.proof_html:
$g$ is $C^{\lfloor s'\rfloor}$ near every point, hence on $\R$, and the derivatives within the small
  intervals agree with the global ones. On a compact $[a,b]$ the values of the derivatives are bounded by
  covering $[a,b]$ with finitely many intervals of length $1$; for the H\"older quotient of
  $g^{(\lfloor s'\rfloor)}$ use the local H\"older constant of the interval centred at $x$ when
  $|x-x'|\le\frac12$, and the sup bound ($\le 8\sup|g^{(\lfloor s'\rfloor)}|\,|x-x'|^{\theta}$) when $|x-x'|>\frac12$.

nodes.title: Localization of the fractional operator, wide version
nodes.statement_html: Under the hypotheses of lem:c03_gain_localization ($0<p<1$, $s>0$, $s\notin\N$, $\eta\in C^\infty(\R;[0,1])$, $\eta=1$ on $[-2,2]$, $\eta=0$ for $|x|>3$; $g$ bounded, locally Lipschitz, $g\in C^s_{\textup{loc}}(\R)$, $z\mapsto\frac{g(y)-g(z)}{|y-z|^{1+p}}$ integrable for every $y$, and $|D|^pg\in C^s_{\textup{loc}}(\R)$), one has $|D|^p(\eta g)\in C^s([-\frac32,\frac32])$.
nodes.proof_html: As for the localization lemma above (with a wider evaluation interval): on $[-\frac32,\frac32]$, $|D|^p(\eta g)=|D|^pg-T$ with the tail $T(y)=-c_p\int(1-\eta(z))g(z)|z-y|^{-1-p}dz$ ($c_p=c_\alpha$ by lem:c03_frac_kernel_formula). Since $|z-y|\ge\frac12$ on the support of $1-\eta$, $T$ is smooth on a neighbourhood of $[-\frac32,\frac32]$, with integrable majorants $C\|g\|_\infty\mathbf 1_{|z|\ge2}\ang z^{-1-p-j}$ for its derivatives; its $C^s$ norm is then bounded via lem:c03_parametric_holder.

nodes.title: Mollification, wide version
nodes.statement_html: Under the hypotheses of lem:c03_gain_mollification, but with $|D|^pv\in C^s([-\frac32,\frac32])$ in place of $C^s([-1,1])$, for every $0<\delta<\frac12$ the mollification $w_\delta=v*\rho_\delta$ satisfies $w_\delta\in C^s(\R)$, $|D|^pw_\delta\in C^s([-1,1])$ and $\||D|^pw_\delta\|_{C^s([-1,1])}\le\||D|^pv\|_{C^s([-\frac32,\frac32])}$.
nodes.proof_html: lem:c03_gain_mollification (applied with the restriction of $|D|^pv$ to $[-1,1]$) gives smoothness and $|D|^pw_\delta=(|D|^pv)*\rho_\delta$. For $|x|\le1$ and $\delta<\frac12$ the convolution only samples $|D|^pv$ on $[-\frac32,\frac32]$; averaging the translates (each with $C^s([-1,1])$ norm at most $\||D|^pv\|_{C^s([-\frac32,\frac32])}$) against the probability density $\rho_\delta$ gives the bound.

nodes.title: Regularity gain for the linear part
nodes.statement_html: Let $0<p<1$, $s>0$ with $s\notin\N$, $s+p\notin\N$. Let $g\in L^\infty(\R)\cap W^{1,\infty}_{\textup{loc}}(\R)\cap C^s_{\textup{loc}}$ and suppose the (pointwise, absolutely convergent) function $h:=|D|^pg$ lies in $C^s_{\textup{loc}}$. Then $g\in C^{s+p}_{\textup{loc}}$.
nodes.proof_html: Lean route (no dilation): for each $x_0$ translate $g$ (lem:c03_frac_translate), localize with lem:c03_gain_localization_wide, mollify with lem:c03_gain_mollification_wide, apply lem:c03_schauder_RS with $\beta=s$ uniformly in $\delta_n=1/(n+3)$, pass to the limit with lem:c03_holder_closed_ball to get $g\in C^{s+p}([x_0-\frac12,x_0+\frac12])$, and conclude with lem:c03_holder_glue. The argument with dilations is as follows. By translation and dilation invariance ($|D|^p[g(x_0+r\,\cdot)]=r^p(|D|^pg)(x_0+r\,\cdot)$) it suffices to show $g\in C^{s+p}([-\frac18,\frac18])$ for $g$ satisfying the hypotheses; covering a compact interval by finitely many such neighbourhoods then gives the claim. Step 1 (localisation). Let $\eta\in C_c^\infty$, $\eta=1$ on $[-2,2]$, $\operatorname{supp}\eta\subset[-3,3]$. Then $\eta g\in C^s(\R)$ (compact support) and, pointwise for $|y|<1$, $|D|^p(\eta g)(y)=h(y)-|D|^p((1-\eta)g)(y)$ with $|D|^p((1-\eta)g)(y)=-c_p\int(1-\eta(w))g(w)|w-y|^{-1-p}dw$. The latter is $C^\infty$ on $(-1,1)$, with $k$-th derivative bounded by $C_k\|g\|_{L^\infty}$ (as $|w-y|\ge1$ on the support; differentiate under the integral). Hence $|D|^p(\eta g)\in C^s([-1,1])$. Step 2 (mollification). Let $\rho_\delta$ be a standard mollifier and $w_\delta=(\eta g)*\rho_\delta\in C^\infty_c$. Then $|D|^pw_\delta=(|D|^p(\eta g))*\rho_\delta$, so $\||D|^pw_\delta\|_{C^s([-1/2,1/2])}\le\||D|^p(\eta g)\|_{C^s([-1,1])}$ for $\delta<1/2$, and $\|w_\delta\|_{C^s(\R)}\le\|\eta g\|_{C^s(\R)}$. Step 3. Apply lem:c03_schauder_RS (rescaled to the pair of intervals $[-\frac14,\frac14]\subset[-\frac12,\frac12]$): $\|w_\delta\|_{C^{s+p}([-1/4,1/4])}\le C$ uniformly in $\delta$. Step 4. $w_\delta\to\eta g=g$ uniformly on $[-\frac14,\frac14]$; by Arzel\`a--Ascoli the derivatives up to order $\lfloor s+p\rfloor$ converge uniformly on $[-\frac18,\frac18]$ and the H\"older bound passes to the limit. So $g\in C^{s+p}([-\frac18,\frac18])$.

nodes.title: Smoothness of profiles
nodes.statement_html: Let $0<p<1$, $\alpha=p+1$, $\epsilon\ge0$. Suppose $f\in W^{2,\infty}_{\textup{loc}}(\R)$, $f'\in L^\infty(\R)$, and $\mc E_\epsilon(f)=0$ in $\mc D'(\R)$ (equivalently, by lem:c03_I_well_defined, pointwise everywhere). Then $f\in C^\infty(\R)$. In particular, for $\epsilon$ small enough the profile $f=\ov f_{\epsilon,\mu_\epsilon}+r_\epsilon$ and the correction $r_\epsilon$ of thm:fixed_point_correction are $C^\infty$.
nodes.proof_html: Step 0 (choice of exponents). The set $\{k-np:k,n\in\N_0\}$ is countable; pick $s_0\in(0,1)$ outside it, so $s_n:=s_0+np\notin\N$ for all $n\ge0$. Step 1. By lem:c03_I_well_defined and prop:analysis_semilinear_kernel, for every $y$: $|D|^pf'(y)=-B_\epsilon(f'(y))(f(y)-yf'(y))-\mc I_\epsilon(f)(y)$. Step 2 (base). $f'$ is locally Lipschitz, so $f'\in C^{s_0}_{\textup{loc}}$. Step 3 (induction). Suppose $f'\in C^{s_n}_{\textup{loc}}$. By lem:c03_I_regularity, the right side of Step 1 is in $C^{s_n}_{\textup{loc}}$. Apply lem:c03_linear_gain with $g=f'$ (bounded, $W^{1,\infty}_{\textup{loc}}$, $C^{s_n}_{\textup{loc}}$; $s_n,s_{n+1}\notin\N$) to get $f'\in C^{s_{n+1}}_{\textup{loc}}$. Step 4. Since $s_n\to\infty$, $f'\in C^k(\R)$ for every $k$, so $f\in C^\infty$. Step 5 (application). By thm:fixed_point_approximation, $\ov f=\ov f_{\epsilon,\mu_\epsilon}\in C^\infty$ with $\ov f'$ bounded (bounds (2) there with $j=0$). By def:X_gamma, $r_\epsilon\in W^{2,\infty}_{\textup{loc}}$ and for $y\ge0$, $|r_\epsilon'|\le\|r_\epsilon\|_{X_\gamma}\ang y^{1/p-\gamma}\le\|r_\epsilon\|_{X_\gamma}$ since $\gamma=\gamma_2>\beta+1/p>1/p$; for $y\le0$, $|r'_\epsilon|\le\|r_\epsilon\|_{X_\gamma}$. So $f$ satisfies the hypotheses. By definition of $\mc N_{\epsilon,\ov f}$ (def:N_eps), $\mc E_\epsilon(\ov f+r)=\mc E_\epsilon(\ov f)+\mc L_\epsilon r+\mc N_{\epsilon,\ov f}(r)$, which vanishes by eqn:fixed_point_correction. Hence $f\in C^\infty$ and $r_\epsilon=f-\ov f\in C^\infty$.

nodes.title: Symbol bounds for $\xi^j\chi\Phi_0^k$
nodes.statement_html: Let $0<p<1$, $\Phi_0(\xi)=\xi|\xi|^p/(p+1)$, and $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\R)$ with $\operatorname{supp}\chi\subset[-2,2]$, $\chi=1$ on $[-1,1]$. For $k\ge1$, $j\in\{0,1,2\}$ let $a_{k,j}(\xi)=(i\xi)^j\chi(\xi)\Phi_0(\xi)^k$. Then $a_{k,j}\in C^{j+1}(\R)\cap C^\infty(\R\setminus\{0\})$, $\operatorname{supp}a_{k,j}\subset[-2,2]$, $\partial^la_{k,j}(0)=0$ for $l\le j+1$, and there are $C_1=C_1(p,\chi)$, $C=C(p)$ with \[ |\partial^la_{k,j}(\xi)|\le C_1C^k|\xi|^{p+1+j-l},\qquad 0<|\xi|\le2,\ 0\le l\le j+3 . \]
nodes.proof_html:
For $\xi>0$, $\xi^j\Phi_0^k=(p+1)^{-k}\xi^{e}$ with $e=j+(p+1)k$; for $\xi<0$ it is $\pm(p+1)^{-k}|\xi|^e$. Hence for $\xi\ne0$,
  $|\partial^l(\xi^j\Phi_0^k)|\le e^l|\xi|^{e-l}\le(5+2k)^5|\xi|^{p+1+j-l}2^{(p+1)(k-1)}$ using $|\xi|\le2$.
  Leibniz with $\chi$: $|\xi|^{p+1+j-i}\le2^{l-i}|\xi|^{p+1+j-l}$. Absorb $(5+2k)^5 4^k$ into $C^k$.
  Regularity at $0$: by induction on $l\le j+1$ (note $p+1+j-l\ge p>0$), $\partial^{l-1}a_{k,j}(\xi)/\xi\to0$, so $\partial^la_{k,j}(0)$ exists and equals $0$, and $\partial^la_{k,j}(\xi)\to0$ as $\xi\to0$.

nodes.title: Decay of the inverse Fourier transform of a symbol with a power singularity
nodes.statement_html: Let $0<p<1$, $n\ge1$, $M\ge0$. Let $a:\R\to\C$ with $\operatorname{supp}a\subset[-2,2]$, $a\in C^{n-1}(\R)\cap C^{n+1}(\R\setminus\{0\})$, $\partial^la(0)=0$ for $l\le n-1$, and $|\partial^la(\xi)|\le M|\xi|^{n-1+p-l}$ for $0<|\xi|\le2$, $0\le l\le n+1$. Then for $|y|\ge1$, $|\widecheck a(y)|\le C(n,p)M|y|^{-n-p}$, and $|\widecheck a(y)|\le C(n,p)M$ for all $y$.
nodes.proof_html:
The second bound: $|\widecheck a|\le\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-2}^2M|\xi|^{n-1+p}d\xi$.
  Step 1. Integrate by parts $n$ times: $\widecheck a(y)=\frac{1}{2\pi}(-iy)^{-n}\int e^{iy\xi}\partial^na(\xi)d\xi$; the first $n-1$ steps use $a\in C^{n-1}$ and compact support; the $n$-th uses that $\partial^{n-1}a$ is absolutely continuous (it is $C^1$ off $0$, continuous at $0$, and $|\partial^na|\le M|\xi|^{p-1}\in L^1$).
  Step 2. $\bigl|\int_{|\xi|\le|y|^{-1}}e^{iy\xi}\partial^na\bigr|\le\int_{|\xi|\le|y|^{-1}}M|\xi|^{p-1}=\frac{2M}{p}|y|^{-p}$.
  Step 3. On $\{|y|^{-1}\le|\xi|\le2\}$ integrate by parts once more: boundary terms at $\pm|y|^{-1}$ are $\le|y|^{-1}M|y|^{1-p}$ each (those at $\pm2$ vanish), and $|y|^{-1}\int_{|\xi|\ge|y|^{-1}}M|\xi|^{p-2}\le\frac{2M}{1-p}|y|^{-p}$.
  Combine: $|\widecheck a(y)|\le C M|y|^{-n}|y|^{-p}$.

nodes.title: Non-smooth Fourier inverse
nodes.statement_html: Let $0<p<1$, $\chi$ as in lem:c03_nonsmooth_symbol_bounds, $\Phi_0(\xi)=\frac{\xi|\xi|^p}{p+1}$ and $m_k=\chi\Phi_0^k$, $k\ge0$. Then $\widecheck{m_k}\in C^\infty(\R)$ and there are $C_0=C_0(p,\chi)$, $C=C(p)$ such that \[ |\partial^j\widecheck{m_k}(y)|\le C_0C^k\ang y^{-p-2-j},\qquad y\in\R,\ j\in\{0,1,2\},\ k\ge0 . \]
nodes.proof_html: $m_k$ is bounded and compactly supported, so $\widecheck{m_k}$ is smooth and $\partial^j\widecheck{m_k}=\widecheck{a_{k,j}}$ (differentiation under the integral). $k=0$: $m_0=\chi\in C_c^\infty$, so $\widecheck{\chi}\in\mc S$ and the bound holds with a constant depending on $\chi$. $k\ge1$: apply lem:c03_power_singularity_decay to $a=a_{k,j}$ with $n=j+2$, $M=C_1C^k$, using lem:c03_nonsmooth_symbol_bounds; for $|y|\ge1$ use $|y|^{-1}\le\sqrt2\ang y^{-1}$, for $|y|\le1$ the trivial bound.

nodes.title: Weighted tail lemma
nodes.statement_html: Let $0<\gamma'<\gamma$, $\omega:\R\to(0,\infty)$ locally bounded, and $h_k,h\in L^\infty_{\textup{loc}}(\R)$ with $\sup_k\|\ang y^{\gamma}\omega h_k\|_{L^\infty}\le M$ and $h_k\to h$ in $L^\infty(-R,R)$ for every $R$. Then $\|\ang y^\gamma\omega h\|_{L^\infty}\le M$ and $\|\ang y^{\gamma'}\omega(h_k-h)\|_{L^\infty}\to0$.
nodes.proof_html:
The first claim: a.e.\ convergence on each $(-R,R)$. For $R>0$:
  $\|\ang y^{\gamma'}\omega(h_k-h)\|_{L^\infty}\le\ang R^{\gamma'}\sup_{[-R,R]}\omega\,\|h_k-h\|_{L^\infty(-R,R)}+\ang R^{\gamma'-\gamma}2M$.
  Take $\limsup_k$, then $R\to\infty$.

nodes.title: Convergence in $X_{\gamma'}$, $Y_{\gamma'}$
nodes.statement_html: Let $0<\gamma'<\gamma<\infty$. If $(g_k)\subset X_\gamma$ with $\sup_k\|g_k\|_{X_\gamma}<\infty$ and $g_k\to g$ in $W^{2,\infty}_{\textup{loc}}$ (i.e.\ in $W^{2,\infty}(-R,R)$ for every $R$), then $g\in X_\gamma$ and $\|g_k-g\|_{X_{\gamma'}}\to0$. If $(G_k)\subset Y_\gamma$ with $\sup_k\|G_k\|_{Y_\gamma}<\infty$ and $G_k\to G$ in $W^{1,\infty}_{\textup{loc}}$, then $G\in Y_\gamma$ and $\|G_k-G\|_{Y_{\gamma'}}\to0$.
nodes.proof_html: Each of the (at most six) terms of the $X_\gamma$ norm is $\sup_{y\in H}\ang y^\gamma\omega_i(y)|g^{(i)}(y)|$ with $H=[0,\infty)$ or $(-\infty,0]$, $i\in\{0,1,2\}$, $\omega_i=\ang y^{-i/p}$ resp.\ $\ang y^{i}$. Apply lem:c03_weighted_tail to $h_k=\mathbbm 1_Hg_k^{(i)}$. The norm of $X_{\gamma'}$ has the same weights with $\gamma'$ in place of $\gamma$. Same for $Y$.

nodes.title: Van der Corput, first derivative, on an interval
nodes.statement_html: Let $a<b$, $\lambda>0$, $\Phi\in C^2([a,b];\R)$ with $\Phi'$ monotone and $|\Phi'|\ge\lambda$ on $[a,b]$. Then $\bigl|\int_a^be^{i\Phi(\xi)}d\xi\bigr|\le 2\max\{|\Phi'(a)|^{-1},|\Phi'(b)|^{-1}\}\le2\lambda^{-1}$.
nodes.proof_html:
$\Phi'$ is continuous and nonvanishing, so of constant sign, and $1/\Phi'$ is monotone. Write $e^{i\Phi}=\frac{1}{i\Phi'}\frac{d}{d\xi}e^{i\Phi}$ and integrate by parts:
  $\int_a^be^{i\Phi}=\bigl[\frac{e^{i\Phi}}{i\Phi'}\bigr]_a^b-\int_a^be^{i\Phi}\frac{d}{d\xi}\frac1{i\Phi'}$.
  The boundary term is $\le|\Phi'(a)|^{-1}+|\Phi'(b)|^{-1}$; the integral is $\le\int_a^b|(1/\Phi')'|=|1/\Phi'(b)-1/\Phi'(a)|$ by monotonicity. With $x=|1/\Phi'(a)|$, $y=|1/\Phi'(b)|$ (same sign): $x+y+|x-y|=2\max(x,y)$.

nodes.title: Van der Corput, second derivative, on an interval
nodes.statement_html: Let $a<b$, $\lambda>0$, $\Phi\in C^2([a,b];\R)$ with $|\Phi''|\ge\lambda$ on $[a,b]$. Then $\bigl|\int_a^be^{i\Phi}\bigr|\le 6\lambda^{-1/2}$.
nodes.proof_html: Replacing $\Phi$ by $-\Phi$ (complex conjugation) we may assume $\Phi''\ge\lambda$, so $\Phi'$ is strictly increasing. Let $\delta=\lambda^{1/2}$ and $J=\{\xi\in[a,b]:|\Phi'(\xi)|<\delta\}$, an interval of length $\le2\delta/\lambda$ (mean value theorem). $[a,b]\setminus J$ consists of at most two intervals on which $\Phi'$ is monotone and $|\Phi'|\ge\delta$; by lem:c03_vdc_first each contributes $\le2/\delta$. Total $\le4/\delta+2\delta/\lambda=6\lambda^{-1/2}$. (If an endpoint of $J$ is open, apply lem:c03_vdc_first on closed subintervals and pass to the limit.)

nodes.title: Van der Corput with amplitude on an interval (sharp cutoff form)
nodes.statement_html: Let $a<b$, $\lambda>0$, $\Phi\in C^2([a,b];\R)$, $\psi\in C^1([a,b];\C)$. Set $c_1=2$, $c_2=6$. If either ($k=1$) $\Phi'$ is monotone and $|\Phi'|\ge\lambda$ on $[a,b]$, or ($k=2$) $|\Phi''|\ge\lambda$ on $[a,b]$, then \[ \Bigl|\int_a^b\psi(\xi)e^{i\Phi(\xi)}d\xi\Bigr|\le c_k\lambda^{-1/k}\Bigl(|\psi(b)|+\int_a^b|\psi'(\xi)|d\xi\Bigr). \] The same holds with $|\psi(b)|$ replaced by $|\psi(a)|$, and in particular with $\|\psi\|_{L^\infty(a,b)}$.
nodes.proof_html: Let $F(x)=\int_a^xe^{i\Phi}$. The hypotheses hold on every $[a,x]$, so $|F(x)|\le c_k\lambda^{-1/k}$. Integrate by parts: $\int_a^b\psi e^{i\Phi}=\psi(b)F(b)-\int_a^bF\psi'$. For the variant with $\psi(a)$ use $\sq F(x)=-\int_x^be^{i\Phi}$.

nodes.title: Van der Corput on a half-line
nodes.statement_html: Let $a\in\R$, $\lambda>0$, $\Phi\in C^2([a,\infty);\R)$ with $\Phi'$ monotone, $|\Phi'|\ge\lambda$ on $[a,\infty)$, and $|\Phi'(\xi)|\to\infty$ as $\xi\to\infty$. Then $\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_a^Re^{i\Phi}$ exists and $\bigl|\int_a^\infty e^{i\Phi}\bigr|\le2|\Phi'(a)|^{-1}\le 2\lambda^{-1}$.
nodes.proof_html: $|1/\Phi'|$ is nonincreasing (it is monotone and tends to $0$). By lem:c03_vdc_first, $|\int_R^{R'}e^{i\Phi}|\le2|\Phi'(R)|^{-1}\to0$ (Cauchy criterion), and $|\int_a^R e^{i\Phi}|\le2|\Phi'(a)|^{-1}$ for all $R$.

nodes.title: Van der Corput, paper form
nodes.statement_html:
Let $I\subset\R$ be a compact interval, $\lambda>0$, $\Phi\in C^2(I;\R)$, $\chi\in C^1(\R;\C)$ with $\operatorname{supp}\chi\subset I$.
  • If $\Phi'$ is monotone and $|\Phi'|\ge\lambda$ on $I$, then $\bigl|\int\chi e^{i\Phi}\bigr|\le2\lambda^{-1}(\|\chi\|_{L^\infty}+\|\chi'\|_{L^1})$.
  • If $|\Phi''|\ge\lambda$ on $I$, then $\bigl|\int\chi e^{i\Phi}\bigr|\le6\lambda^{-1/2}(\|\chi\|_{L^\infty}+\|\chi'\|_{L^1})$.
The sharp-cutoff (interval) form, with $|\psi(b)|+\int_a^b|\psi'|$, is lem:c03_vdc_interval_amplitude; the half-line form is lem:c03_vdc_halfline.
nodes.proof_html: Apply lem:c03_vdc_interval_amplitude on $I=[a,b]$ with $\psi=\chi|_I$, and $|\chi(b)|\le\|\chi\|_\infty$. Reference: \cite[Ch. VIII, Prop. 2 and Cor.]{Stein:harmonic-analysis}.

nodes.title: Existence of the tail integrals
nodes.statement_html: Let $0<p<1$, $\Phi_0(\xi)=\xi|\xi|^p/(p+1)$. For all $y\in\R$, $\eta>0$, the improper integral $E_y(\eta):=\int_\eta^\infty e^{i(\Phi_0(\xi)-y\xi)}d\xi$ exists, and $\eta\mapsto E_y(\eta)$ is $C^1$ on $(0,\infty)$ with $\partial_\eta E_y(\eta)=-e^{i(\Phi_0(\eta)-y\eta)}$.
nodes.proof_html: On $\xi>0$ the phase $\phi_y(\xi)=\Phi_0(\xi)-y\xi$ has $\phi_y'=\xi^p-y$ (increasing, $\to\infty$) and $\phi_y''=p\xi^{p-1}>0$. For $\xi_1=\max(\eta,(|y|+1)^{1/p})$, $\phi'_y\ge1$ on $[\xi_1,\infty)$; apply lem:c03_vdc_halfline there and add the proper integral over $[\eta,\xi_1]$.

nodes.title: Tail integral, $y\le-1$
nodes.statement_html: For $y\le-1$ and $\eta>0$: $|E_y(\eta)|\le2|y|^{-1}$.
nodes.proof_html: $\phi_y'=\xi^p+|y|\ge|y|$, increasing, $\to\infty$. Apply lem:c03_vdc_halfline on $[\eta,\infty)$.

nodes.title: Tail integral, $y\ge1$
nodes.statement_html: There is $C=C(p)$ such that for $y\ge1$, $\eta>0$: $|E_y(\eta)|\le Cy^{\frac{1-p}{2p}}$.
nodes.proof_html: Let $\xi_0=y^{1/p}$ (the stationary point) and split $[\eta,\infty)$ into its intersections with $I_1=(0,\frac12\xi_0]$, $I_2=[\frac12\xi_0,\frac32\xi_0]$, $I_3=[\frac32\xi_0,\infty)$ (each intersection is an interval, possibly empty). On $I_1$: $\phi_y'=\xi^p-y\le-(1-2^{-p})y$, monotone; lem:c03_vdc_first gives $\le\frac{2}{(1-2^{-p})y}$. On $I_2$: $\phi_y''=p\xi^{p-1}\ge p(3/2)^{p-1}y^{(p-1)/p}$; lem:c03_vdc_second gives $\le6p^{-1/2}(3/2)^{(1-p)/2}y^{\frac{1-p}{2p}}$. On $I_3$: $\phi'_y\ge((3/2)^p-1)y$, increasing to $\infty$; lem:c03_vdc_halfline gives $\le\frac2{((3/2)^p-1)y}$. Sum, using $y^{-1}\le1\le y^{\frac{1-p}{2p}}$.

nodes.title: Tail integral, $|y|\le1$
nodes.statement_html: For $|y|\le1$, $\eta>0$: $|E_y(\eta)|\le2+\frac{2}{2^p-1}$.
nodes.proof_html: If $\eta\ge2$: $\phi'_y\ge2^p-1>0$ on $[\eta,\infty)$, increasing to $\infty$; use lem:c03_vdc_halfline. If $\eta<2$: $E_y(\eta)=\int_\eta^2e^{i\phi_y}+E_y(2)$ and $|\int_\eta^2|\le2$.

nodes.title: Uniform bound for the tail integrals
nodes.statement_html: Let $0<p<1$, $\Phi_0(\xi)=\frac{\xi|\xi|^p}{p+1}$. There is $C=C(p)$ such that for all $y\in\R$ the improper integrals $\int_\eta^\infty e^{i(\Phi_0(\xi)-y\xi)}d\xi$ exist for all $\eta>0$ and \[ \sup_{\eta>0}\Bigl|\int_\eta^\infty e^{i(\Phi_0(\xi)-y\xi)}d\xi\Bigr|\le \begin{cases}C\ang y^{-1},&y\le0,\\ C\ang y^{\frac{1-p}{2p}},&y\ge0.\end{cases} \]
nodes.proof_html: Combine the three regimes, using $|y|^{-1}\le\sqrt2\ang y^{-1}$ for $|y|\ge1$ and $\ang y\le\sqrt2$ for $|y|\le1$.

nodes.title: Reciprocal derivative bounds by a finite recurrence
nodes.statement_html: Fix $n\in\N$ and nonnegative constants $A_1,\ldots,A_n$. There are constants $D_j=D_j(A_1,\ldots,A_j)>0$, $0\le j\le n$, such that the following holds. Let $U\subset\R$ be open, $v\in C^n(U;\C)$, $\lambda>0$, and $w:U\to(0,\infty)$. If $|v(x)|\ge\lambda$ and $|v^{(j)}(x)|\le A_j\lambda w(x)^{-j}$ for $x\in U$, $1\le j\le n$, then $v^{-1}\in C^n(U)$ and $|(v^{-1})^{(j)}(x)|\le D_j\lambda^{-1}w(x)^{-j}$ for $0\le j\le n$. No regularity of the comparison weight $w$ is required.
nodes.proof_html:
The nonvanishing of $v$ gives regularity. Differentiate $v v^{-1}=1$:
  $(v^{-1})^{(j)}=-v^{-1}\sum_{\ell=1}^j\binom j\ell v^{(\ell)}(v^{-1})^{(j-\ell)}$.
  Starting with $D_0=1$, take $D_j=1+\sum_{\ell=1}^j\binom j\ell A_\ell D_{j-\ell}$.
  The powers of $\lambda$ and $w(x)$ cancel pointwise. This recurrence is the implementation,
  not a citation of a general high-order chain rule.

nodes.title: A finite sequence of integrations by parts
nodes.statement_html: Let $U\subset\R$ be open, $n\in\N$, $\phi\in C^{n+1}(U;\R)$ with $\phi'\ne0$ on $U$, and $a\in C_c^n(U;\C)$, extended by zero to $\R$. Set $L_\phi a=(a/(i\phi'))'$ on $U$ and zero outside $U$, and iterate this definition. For $0\le j\le n$, $L_\phi^j a$ is continuous, compactly supported in $\operatorname{supp}a$, and belongs to $C^{n-j}(\R)$. All the following integrals converge absolutely: \[ \int_\R a(x)e^{i\phi(x)}\,dx=(-1)^n\int_\R L_\phi^n a(x)e^{i\phi(x)}\,dx. \] The values chosen for $\phi$ outside $U$ do not affect either side.
nodes.proof_html:
Work on a finite union of bounded intervals compactly contained in $U$ and containing
  the compact support of $a$. On each interval the quotient is $C^{n}$ and vanishes near
  both endpoints. The ordinary interval integration-by-parts formula gives the case $n=1$.
  Differentiation does not enlarge support, so zero extension is regular and induction gives the result.
  To obtain the finite union, cover the compact support by finitely many intervals whose closures lie
  in $U$, then merge overlapping intervals. Each endpoint lies outside the support after a small enlargement.
  Sum the interval identities; no partition of unity is needed.

nodes.title: Symbol bounds after iterated integration by parts
nodes.statement_html: Fix integers $n,j\ge0$, $\sigma\in\R$, and nonnegative finite lists $(A_\ell)$ and $(Q_\ell)$ for $0\le\ell\le n+j+1$. There is $C>0$ depending only on these data such that: if $U\subset\R\setminus\{0\}$ is open, $a\in C_c^\infty(U;\C)$, $\phi\in C^\infty(U;\R)$, $B\ge0$, $\Lambda>0$, $\phi'\ne0$ on $U$, and \[ |a^{(\ell)}(z)|\le A_\ell B|z|^{\sigma-\ell},\qquad |(1/\phi')^{(\ell)}(z)|\le Q_\ell\Lambda^{-1}|z|^{-\ell} \quad(z\in U,\ 0\le\ell\le n+j+1), \] then $|(L_\phi^n a)^{(j)}(z)|\le C B\Lambda^{-n}|z|^{\sigma-n-j}$ on $U$.
nodes.proof_html: Use $(L_\phi a)^{(j)}=\sum_{\ell=0}^{j+1}\binom{j+1}{\ell} a^{(\ell)}(1/(i\phi'))^{(j+1-\ell)}$. Each summand has the same power $|z|^{\sigma-j-1}$ and one factor $\Lambda^{-1}$. Induct on $n$, carrying the finite list of constants for the derivative orders still required. No infinite-order estimate is needed.

nodes.title: Zero extension of a supported oscillatory amplitude
nodes.statement_html: Let $U\subset\R$ be open, $a\in C_c^\infty(U;\C)$ extended by zero, and $\phi\in C^\infty(U;\R)$ with arbitrary values outside $U$. Then $a e^{i\phi}\in C_c^\infty(\R)$ and its support is contained in $\operatorname{supp}a$. Every derivative equals its ordinary product/chain-rule expression on $U$ and is zero in a neighbourhood of each point outside $\operatorname{supp}a$.
nodes.proof_html:
Regularity is local: on $U$ use the product and chain rules; outside the closed support of $a$
  the product is identically zero on a neighbourhood. These two open sets cover $\R$ because
  $\operatorname{supp}a\subset U$. Compact support also proves integrability of every derivative.

nodes.title: Stationary-phase functions, amplitude class and Euler operator
nodes.statement_html: For $0<p<1$, the functions $h,\lambda_0,\Psi_0,\phi_y,\mu$ and the normalized remainder $\rho(\mu;c)$ have the formulas displayed at the start of this subsection. Put \[ P(y)=e^{i(\Psi_0(y)-\pi/4)}\sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{p\lambda_0(y)^{p-1}}},\qquad b_y(s)=\lambda_0(y)^{-m}a(\lambda_0(y)s), \] \[ q(s)=\begin{cases}(h(s)-h(1))/(1-s^p),&s\ne1,\\0,&s=1,\end{cases} \qquad Tc(s)=c(s)/2-\partial_s(c(s)q(s)). \] The symbol class $\mathcal S^m_+$ here consists of $a:(0,\infty)\to\C$ smooth, zero on $(0,1]$, such that for every $k\in\N$ there is $C_k\ge0$ with $|a^{(k)}(\xi)|\le C_k\xi^{m-k}$ for $\xi\ge1$. These are data definitions only. Smoothness of the quotient at $1$, the operator bounds, and the stationary-phase estimates are separate lemmas below.

nodes.title: Near, far and full stationary integrals
nodes.statement_html: With the fixed cutoff $\chi_{\rm sp}$, set \[ I_{\rm near}(y)=\int_0^\infty a(\xi)\chi_{\rm sp}(\xi/\lambda_0(y))e^{i\phi_y(\xi)}d\xi, \] \[ I_{\rm far}(y)=\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_0^R a(\xi)(1-\chi_{\rm sp}(\xi/\lambda_0(y)))e^{i\phi_y(\xi)}d\xi, \quad I(y)=\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_0^R a(\xi)e^{i\phi_y(\xi)}d\xi, \quad r(y)=I(y)/P(y)-a(\lambda_0(y)). \] The first formula is a total Bochner integral. The limits denote Lean's total limit operator; their existence is a separate assertion, not part of this definition.

nodes.title: Complex Gaussian integral
nodes.statement_html: For $b\in\C$ with $\operatorname{Re}b>0$: $\int_\R e^{-bx^2}dx=(\pi/b)^{1/2}$ (principal branch).

nodes.title: Fresnel expansion with remainder
nodes.statement_html: There is an absolute constant $C$ such that for all $ u>0$, $L\ge1$ and $e\in C^3(\R;\C)$ with $\operatorname{supp}e\subset[-L,L]$, \[ \Bigl|\int_\R e(w)e^{-i u w^2/2}dw-\Bigl( rac{2\pi}{ u}\Bigr)^{1/2}e^{-i\pi/4}e(0)\Bigr|\le CL u^{-3/2}\|e\|_{C^3(\R)}. \]
nodes.proof_html: Let $g(w)=e^{-w^2/2}$ and $d(w)=(e(w)-e(0)g(w))/w=\int_0^1(e'-e(0)g')(tw)dt$ (smooth extension at $0$). Step 1. By lem:c03_gaussian_complex with $b=(1+i u)/2$: $\int ge^{-i u w^2/2}=(2\pi/(1+i u))^{1/2}=(2\pi/ u)^{1/2}e^{-i\pi/4}(1-i/ u)^{-1/2}$, and $|(1-i/ u)^{-1/2}-1|\le2/ u$ (for $ u\le1$ since $|1-i/ u|\ge1$; for $ u\ge1$ by the mean value theorem). Step 2. $we^{-i u w^2/2}= rac i u\partial_we^{-i u w^2/2}$; integrating by parts on $[-R,R]$ and letting $R o\infty$ ($d(w)=O(|w|^{-1})$, $d'\in L^1$): $\int wd(w)e^{-i u w^2/2}dw=- rac i u\int d'(w)e^{-i u w^2/2}dw$. Step 3. By lem:c03_vdc_interval_amplitude ($k=2$, $\Phi''=- u$) on $[-R,R]$ and $R o\infty$: $|\int d'e^{-i u w^2/2}|\le6 u^{-1/2}(\|d'\|_\infty+\|d''\|_{L^1})$. Step 4. $\|d'\|_\infty+\|d''\|_{L^\infty}\le C\|e\|_{C^3}$ from the integral formula; for $|w|\ge1$, $|d''(w)|\le C(|e''|+|e'|+|e|)\mathbbm 1_{[-L,L]}+C|e(0)|(1+|w|)^{-3}$, so $\|d''\|_{L^1}\le CL\|e\|_{C^2}$. Combine: $e=e(0)g+wd$.

nodes.title: Morse coordinate for $h$ near $s=1$
nodes.statement_html: Define on $(0,\infty)$ $w(s):=(s-1)\Bigl(\frac2p\int_0^1(1-t)\,p\,(1+t(s-1))^{p-1}dt\Bigr)^{1/2}$. Then $w\in C^\infty((0,\infty))$, $h(s)-h(1)=-\frac p2w(s)^2$, $w(1)=0$, $w'(1)=1$, and $w'>0$ on $(0,\infty)$. Hence $w$ is a $C^\infty$ diffeomorphism of $[\frac12,2]$ onto $[w(\frac12),w(2)]$; its inverse $s(w)$ has $C^k$ norms bounded by constants depending only on $p,k$.
nodes.proof_html: Taylor: $h(s)-h(1)=(s-1)^2\int_0^1(1-t)h''(1+t(s-1))dt$ with $-h''(\sigma)=p\sigma^{p-1}>0$; the radicand is positive and smooth, so $w$ is smooth and $w^2=\frac2p(h(1)-h(s))$. $w'(1)=(\frac2p\cdot\frac p2)^{1/2}=1$. For $s\ne1$: $2ww'=-\frac2ph'(s)$ and $h'(s)=1-s^p$ has the sign of $1-s$ while $w$ has the sign of $s-1$, so $w'>0$. Inverse function theorem on the compact interval.

nodes.title: Transport of a compact amplitude through the Morse coordinate
nodes.statement_html: Fix $0<p<1$ and let $w$ be the coordinate of lem:c03_morse_h. Write $J=(w(1/2),w(2))$ and let $s:J\to(1/2,2)$ be its inverse. There are $L=L(p)\ge1$ and $C=C(p)>0$ such that for every $c\in C^3(\R;\C)$ with compact support in $(1/2,2)$, the function $e(v)=c(s(v))s'(v)$ on $J$, extended by zero, lies in $C_c^3(\R)$, has support in $[-L,L]$, satisfies $e(0)=c(1)$, and $\|e\|_{C^3(\R)}\le C\|c\|_{C^3(\R)}$.
nodes.proof_html: The inverse coordinate has bounded derivatives through order four on the closed image of $[1/2,2]$. Expand the first three derivatives of $c(s(v))s'(v)$ by product and chain rules. The extension is smooth at the endpoints because $c$ vanishes in neighbourhoods of $1/2$ and $2$; the bound uses only inverse-coordinate derivative bounds, not the size of those neighbourhoods.

nodes.title: Morse change of variables in the stationary integral
nodes.statement_html: With $0<p<1$, $c$ and $e$ as in lem:c03_sp_morse_amplitude, for every $\mu>0$, \[ \int_0^\infty c(s)e^{i\mu h(s)}\,ds =e^{i\mu h(1)}\int_\R e(v)e^{-ip\mu v^2/2}\,dv. \] Both integrands are absolutely integrable.
nodes.proof_html: Restrict to $(1/2,2)$, apply the one-dimensional change-of-variables theorem for the increasing $C^1$ diffeomorphism $w$, and use $h(s)-h(1)=-p w(s)^2/2$. Extend the transformed integrand by zero and use compact support for absolute convergence.

nodes.title: Stationary phase for compactly supported amplitudes
nodes.statement_html: There is $C=C(p)$ such that for all $\mu>0$ and $c\in C^3(\R)$ with $\operatorname{supp}c\subset(\frac12,2)$: $|\rho(\mu;c)|\le C\mu^{-1}\|c\|_{C^3}$.
nodes.proof_html: Change variables $s=s(w)$ (lem:c03_morse_h): $\int c(s)e^{i\mu h(s)}ds=e^{i\mu h(1)}\int e(w)e^{-ip\mu w^2/2}dw$ with $e(w)=c(s(w))s'(w)$ extended by $0$, $e\in C^3$, $\operatorname{supp}e\subset[-L,L]$ with $L=L(p)$, $\|e\|_{C^3}\le C(p)\|c\|_{C^3}$, $e(0)=c(1)$. Apply lem:c03_fresnel_expansion with $\nu=p\mu$; the main term times $e^{i\pi/4}(p\mu/2\pi)^{1/2}e^{-i\mu h(1)}$ equals $c(1)$.

nodes.title: Removal of the apparent singularity in the Euler quotient
nodes.statement_html: For $0<p<1$, define $N(s)=\int_0^1h'(1+t(s-1))dt$ and $D(s)=\int_0^1h''(1+t(s-1))dt$ for $s>0$. Both are smooth, $D(s)<0$, and $q=N/D$ agrees with $(h(s)-h(1))/h'(s)$ for $s\ne1$. Moreover $q(1)=0$, $q'(1)=1/2$, and every derivative of $q$ is bounded on $[1/2,2]$ by a constant depending only on $p$ and its order.
nodes.proof_html:
Differentiate the parameter integrals on compact subintervals of $(0,\infty)$;
  their integrands and all derivatives have uniform integrable bounds on $t\in[0,1]$.
  The fundamental theorem of calculus gives the quotient identities. At $s=1$,
  $N=0$, $N'=h''(1)/2$, and $D=h''(1)=-p$. Compactness gives the derivative bounds.

nodes.title: Support, cancellation and norm bound for the Euler amplitude operator
nodes.statement_html: For $0<p<1$ set $Tc=c/2-(cq)'$, with $q$ of lem:c03_sp_q_extension. If $c\in C_c^\infty((1/2,2);\C)$, extended by zero, then $Tc\in C_c^\infty((1/2,2))$ and $Tc(1)=0$. For every integer $k\ge0$ there is $C_k=C_k(p)>0$, independent of $c$, with $\|Tc\|_{C^k(\R)}\le C_k\|c\|_{C^{k+1}(\R)}$.
nodes.proof_html: On the support interval use Leibniz and the bounds for $q^{(j)}$, $j\le k+1$. Outside the support the expression is locally zero. The identity at $1$ follows from $q(1)=0$ and $q'(1)=1/2$.

nodes.title: Differentiation of the compact stationary integral
nodes.statement_html: Fix $0<p<1$ and $c\in C_c^\infty((1/2,2);\C)$. Then $J(\mu;c)=\int_0^\infty c(s)e^{i\mu h(s)}ds$ is smooth for $\mu\in\R$ and \[ \partial_\mu^jJ(\mu;c)=\int_0^\infty (ih(s))^j c(s)e^{i\mu h(s)}ds \quad(j\in\N). \] More generally, let $V\subset\R$ be open and $c:V\times\R\to\C$ smooth, with a common compact support in $(1/2,2)$ for $y$ in each compact subinterval of $V$. Then mixed derivatives in $y\in V$ and $\mu\in\R$ pass under the integral. The same assertions hold for the normalized remainder $\rho$ when $\mu>0$.
nodes.proof_html:
On the fixed support, each differentiated integrand is continuous and bounded uniformly
  for parameters in a compact set. Dominate by a constant times its indicator and iterate
  differentiation under the integral. The normalizing factor of $\rho$ is smooth on $(0,\infty)$.

nodes.title: Integration-by-parts identity for the normalized stationary remainder
nodes.statement_html: For $0<p<1$, $c\in C_c^\infty((1/2,2);\C)$, and $\mu>0$, $\mu\partial_\mu\rho(\mu;c)=\rho(\mu;Tc)$.
nodes.proof_html: Differentiate the normalization of $J$. Its derivative contributes $J/2-i\mu h(1)J$, while $\mu J'$ contributes $i\mu\int h c e^{i\mu h}$. Use $q h'=h-h(1)$ and integrate the latter difference by parts in $s$; the boundary term vanishes because $cq$ is compactly supported. The result is the normalized integral with amplitude $Tc$, with no extra value term since $Tc(1)=0$.

nodes.title: Euler identity for $\rho$
nodes.statement_html: Let $q(s):=\frac{h(s)-h(1)}{h'(s)}$ for $s\in(0,\infty)\setminus\{1\}$, $q(1):=0$. Then $q\in C^\infty((0,\infty))$, $q'(1)=\frac12$. For $c\in C^\infty$ with $\operatorname{supp}c\subset(\frac12,2)$ set $Tc:=\frac12c-(cq)'$. Then $\operatorname{supp}Tc\subset(\frac12,2)$, $Tc(1)=0$, $\|Tc\|_{C^k}\le C_k(p)\|c\|_{C^{k+1}}$, $\mu\mapsto\rho(\mu;c)$ is $C^\infty$ on $(0,\infty)$, and $\mu\partial_\mu\rho(\mu;c)=\rho(\mu;Tc)$.
nodes.proof_html: $q=N/D$ with $N(s)=\int_0^1h'(1+t(s-1))dt=\frac{h(s)-h(1)}{s-1}$ and $D(s)=\int_0^1h''(1+t(s-1))dt=\frac{h'(s)}{s-1}$, both smooth, $D<0$ on $(0,\infty)$ (as $h''<0$). $N(1)=0$, $N'(1)=h''(1)/2$, $D(1)=h''(1)$, so $q'(1)=\frac12$, and $Tc(1)=\frac12c(1)-c(1)q'(1)-c'(1)q(1)=0$. Differentiating under the (compactly supported) integral, with $J(\mu;c)=\int ce^{i\mu h}$: $\mu\partial_\mu J(\mu;c)=i\mu h(1)J(\mu;c)+\int c\,i\mu(h-h(1))e^{i\mu h}$, and $i\mu(h-h(1))e^{i\mu h}=q\,\partial_se^{i\mu h}$, so the last integral is $-J(\mu;(cq)')$ (no boundary terms). Hence $\mu\partial_\mu[(p\mu/2\pi)^{1/2}e^{-i\mu h(1)}J(\mu;c)]=(p\mu/2\pi)^{1/2}e^{-i\mu h(1)}J(\mu;\frac12c-(cq)')$; multiply by $e^{i\pi/4}$ and use $Tc(1)=0$.

nodes.title: Symbol bounds and Euler differentiation after rescaling
nodes.statement_html: Fix $0<p<1$, $m\in\R$, and $a\in C^\infty((0,\infty);\C)$ with $a=0$ on $(0,1]$ and $|a^{(k)}(\xi)|\le C_k\xi^{m-k}$ for $\xi\ge1$, where $C_k\ge0$. For $y,s>0$ put $b_y(s)=\lambda_0(y)^{-m}a(\lambda_0(y)s)$ and $\mathfrak E=p^{-1}(-m+s\partial_s)$. The map $(y,s)\mapsto b_y(s)$ is smooth and \[ \partial_s^k b_y(s)=\lambda_0(y)^{k-m}a^{(k)}(\lambda_0(y)s),\quad |\partial_s^kb_y(s)|\le C_ks^{m-k},\quad y\partial_yb_y=\mathfrak E b_y. \] For each $j,k\in\N$ there is $D=D(p,m,j,k,C_0,\ldots,C_{j+k})$, independent of $y$, with $\sup_{s\in[1/2,2]}|\partial_s^k\mathfrak E^j b_y(s)|\le D$.
nodes.proof_html:
The first formula follows by repeated differentiation of a linear rescaling.
  When $\lambda_0s\le1$, every derivative of $a$ vanishes (including at $1$ by smoothness).
  Otherwise apply the given symbol bound. The Euler identity is the chain rule and
  $y\lambda_0'=\lambda_0/p$. Expand the finite-order differential operator
  $\partial_s^k\mathfrak E^j$ inductively; it is a finite sum of bounded powers of $s$
  times derivatives of order at most $j+k$ on $[1/2,2]$.

nodes.title: Exact scaling of the near stationary contribution
nodes.statement_html: Under the hypotheses of lem:c03_sp_scaled_symbol, fix the cutoff $\chi_{\rm sp}$ of this subsection. For every $y>0$, $c_y=\chi_{\rm sp}b_y$ is smooth and compactly supported in $(1/2,2)$, the integral defining $I_{\rm near}(y)$ converges absolutely, $P(y)\ne0$, and \[ I_{\rm near}(y)/P(y)-a(\lambda_0(y)) =\lambda_0(y)^m\rho(\mu(y);c_y). \] Both sides are smooth functions of $y>0$.
nodes.proof_html: Substitute $\xi=\lambda_0s$ in the compact integral. Use $\phi_y(\lambda_0s)=\mu h(s)$, $\mu=\lambda_0^{p+1}$ and $c_y(1)=\lambda_0^{-m}a(\lambda_0)$. Match the positive square-root factors in $P$ and $\rho$. The family $c_y$ has its support in the fixed support of $\chi_{\rm sp}$, so parameter differentiation proves smoothness without differentiating an improper integral.

nodes.title: Euler recurrence for the parameter-dependent stationary remainder
nodes.statement_html: With the same data, let $F(y)=\rho(\mu(y);\chi_{\rm sp}b_y)$ and $E=y\partial_y$. For every $l\in\N$ and $y>0$, \[ E^lF(y)=\sum_{i=0}^l\binom li(1+1/p)^i \rho\bigl(\mu(y);T^i(\chi_{\rm sp}\mathfrak E^{l-i}b_y)\bigr). \] For each $l$ there is $C_l=C_l(p,m,\chi_{\rm sp},C_0,\ldots,C_{l+4})>0$ such that $|E^lF(y)|\le C_l\mu(y)^{-1}$ for all $y>0$.
nodes.proof_html: Differentiate both the parameter $\mu$ and the amplitude; $E\mu=(1+1/p)\mu$. The $s$-operator $T$ commutes with $y$ differentiation, while $E(\chi_{\rm sp}b_y)=\chi_{\rm sp}\mathfrak E b_y$. Induction and Pascal's identity give the displayed sum. Apply the compact stationary remainder bound, the $T$ norm bound, and the rescaled-symbol estimate to each of its finitely many amplitudes.

nodes.title: Conversion of Euler bounds to ordinary derivatives
nodes.statement_html: Let $F\in C^\infty((0,\infty);\C)$ and $E=y\partial_y$. For $j\in\N$ define real coefficients $a_{j,l}$ by $\prod_{r=0}^{j-1}(X-r)=\sum_{l=0}^j a_{j,l}X^l$. Then $y^j F^{(j)}(y)=\sum_{l=0}^j a_{j,l}E^lF(y)$ for $y>0$. Consequently, if $|E^lF(y)|\le B_l y^\sigma$ for $y\ge1$, $0\le l\le j$, $B_l\ge0$, then $|F^{(j)}(y)|\le(\sum_{l=0}^j|a_{j,l}|B_l)y^{\sigma-j}$ for $y\ge1$.
nodes.proof_html:
Induct on $j$ using $E(y^jF^{(j)})=j y^jF^{(j)}+y^{j+1}F^{(j+1)}$.
  This is precisely multiplication of the coefficient polynomial by $X-j$.
  The estimate follows from the finite sum and division by the positive number $y^j$.

nodes.title: Rescaling and the near part
nodes.statement_html:
Let $m\in\R$ and $a\in C^\infty((0,\infty))$ with $a=0$ on $(0,1]$ and $|a^{(k)}(\xi)|\le C_k\xi^{m-k}$ for $\xi\ge1$ (hence for all $\xi>0$). For $y>0$ let $b_y(s)=\lambda_0^{-m}a(\lambda_0s)$, $c_y=\chi_{\textup{sp}}b_y$, and $I_{\textup{near}}(y)=\int_0^\infty a(\xi)\chi_{\textup{sp}}(\xi/\lambda_0)e^{i\phi_y(\xi)}d\xi$, $P(y)=e^{i(\Psi_0(y)-\pi/4)}\bigl(\frac{2\pi}{p\lambda_0^{p-1}}\bigr)^{1/2}$. Then
  • $|\partial_s^kb_y(s)|\le C_ks^{m-k}$ for $s>0$, and $y\partial_yb_y=\mathfrak Eb_y$ with $\mathfrak Eb:=\frac1p(-mb+sb')$;
  • $I_{\textup{near}}(y)/P(y)-a(\lambda_0(y))=\lambda_0^m\rho(\mu(y);c_y)$, and $y\mapsto\lambda_0^m\rho(\mu(y);c_y)$ is $C^\infty$ on $(0,\infty)$;
  • for each $j\ge0$ there is $C$ (depending on $p,m,j$ and $C_0,\dots,C_{j+4}$) with $|\partial_y^j[\lambda_0^m\rho(\mu;c_y)]|\le C\lambda_0^{m-p-1}y^{-j}$ for $y\ge1$.
nodes.proof_html: (1) Chain rule; $y\partial_y\lambda_0=\lambda_0/p$. (2) Substitute $\xi=\lambda_0s$: $I_{\textup{near}}=\lambda_0^{1+m}\int c_y(s)e^{i\mu h(s)}ds$; and $\lambda_0^{1+m}(p\lambda_0^{p-1}/2\pi)^{1/2}=\lambda_0^m(p\mu/2\pi)^{1/2}$, $\Psi_0=\mu h(1)$, $c_y(1)=\lambda_0^{-m}a(\lambda_0)$. (3) Let $F(y)=\rho(\mu(y);c_y)$. Since $y\partial_y\mu=(1+\frac1p)\mu$, $\rho$ is linear in $c$, and $y\partial_yc_y=\chi_{\textup{sp}}\mathfrak Eb_y$, lem:c03_sp_euler gives by induction $(y\partial_y)^lF=\sum_{i=0}^l\binom li(1+\frac1p)^i\rho(\mu;T^i(\chi_{\textup{sp}}\mathfrak E^{l-i}b_y))$. On $[\frac12,2]$, $\mathfrak E^{l-i}b_y$ has $C^{3+i}$ norm bounded uniformly in $y>0$ by (1); hence $\|T^i(\dots)\|_{C^3}\le C$ and by lem:c03_sp_compact $|(y\partial_y)^lF|\le C\mu^{-1}$. Next $(y\partial_y)^l(\lambda_0^mF)=\lambda_0^m(\frac mp+y\partial_y)^lF$, so $|(y\partial_y)^l(\lambda_0^mF)|\le C\lambda_0^m\mu^{-1}=C\lambda_0^{m-p-1}$. Finally $y^j\partial_y^j=\prod_{i=0}^{j-1}(y\partial_y-i)$.

nodes.title: Nonstationarity and reciprocal phase bounds away from the critical point
nodes.statement_html: For $0<p<1$ there is $c=c(p)>0$ such that, for $y,\xi>0$ with $\xi\le3\lambda_0(y)/4$ or $\xi\ge3\lambda_0(y)/2$, $|y-\xi^p|\ge c(y+\xi^p)$. For every $k,j\in\N$ there is $C_{k,j}=C_{k,j}(p)>0$ with \[ \left|\partial_y^j\partial_\xi^k\frac1{y-\xi^p}\right| \le C_{k,j}\xi^{-k}(y+\xi^p)^{-1-j} \] on the same set. These bounds also hold with enlarged constants on the wider open set $\xi<7\lambda_0(y)/8$ or $\xi>5\lambda_0(y)/4$.
nodes.proof_html: Divide by $y$ and put $r=\xi/\lambda_0$ to obtain a positive lower bound on $|1-r^p|/(1+r^p)$ in each stated region. Differentiating in $y$ gives a factorial times $(y-\xi^p)^{-1-j}$; apply the reciprocal recurrence in $\xi$, using $|\partial_\xi^k\xi^p|\le C(p,k)\xi^{p-k}$ and $\xi^p\le y+\xi^p$.

nodes.title: Symbols produced by the far-region integration-by-parts operator
nodes.statement_html: Let $0<p<1$, $m\in\R$, and $a$ satisfy the symbol hypotheses of lem:c03_sp_scaled_symbol. Set $g_y(\xi)=a(\xi)(1-\chi_{\rm sp}(\xi/\lambda_0(y)))$, $a_0=g_y$, and $a_{n+1}=\partial_\xi(a_n/(i(y-\xi^p)))$, with value zero near $\xi=\lambda_0(y)$. The functions $a_n(y,\xi)$ are smooth for $y,\xi>0$, vanish for $\xi\le1$ and for $3\lambda_0(y)/4\le\xi\le3\lambda_0(y)/2$. For all $n,k,j\in\N$ there is $D=D(p,m,n,k,j,\chi_{\rm sp},C_0,\ldots,C_{n+k+j+2})>0$, independent of $y,\xi$, such that \[ |\partial_y^j\partial_\xi^k a_n(y,\xi)| \le D\xi^{m-n-k}(y+\xi^p)^{-n}y^{-j} \quad(y>0,\ \xi\ge1). \]
nodes.proof_html: Derivatives of the cutoff are supported where $\xi$ and $\lambda_0(y)$ are comparable; every $\xi$ derivative costs $\xi^{-1}$ and every $y$ derivative costs $y^{-1}$. The division is smooth after extension by zero because the numerator vanishes on a whole neighbourhood of the zero denominator. Induct on $n$, expanding the finite Leibniz sum; apply the reciprocal bounds and $(y+\xi^p)^{-1}\le y^{-1}$ for the extra $y$ derivatives. Keep all mixed derivatives through the finite order needed in the induction.

nodes.title: Boundary terms and the improper far integral
nodes.statement_html: Under the preceding hypotheses with $m<p$, for every $y>0$ and integer $n\ge1$, the function $\xi\mapsto a_n(y,\xi)$ is integrable on $[1,\infty)$ and \[ \lim_{R\to\infty}\int_1^R g_y(\xi)e^{i\phi_y(\xi)}d\xi =(-1)^n\int_1^\infty a_n(y,\xi)e^{i\phi_y(\xi)}d\xi. \] Every boundary term $a_l(y,R)e^{i\phi_y(R)}/(i(y-R^p))$, $0\le l<n$, tends to zero; the boundary terms at $1$ vanish exactly.
nodes.proof_html: Integrate by parts on $[1,R]$, interpreting the quotient as its smooth zero extension. The upper boundary term is $O_y(R^{m-l(p+1)-p})$, whose exponent is negative because $m<p$. The final amplitude is $O_y(\xi^{m-n(p+1)})$, integrable for $n\ge1$. Flatness of $a$ at $1$ gives the lower boundary identities. Iterate the finite formula before taking limits.

nodes.title: Integrable parameter-derivative majorants for the far representation
nodes.statement_html: With $a_n$ as in lem:c03_sp_far_symbol_iteration, for every $n,j\in\N$ there is $C=C(p,m,n,j,\chi_{\rm sp},C_0,\ldots,C_{n+j+2})$ such that for $y,\xi\ge1$, \[ |\partial_y^j(a_n(y,\xi)e^{i\phi_y(\xi)})| \le C\xi^{m-n+j}(y+\xi^p)^{-n} \le C y^{-n/2}\xi^{m-n+j-pn/2}. \] On a fixed compact interval $J\subset(0,\infty)$ the same derivatives are bounded by $C_J\xi^{m-(p+1)n+j}$ for $\xi\ge1$. Thus choosing $n$ with $m-(p+1)n+j<-1$ gives an integrable majorant on $J$; choosing additionally $n/2\ge M$ and $m-n+j-pn/2<-1$ gives a bound $C_M y^{-M}$ for the integral of the derivative for $y\ge1$. Constants are independent of the truncation radius.
nodes.proof_html: Apply Leibniz; a derivative of $e^{i\phi_y}$ contributes $i\xi$, and the other factors are bounded by the preceding mixed-symbol estimate. On $y\ge1$ discard factors $y^{-1}$; use $y+\xi^p\ge\sqrt{y\xi^p}$. On $J$, the factors $y^{-1}$ are uniformly bounded. Integrate the resulting explicit powers on $[1,\infty)$.

nodes.title: Finite-order differentiation of a parametric integral over $(1,\infty)$
nodes.statement_html: Let $N\in\N$ and $F:\R\times\R\to\C$ with $(y,\xi)\mapsto F(y,\xi)$ of class $C^\infty$ on $(0,\infty)\times(1,\infty)$. Assume that for every $j\le N$ and all $0<y_1$, $y_2\in\R$ there is $g\in L^1((1,\infty))$ with $|\partial_y^jF(y,\xi)|\le g(\xi)$ for all $y\in[y_1,y_2]$ and $\xi>1$. Then $y\mapsto\int_{(1,\infty)}F(y,\xi)\,d\xi$ is $C^N$ on $(0,\infty)$ and for every $j\le N$ and $y>0$, \[ \partial_y^j\int_{(1,\infty)}F(y,\xi)\,d\xi=\int_{(1,\infty)}\partial_y^jF(y,\xi)\,d\xi . \]
nodes.proof_html:
Induction on $j<N$: the $\xi$-integrand $\partial_y^jF(y,\cdot)$ is continuous (hence measurable) and
  integrable by the majorant; its $y$-derivative $\partial_y^{j+1}F$ is dominated on $[y_1,y_2]$ by the
  majorant of order $j+1$, so the dominated differentiation theorem gives
  $\partial_y\int\partial_y^jF=\int\partial_y^{j+1}F$ on every interval $(y_1,y_2)\subset(0,\infty)$.
  Continuity of the order-$N$ integral follows by dominated convergence, which gives $C^N$.

nodes.title: Nonstationary (far) part
nodes.statement_html: Let $m<p$ and $a$ as in lem:c03_sp_near. For $y>0$ the improper integral $I_{\textup{far}}(y)=\int_0^\infty a(\xi)(1-\chi_{\textup{sp}}(\xi/\lambda_0))e^{i\phi_y(\xi)}d\xi$ exists, $I_{\textup{far}}\in C^\infty((0,\infty))$, and for all $j,M\ge0$ there is $C$ (depending on $p,m,j,M$ and finitely many $C_k$) with $|\partial_y^jI_{\textup{far}}(y)|\le Cy^{-M}$ for $y\ge1$.
nodes.proof_html: Step 1 (nonstationarity). On the support ($\xi\ge1$, $\xi\le\frac34\lambda_0$ or $\xi\ge\frac32\lambda_0$): $|\phi_y'(\xi)|=|y-\xi^p|\ge c_p(y+\xi^p)$ with $c_p=\frac12\min(1-(3/4)^p,1-(2/3)^p)$. Step 2 (symbol class). Say $G$ (smooth, supported in the set of Step 1) is of type $(\sigma,\tau)$ if $|\partial_\xi^kG|\le C_k\xi^{\sigma-k}(y+\xi^p)^{-\tau}$ uniformly in $y\ge1$. $g_y:=a(1-\chi_{\textup{sp}}(\cdot/\lambda_0))$ is of type $(m,0)$ (derivatives of $\chi_{\textup{sp}}(\xi/\lambda_0)$ are supported where $\xi\approx\lambda_0$). Since $|\partial_\xi^k(1/\phi'_y)|\le C_k\xi^{-k}(y+\xi^p)^{-1}$ (Fa\`a di Bruno with $|\partial^k\xi^p|\le C\xi^{p-k}$), $L_yG:=\partial_\xi(G/(i\phi_y'))$ maps type $(\sigma,\tau)$ to type $(\sigma-1,\tau+1)$. Step 3 (integration by parts). $\int_1^Rge^{i\phi_y}=[ge^{i\phi_y}/(i\phi_y')]_1^R-\int_1^RL_yg\,e^{i\phi_y}$; the boundary term at $R$ is $O(R^{m-p})\to0$ since $m<p$, at $1$ it vanishes. This proves existence and, iterating ($L_y^kg$ is absolutely integrable for $k\ge1$), $I_{\textup{far}}(y)=(-1)^N\int_1^\infty(L_y^Ng_y)e^{i\phi_y}d\xi$ for every $N\ge1$. Step 4 (derivatives). $\partial_y$ applied to the integrand produces: $i\xi$ from $e^{i\phi_y}$ (type $(\sigma+1,\tau)$), $\partial_y(1/\phi'_y)=-1/\phi_y'^2$ (type raises $\tau$), and $\partial_y[\chi_{\textup{sp}}(\xi/\lambda_0)]=-\frac1{py}\frac\xi{\lambda_0}\chi_{\textup{sp}}'(\xi/\lambda_0)$ (type $(0,0)$ times $y^{-1}$). So $\partial_y^j[(L^N_yg_y)e^{i\phi_y}]$ is a finite sum of terms bounded by $C\xi^{m-N+j}(y+\xi^p)^{-N}\le C\xi^{m-N+j-pN/2}y^{-N/2}$; for $N>2(m+j+1)$ these are integrable uniformly for $y$ in compacts of $[1,\infty)$ (similarly of $(0,\infty)$), which justifies differentiating under the integral, and give $|\partial_y^jI_{\textup{far}}|\le Cy^{-N/2}$. Take $N\ge2M$.

nodes.title: Homogeneous stationary phase
nodes.statement_html: Let $0<p<1$, $m\le0$, and $a\in C^\infty((0,\infty))$ with $a=0$ on $(0,1]$ and $|\partial_\xi^ka(\xi)|\le C_k\xi^{m-k}$ for $\xi\ge1$, $k\ge0$. Let $\lambda_0(y)=y^{1/p}$, $\Psi_0(y)=\frac p{p+1}y^{1+1/p}$. For $y>0$ the improper integral $I(y)=\int_0^\infty a(\xi)e^{i(y\xi-\xi^{p+1}/(p+1))}d\xi$ exists, and defining $r:(0,\infty)\to\C$ by \begin{equation} I(y)=e^{i(\Psi_0(y)-\pi/4)}\Bigl(\frac{2\pi}{p\lambda_0(y)^{p-1}}\Bigr)^{1/2}\bigl[a(\lambda_0(y))+r(y)\bigr], \end{equation} $r$ is $C^\infty$ and for every $j\ge0$ there is $C$ depending only on $p,m,j$ and finitely many $C_k$ with \begin{equation} |\partial_y^jr(y)|\le C\lambda_0(y)^{m-(p+1)}y^{-j},\qquad y\ge1 . \end{equation}
nodes.proof_html: $I=I_{\textup{near}}+I_{\textup{far}}$ (the near part is a proper integral), so $I$ exists and is smooth. Then $r=\lambda_0^m\rho(\mu;c_y)+I_{\textup{far}}/P$ by lem:c03_sp_near(2). The first term is bounded by lem:c03_sp_near(3). For the second, $1/P=e^{-i(\Psi_0-\pi/4)}(p\lambda_0^{p-1}/2\pi)^{1/2}$ with $\Psi_0'=\lambda_0$, so $|\partial_y^i(1/P)|\le Cy^{i/p}$ for $y\ge1$; by Leibniz and lem:c03_sp_far with $M$ large, $|\partial_y^j(I_{\textup{far}}/P)|\le Cy^{j/p-M}\le C\lambda_0^{m-p-1}y^{-j}$.

nodes.title: Stationary phase against a tail integral
nodes.statement_html:
Let $x_0\in\R$, $L>0$, $I=(x_0-L,x_0+L)$, $\kappa>0$, $A,M\ge0$, $\omega,\omega_0\in\R$, and constants $c_1,\dots,c_4>0$. Assume:
  • $\Phi\in C^3(\ov I;\R)$, $\Phi'(x_0)=0$, $c_1\kappa\le|\Phi''|\le c_2\kappa$ and $|\Phi'''|\le c_3\kappa L^{-1}$ on $I$;
  • $a\in C^2_c(I;\C)$ with $|a^{(j)}|\le c_4AL^{-j}$, $j=0,1,2$;
  • $\Psi\in C([x_0-L,\infty);\R)$ is such that $E(t)=\int_t^\infty e^{i\Psi(s)}ds$ exists (improper) for every $t\in I$, and $|E(t)|\le M$ on $I$;
  • $\Phi(t)+\Psi(t)=\omega t+\omega_0$ for $t\in I$.
Then $\bigl|\int_Ia(t)e^{i\Phi(t)}E(t)dt\bigr|\le C\,A(M\kappa^{-1/2}+\kappa^{-1})$ with $C=C(c_1,\dots,c_4)$.
nodes.proof_html:
WLOG $x_0=0$. $E\in C^1(I)$ with $E'=-e^{i\Psi}$. $\Phi''$ is continuous and nonvanishing, hence of constant sign, so $|\Phi'(t)|\ge c_1\kappa|t|$.
  Case $L\le\kappa^{-1/2}$: bound absolutely, $\le2Lc_4AM\le2c_4AM\kappa^{-1/2}$.
  Case $L>\kappa^{-1/2}$. Step 1: $|\int_{|t|\le\kappa^{-1/2}}|\le2c_4AM\kappa^{-1/2}$.
  Step 2 (bounds for $|t|\ge\kappa^{-1/2}$): $|a/\Phi'|\le CA/(\kappa|t|)$ and $|(a/\Phi')'|\le|a'|/|\Phi'|+|a||\Phi''|/\Phi'^2\le CA/(\kappa L|t|)+CA/(\kappa t^2)\le CA/(\kappa t^2)$ (as $|t|<L$).
  Step 3 (integration by parts on $\kappa^{-1/2}<|t|<L$), writing $e^{i\Phi}=\frac1{i\Phi'}\partial_te^{i\Phi}$ and using $aEe^{i\Phi}\to0$ at $\pm L$ (compact support):
  the integral equals the boundary terms at $\pm\kappa^{-1/2}$, each $\le CAM/(\kappa\cdot\kappa^{-1/2})$, minus $\frac1i\int(a/\Phi')'Ee^{i\Phi}$, bounded by $M\int_{|t|>\kappa^{-1/2}}CA/(\kappa t^2)=2CAM\kappa^{-1/2}$, plus
  $\frac1i\int_{\kappa^{-1/2}<|t|<L}\frac{a}{\Phi'}e^{i\Psi+i\Phi}=\frac{e^{i\omega_0}}i\int_{\kappa^{-1/2}<|t|<L}\frac{a(t)}{\Phi'(t)}e^{i\omega t}dt$.
  Step 4. Let $h(t)=ta(t)/\Phi'(t)$; since $\Phi'(t)/t=\int_0^1\Phi''(\sigma t)d\sigma$ (modulus $\ge c_1\kappa$) and $\partial_t(\Phi'(t)/t)=\int_0^1\sigma\Phi'''(\sigma t)d\sigma$, $h$ extends to a $C^1$ function on $I$ with $h(0)=a(0)/\Phi''(0)$ and $|h'|\le CA/(\kappa L)$. Hence $|a/\Phi'-h(0)/t|\le CA/(\kappa L)$, whose integral over $|t|<L$ is $\le2CA/\kappa$.
  Step 5. $\int_{\kappa^{-1/2}<|t|<L}\frac{e^{i\omega t}}tdt=2i\int_{\kappa^{-1/2}}^L\frac{\sin\omega t}tdt$, bounded by $2\sup_{0\le u<v}|\int_u^v\frac{\sin x}xdx|\le 2\pi$ (finite absolute constant), and $|h(0)|\le c_4A/(c_1\kappa)$.

nodes.title: Uniform Gaussian and cutoff symbol bounds
nodes.statement_html: Fix $0<p<1$, $K>p$, an integer $n\ge0$, and a smooth cutoff $\chi_1:\R\to[0,1]$ equal to one on $[-1,1]$ and supported in $[-2,2]$. For every $j\le n$ there is $D_j>0$ with $|\partial_z^j e^{-\eta z^2}|\le D_j|z|^{-j}$ for $\eta\ge0$, $z\ne0$. If $b\in C^\infty(\R;\C)$ and $|b^{(j)}(z)|\le C_j B|z|^{K-j}$ for $0\le j\le n$, $z\ne0$, $B\ge0$, then for every $\Lambda>0$, $\eta\ge0$, \[ g_{\eta,\Lambda}(z)=(1-\chi_1(\Lambda z))e^{-\eta z^2}b(z)|z|^{-1-p} \] extends smoothly through $0$, vanishes on $|z|\le1/\Lambda$, and $|g_{\eta,\Lambda}^{(j)}(z)|\le D B|z|^{K-1-p-j}$ for $z\ne0$, $j\le n$, where $D$ depends only on $p,K,n,\chi_1,C_0,\ldots,C_n$.
nodes.proof_html:
For $\eta>0$, induction expresses the Gaussian derivative as a polynomial in $\sqrt\eta z$
  times $|z|^{-j}e^{-\eta z^2}$; each polynomial times the Gaussian is bounded on $\R$.
  At $\eta=0$ the assertion is immediate. Nonzero derivatives of $\chi_1(\Lambda z)$ are
  supported where $1\le\Lambda|z|\le2$, so they cost $C_j|z|^{-j}$.
  Leibniz and the explicit derivatives of $|z|^{-1-p}$ give the finite-order bound.

nodes.title: Absolute near-diagonal bound for the homogeneous kernel
nodes.statement_html: Let $0<p<1$, $K>p$, $B,C_0\ge0$, $\Lambda>0$, $\eta\ge0$, and let $b$ be measurable with $|b(z)|\le C_0B|z|^K$ for $z\ne0$. For a measurable real phase $\phi$ and any measurable cutoff $0\le\chi_1\le1$ supported in $[-2,2]$, the near integrand is absolutely integrable and \[ \left|\int_\R\chi_1(\Lambda z)e^{i\phi(z)-\eta z^2}b(z)|z|^{-1-p}dz\right| \le\frac{2C_0B}{K-p}(2/\Lambda)^{K-p}. \]
nodes.proof_html:
Bound the modulus by $C_0B\mathbf1_{|z|\le2/\Lambda}|z|^{K-1-p}$.
  Integrate on the two half-lines; the exponent is greater than $-1$ because $K>p$.

nodes.title: Far homogeneous-kernel bound after an explicit integer number of integrations
nodes.statement_html: Let $0<p<1$, $K>p$, $B\ge0$, $\Lambda>0$, $c_0>0$, $U\subset\R$ open, $b\in C_c^\infty(U;\C)$, and $\phi\in C^\infty(U;\R)$. Assume on $U$, for $z\ne0$, $|b^{(j)}(z)|\le C_jB|z|^{K-j}$ and $|(1/\phi')^{(j)}(z)|\le C_j\Lambda^{-1}|z|^{-j}$, with $c_0^{-1}\Lambda\le|\phi'|\le c_0\Lambda$. Fix $\chi_1$ as in lem:c03_homogeneous_cutoff_symbol and an integer $L>K-p$; the derivative hypotheses are required only for $0\le j\le L+1$. There is $C=C(p,K,L,c_0,\chi_1,C_0,\ldots,C_{L+1})>0$, independent of $b,B,\Lambda,\eta$, such that, with $g=g_{\eta,\Lambda}$, \[ \int e^{i\phi}g=(-1)^L\int e^{i\phi}L_\phi^Lg,\qquad |L_\phi^Lg(z)|\le CB\Lambda^{-L}|z|^{K-1-p-L} \mathbf1_{|z|\ge1/\Lambda}. \] All integrals converge absolutely and their modulus is bounded by $2CB\Lambda^{p-K}/(L+p-K)$.
nodes.proof_html: The cutoff removes the origin and $b$ provides compact support, so the finite IBP identity has zero boundary terms. Apply the symbol iteration with $\sigma=K-1-p$ and integrate $|z|^{K-1-p-L}$ on $|z|\ge1/\Lambda$. The denominator $L+p-K$ is strictly positive.

nodes.title: Integration by parts against the homogeneous kernel
nodes.statement_html: Let $0<p<1$, $\Lambda>0$, $B\ge0$, $K>p$, and $c_0,(C_s)_{s\ge0}$ constants. Let $U\subset\R$ be open, $b\in C^\infty(\R;\C)$ with $\operatorname{supp}b\subset U$ compact, $\phi\in C^\infty(U;\R)$, such that on $U$: $|\partial^s_zb(z)|\le C_sB|z|^{K-s}$, $c_0^{-1}\Lambda\le|\phi'(z)|\le c_0\Lambda$, $|\partial_z^s(1/\phi'(z))|\le C_s\Lambda^{-1}|z|^{-s}$ ($s\ge0$). Then for all $\eta\ge0$ \[ \Bigl|\int_\R e^{i\phi(z)}e^{-\eta z^2}\frac{b(z)}{|z|^{1+p}}dz\Bigr|\le C B\Lambda^{p-K}, \] with $C$ depending only on $p,K,c_0$ and finitely many $C_s$; and the integral is continuous in $\eta\ge0$.
nodes.proof_html: Let $\chi_\Lambda(z)=\chi_1(\Lambda z)$ with $\chi_1\in C_c^\infty([-2,2])$, $\chi_1=1$ on $[-1,1]$. Near part: $\le\int_{|z|\le2/\Lambda}C_0B|z|^{K-1-p}=CB\Lambda^{p-K}$ (as $K>p$). Far part: integrate by parts $L>K-p$ times with $e^{i\phi}=\frac1{i\phi'}\partial_ze^{i\phi}$ (no boundary terms: compact support, and the integrand vanishes near $0$). The amplitude $g=(1-\chi_\Lambda)e^{-\eta z^2}b|z|^{-1-p}$ satisfies $|\partial^sg|\le CB|z|^{K-1-p-s}$ on $|z|\ge1/\Lambda$, uniformly in $\eta$ (since $|\partial^s\chi_\Lambda|\le C\Lambda^s\le C|z|^{-s}$ on its support and $|\partial_z^se^{-\eta z^2}|\le C_s|z|^{-s}$ uniformly in $\eta\ge0$). Each step multiplies by $\Lambda^{-1}|z|^{-1}$, giving $\le CB\Lambda^{-L}\int_{|z|\ge1/\Lambda}|z|^{K-1-p-L}=CB\Lambda^{p-K}$. Continuity in $\eta$: dominated convergence on the compact support.

nodes.title: Moments of the kernel
nodes.statement_html: For $\lambda>0$ and integers $k\ge1$, $\int^{\textup{osc}}e^{i\lambda z}z^k|z|^{-1-p}dz$ exists and \begin{equation} -c_p\int^{\textup{osc}}e^{i\lambda z}\frac{z^k}{|z|^{1+p}}dz=(-i)^km^{(k)}(\lambda), \end{equation} locally uniformly in $\lambda\in(0,\infty)$. Also $c_p\int^{\textup{osc}}(1-e^{i\lambda z})|z|^{-1-p}dz=c_p\int(1-e^{i\lambda z})|z|^{-1-p}dz=\lambda^p$.
nodes.proof_html: Let $g_\eta(\lambda)=c_p\int(1-e^{i\lambda z})e^{-\eta z^2}|z|^{-1-p}dz$, $\eta>0$; it is $C^\infty$ in $\lambda$ with $g_\eta^{(k)}(\lambda)=-c_p\int(iz)^ke^{i\lambda z-\eta z^2}|z|^{-1-p}dz$ for $k\ge1$, and $g_\eta\to\lambda^p$ pointwise by dominated convergence and lem:c03_frac_kernel_formula. For $k\ge1$, $g_\eta^{(k)}$ converges locally uniformly on $(0,\infty)$ as $\eta\downarrow0$: split with $\chi_1(z)$; the part $|z|\le2$ converges by dominated convergence ($|z|^{k-1-p}$ integrable); on $|z|\ge1$ integrate by parts $L>k-p$ times in $z$ using $\partial_ze^{i\lambda z}=i\lambda e^{i\lambda z}$, obtaining absolutely convergent integrals, dominated uniformly in $\eta$ and $\lambda\in[\lambda_1,\lambda_2]$. A sequence of functions converging pointwise whose derivatives converge locally uniformly has a differentiable limit with derivative the limit of the derivatives; iterate in $k$. Lean route: no integration by parts on $|z|\ge1$. With $Q_m(\eta,l)=c_p\int P_m(l,z)e^{-\eta z^2}|z|^{-1-p}dz$ ($P_0=1-e^{ilz}$, $P_m=-e^{ilz}z^m$): $\partial_lQ_m=iQ_{m+1}$ for $\eta>0$; $|Q_m(\eta,l)|\le C$ uniformly for $\eta>0$, $l\ge a>0$, $m\ge1$ (from lem:c03_ibp_homogeneous applied to truncations $z^m\chi(z/R)$, $R\to\infty$); $k=0$ by dominated convergence; induction on $m$ using convergence of functions plus uniform second-derivative bounds; uniformity on $[\lambda_1,\lambda_2]$ from the scaling $Q_m(\eta,l)=l^{p-m}Q_m(\eta/l^2,1)$.

nodes.title: Phase data for the oscillatory multiplier
nodes.statement_html: For $a:\R\to\C$, $\Psi:\R\to\R$, $Y\in\R$, put $\lambda=\Psi'$ and \[ \Theta_y(z)=\Psi(y+z)-\Psi(y)-\lambda(y)z,\qquad F_y(z)=\begin{cases}a(y+z)e^{i\Theta_y(z)},&y+z\in(Y/4,4Y),\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} \] For $k_0\in\N$, $C_k\in\R$ and real $\Lambda,A,c_0$, the predicate $\mathsf H(Y,\Lambda,A,c_0,(C_k),k_0;a,\Psi)$ means that $a\in C^\infty(\R)$, $\operatorname{supp}a\subset(Y/4,4Y)$, $\Psi\in C^\infty((Y/4,4Y))$, and for all $x\in(Y/4,4Y)$ and $0\le k\le k_0$, \[ c_0^{-1}\Lambda\le\lambda(x)\le c_0\Lambda,\quad |\partial^k\lambda(x)|\le C_k\Lambda Y^{-k},\quad |\partial^ka(x)|\le C_kAY^{-k}. \] Positivity and size restrictions on $Y,\Lambda,A,c_0$ are hypotheses of the lemmas using this predicate.

nodes.title: Multiplier coefficients and remainders
nodes.statement_html: Let $m(\xi)=\xi^p$. For $k\in\N$ and $N\ge1$ define \[ B_k(y)=\frac{(-i)^k}{k!}m^{(k)}(\lambda(y))F_y^{(k)}(0),\qquad R_{2N-1}(z)=F_y(z)-\sum_{k=0}^{2N-2}\frac{F_y^{(k)}(0)}{k!}z^k, \] \[ \mc R_{\mathrm{mult},N}(y)=e^{-i\Psi(y)}|D|^p(ae^{i\Psi})(y)-\sum_{k=0}^{2N-2}B_k(y),\qquad \sq{\mc R}_{\mathrm{mult},2}(y)=\mc R_{\mathrm{mult},2}(y) -\frac{p(p-1)}2\lambda(y)^{p-2}a''(y). \] The finite index set consists of $(r,q)$ with $r\in\{0,\ldots,2N-1\}$, $q=(q_1,\ldots,q_{2N-1})\in\{0,\ldots,2N-1\}^{2N-1}$, and $r+\sum_{j=1}^{2N-1}j q_j=2N-1$. Its coefficient is $d_{r,q}=i^{\sum_jq_j}/(r!\prod_j q_j!(j!)^{q_j})$. These are definitions; their integral representations and bounds require the lemmas below.

nodes.title: Individual multiplier summands
nodes.statement_html: For an index $(r,q)$ as above, let $q_1$ be its first component and $\ell=\sum_{j\ge2}q_j$. Define \[ b_t(z)=z^{2N-1}a^{(r)}(y+tz)\prod_{j=1}^{2N-1}(\Theta_y^{(j)}(tz))^{q_j} \] when $y+tz\in(Y/4,4Y)$, and $b_t(z)=0$ otherwise. Put \[ \phi_t(z)=\lambda(y)z+\Theta_y(tz),\qquad I_\eta(y,t)=\int_\R e^{i\phi_t(z)-\eta z^2}\frac{b_t(z)}{|z|^{1+p}}\,dz, \qquad B=A\Lambda^{q_1+\ell}Y^{-2N+1+\ell}t^{q_1}. \] Here $I_\eta$ is the total Bochner integral; the hypotheses ensuring convergence and estimates are imposed in the following lemmas.

nodes.title: Recursive jets of an exponential
nodes.statement_html: Let $U\subset\R$ be open and $\Theta\in C^\infty(U;\R)$. Define $E_0=1$ and $E_{n+1}=E_n'+i\Theta'E_n$ on $U$. For every $n\in\N$, $E_n$ is smooth and $\partial^n e^{i\Theta}=e^{i\Theta}E_n$ on $U$. In particular $E_1=i\Theta'$ and $E_2=i\Theta''-(\Theta')^2$.
nodes.proof_html:
Induct on $n$, applying the product rule and $(e^{i\Theta})'=i\Theta'e^{i\Theta}$.
  This fixes a recursive implementation of the jets before any closed combinatorial formula is used.

nodes.title: Finite multiindex formula for exponential jets
nodes.statement_html: For the jets of lem:c03_exp_jet_recursion, and every $n\ge1$, \[ E_n=n!\sum_{\substack{q_1,\ldots,q_n\ge0\\\sum_{j=1}^n j q_j=n}} \frac{i^{\sum_jq_j}}{\prod_jq_j!(j!)^{q_j}} \prod_{j=1}^n(\Theta^{(j)})^{q_j}. \] The index set is finite because each $q_j\le n$.
nodes.proof_html: Induct in the recursion. Multiplication by $i\Theta'$ increments $q_1$. Differentiating the $j$-th factor removes one $\Theta^{(j)}$ and adds one $\Theta^{(j+1)}$, contributing its multiplicity $q_j$. Reindex these finite sums; factorial cancellation gives the displayed coefficient at order $n+1$. The required finite-index reindexing and coefficient arithmetic are the concrete subtask here; no analytic estimates enter it.

nodes.title: Absolutely convergent kernel identity for a localized oscillatory profile
nodes.statement_html: Let $0<p<1$, $Y\ge1$, $a\in C_c^\infty((Y/4,4Y);\C)$, and $\Psi\in C^\infty((Y/4,4Y);\R)$ with $\lambda=\Psi'>0$. For every $y\in[Y,2Y]$, $F_y\in C_c^\infty(\R)$, $F_y(0)=a(y)$, and \[ e^{-i\Psi(y)}|D|^p(ae^{i\Psi})(y)-\lambda(y)^pa(y) =-c_p\int e^{i\lambda(y)z}(F_y(z)-a(y))|z|^{-1-p}dz. \] The integral on the right converges absolutely, as does the defining kernel integral on the left.
nodes.proof_html: Apply the fractional-kernel formula to the smooth supported product and subtract the plane-wave identity for $\lambda^p$. Near zero, $F_y(z)-F_y(0)=O(|z|)$; at infinity $F_y$ vanishes and the remaining constant is integrable against $|z|^{-1-p}$. These two majorants justify subtraction and all changes of variables.

nodes.title: Integral Taylor remainder with explicit amplitude and phase factors
nodes.statement_html: With the data of lem:c03_mult_kernel_identity, $N\ge1$, and $y\in[Y,2Y]$, put $n=2N-1$. For every $z\in\R$, \[ R_n(z)=n\sum_{r+\sum_{j=1}^n j q_j=n}d_{r,q} \int_0^1(1-t)^{n-1}e^{i\Theta_y(tz)}b_t(z)\,dt. \] Each integral is absolutely convergent. Here the amplitude $b_t$ includes the factor $z^n$ and is zero when $y+tz\notin(Y/4,4Y)$, as in def:c03_multiplier_summands.
nodes.proof_html: Taylor's integral remainder for the globally smooth $F_y$ gives $R_n(z)=z^n/(n-1)!\int_0^1(1-t)^{n-1}F_y^{(n)}(tz)dt$. Expand by Leibniz and the exponential-jet formula. Outside the phase domain, every amplitude derivative vanishes on a neighbourhood, so the zero-extension convention is legitimate. Cancel $n!/(n-1)!=n$ after collecting the finite index set.

nodes.title: Removal of Gaussian regularization from the Taylor remainder
nodes.statement_html: Under the same hypotheses, for every $N\ge1$, $y\in[Y,2Y]$, and $\eta>0$, $e^{i\lambda(y)z-\eta z^2}R_{2N-1}(z)|z|^{-1-p}$ is integrable, and \[ \lim_{\eta\downarrow0}-c_p\int e^{i\lambda(y)z-\eta z^2} R_{2N-1}(z)|z|^{-1-p}dz=\mc R_{\rm mult,N}(y). \]
