nodes.proof_html: The Taylor remainder vanishes to order $2N-1\ge1$ at zero and grows polynomially at infinity, giving integrability for $\eta>0$. Expand it into $F_y-a(y)$ minus the finite polynomial with degrees $1$ through $2N-2$. Dominated convergence applies to the first term, and the regularized moment lemma evaluates every polynomial term. This proves existence and value of the limit before any uniform remainder estimate is used.

nodes.title: Kernel representation and Taylor expansion
nodes.statement_html: Let $Y,\Lambda\ge1$, $a\in C_c^\infty((Y/4,4Y);\C)$, $\Psi\in C^\infty((Y/4,4Y);\R)$, $\lambda=\Psi'>0$ there. For $Y\le y\le2Y$ set $\Theta_y(z)=\Psi(y+z)-\Psi(y)-\lambda(y)z$ and $F_y(z)=a(y+z)e^{i\Theta_y(z)}$ for $y+z\in(Y/4,4Y)$, $F_y(z)=0$ otherwise ($F_y\in C_c^\infty(\R)$). Then \begin{equation} e^{-i\Psi(y)}|D|^p(ae^{i\Psi})(y)-\lambda(y)^pa(y)=-c_p\int_\R e^{i\lambda(y)z}\frac{F_y(z)-a(y)}{|z|^{1+p}}dz \end{equation} (absolutely convergent), and with $B_k$ as in eqn:appendix_oscillatory_multiplier_coefficients, $N\ge1$, and $R_{2N-1}(z):=F_y(z)-\sum_{k=0}^{2N-2}\frac{F_y^{(k)}(0)}{k!}z^k$, \[ \mc R_{\textup{mult},N}(y):=e^{-i\Psi(y)}|D|^p(ae^{i\Psi})(y)-\sum_{k=0}^{2N-2}B_k(y)=-c_p\int^{\textup{osc}}e^{i\lambda(y)z}\frac{R_{2N-1}(z)}{|z|^{1+p}}dz . \] Moreover eqn:appendix_oscillatory_multiplier_taylor_remainder holds: \begin{equation} R_{2N-1}(z)=(2N-1)z^{2N-1}\!\!\sum_{\substack{r,q_1,\dots,q_{2N-1}\ge0\\ r+\sum_jjq_j=2N-1}}\!\!\frac{i^{\sum_jq_j}}{r!\prod_jq_j!(j!)^{q_j}}\int_0^1(1-t)^{2N-2}e^{i\Theta_y(tz)}a^{(r)}(y+tz)\prod_{j=1}^{2N-1}\bigl(\Theta_y^{(j)}(tz)\bigr)^{q_j}dt, \end{equation} where each summand is interpreted as $0$ when $y+tz\notin(Y/4,4Y)$.
nodes.proof_html: Step 1. $ae^{i\Psi}\in C_c^\infty(\R)$; by lem:c03_frac_kernel_formula, $e^{-i\Psi(y)}|D|^p(ae^{i\Psi})(y)=c_p\int(a(y)-e^{i\lambda z}F_y(z))|z|^{-1-p}dz$; subtract $\lambda^pa(y)=c_pa(y)\int(1-e^{i\lambda z})|z|^{-1-p}$; both integrals absolutely convergent ($F_y(z)-a(y)=O(|z|)$ at $0$). Step 2. Insert $e^{-\eta z^2}$ (dominated convergence) and expand $F_y-a(y)=\sum_{k=1}^{2N-2}\frac{F_y^{(k)}(0)}{k!}z^k+R_{2N-1}$; every piece is integrable against $e^{-\eta z^2}|z|^{-1-p}$ for $\eta>0$. By lem:c03_frac_moments, the $k$-th piece tends to $\frac{(-i)^k}{k!}m^{(k)}(\lambda)F_y^{(k)}(0)=B_k$ (and $B_0=\lambda^pa$). So the limit for $R_{2N-1}$ exists and gives the formula. Step 3. Taylor's formula with integral remainder, then Fa\`a di Bruno/Leibniz for $F_y^{(2N-1)}(w)=\sum\frac{(2N-1)!}{r!\prod q_j!(j!)^{q_j}}a^{(r)}(y+w)e^{i\Theta_y(w)}\prod(i\Theta_y^{(j)}(w))^{q_j}$; and $(2N-1)!/(2N-2)!=2N-1$.

nodes.title: Support and mixed symbol bounds for a Taylor summand
nodes.statement_html: Fix $N\ge1$ and an index $r+\sum_{l=1}^{2N-1}lq_l=2N-1$. For $Y,\Lambda\ge1$, $A>0$, $c_0>0$, assume the phase-data hypothesis $\mathsf H$ through order $2N+j+s+2$, where $j,s\in\N$ are prescribed. Put $K=2N-1+q_1$ and $B=A\Lambda^{q_1+\ell}Y^{-2N+1+\ell}t^{q_1}$. For $0<t\le1$, $y\in[Y,2Y]$, the amplitude $b_t$ is smooth and compactly supported in $\{z:y+tz\in(Y/4,4Y)\}$, and \[ |\partial_y^j\partial_z^s b_t(z)|\le C B Y^{-j}|z|^{K-s}\qquad(z\ne0). \] Here $C$ depends only on $N,j,s,c_0,C_0,\ldots,C_{2N+j+s+2}$ and is uniform in $Y,\Lambda,A,y,t$. The same local smoothness and estimates, with enlarged constants, hold for $Y/2<y<3Y$.
nodes.proof_html:
Use $\Theta_y'(tz)=\lambda(y+tz)-\lambda(y)$ and the fundamental theorem of calculus
  along the segment inside the phase interval. Each mixed $y$ derivative costs $Y^{-1}$;
  each $z$ derivative costs $t/Y\le4/|z|$ on the support. The factor $\Theta_y'(tz)$
  contributes $\Lambda Y^{-1}t|z|$, and every higher phase derivative contributes
  $\Lambda Y^{1-l}$. Leibniz and $r+\sum lq_l=2N-1$ give the displayed powers.
  Smooth zero extension follows because every derivative of $a$ is supported in the fixed compact
  support of $a$, strictly inside the phase interval.

nodes.title: Mixed phase bounds and convex interpolation
nodes.statement_html: Fix $j,s\in\N$, $Y,\Lambda\ge1$, $c_0>0$, and assume the phase bounds in $\mathsf H$ through order $j+s+2$. For $0<t\le1$, $y\in[Y,2Y]$, and $y+tz\in(Y/4,4Y)$, \[ \phi_t'(z)=(1-t)\lambda(y)+t\lambda(y+tz),\qquad c_0^{-1}\Lambda\le\phi_t'(z)\le c_0\Lambda, \] \[ |\partial_y^j\partial_z^s(1/\phi_t')(z)| \le C\Lambda^{-1}Y^{-j}(t/Y)^s. \] For $j\ge1$, $z\ne0$, also $|\partial_y^j\partial_z^s\phi_t(z)|\le C\Lambda Y^{-j}|z|^{1-s}$. These bounds hold uniformly for convex combinations of two such phases with the same constants, and extend to $Y/2<y<3Y$ with enlarged constants. Constants depend only on $j,s,c_0$ and the displayed finite list of symbol bounds.
nodes.proof_html: The first identity is direct differentiation and positivity follows by convexity. Mixed derivatives of $\phi_t'$ cost $Y^{-1}$ in $y$ and $t/Y$ in $z$. Apply the reciprocal recurrence, now inducting on the two derivative orders. For derivatives of $\phi_t$ itself use its vanishing at $z=0$ and the fundamental theorem of calculus for the $s=0$ bound; for $s\ge1$ use $t|z|\le4Y$ on the controlled domain.

nodes.title: Pointwise parameter-derivative bound for one summand integral
nodes.statement_html: Let $0<p<1$, $c_0>0$, $N\ge1$ and an index $(r,q)$, $q=(q_1,\dots,q_{2N-1})$, with $r+\sum_jjq_j=2N-1$; put $K=2N-1+q_1$. For every $j\in\N$ there is $k_0\in\N$ such that for every sequence $(C_k)$ there is $C>0$ with the following property: for all $Y\ge1$, $\Lambda\ge1$, $A>0$ and data $(a,\Psi)$ satisfying $\mathsf H(Y,\Lambda,A,c_0,(C_k),k_0)$, all $0<t\le1$, $\eta\ge0$ and $Y/2<y<3Y$, \[ |\partial_y^jI_\eta(y,t)|\le C\,B\,Y^{-j}\Lambda^{p-K}, \] where $B=B(N,q,Y,\Lambda,A,t)$ is the size of def:c03_multiplier_summands.
nodes.proof_html: The differentiated amplitudes $E_{0,0}=b_t$, $E_{j+1,l}=\partial_yE_{j,l}+i(\partial_y\phi_t)E_{j,l-1}$ satisfy $\partial_y^j(e^{i\phi_t}b_t)=e^{i\phi_t}\sum_{l\le j}E_{j,l}$, and (using commutation of $\partial_y$ and $\partial_z$ together with lem:c03_mult_amplitude_symbol and lem:c03_mult_phase_symbol) $E_{j,l}$ obeys symbol bounds of order $K+l$ and size $B\Lambda^lY^{-j}$. Localize each $E_{j,l}$ to a $C^\infty_c$ amplitude and apply lem:c03_ibp_homogeneous with order $K+l>p$; the factor $\Lambda^l$ cancels the gain $\Lambda^{-l}$. The finitely many orders used fix $k_0$.

nodes.title: Differentiated amplitudes and the summand integral bound
nodes.statement_html: For $0<p<1$, fix the data and index of lem:c03_mult_amplitude_symbol. For each $j\in\N$ there is a finite order $k_0=k_0(p,N,j)$ such that bounds in $\mathsf H$ through order $k_0$ imply: $I_\eta(y,t)$ is smooth in $y\in(Y/2,3Y)$ for each $\eta\ge0$, $t>0$, its derivatives are obtained by differentiating its absolutely integrable integrand, and \[ |\partial_y^jI_\eta(y,t)|\le C B Y^{-j}\Lambda^{p-K} \le C A Y^{-N-j}\Lambda^{p-N}\quad(y\in[Y,2Y],\ 0<t\le1,\ \eta\ge0). \] The constant depends only on $p,N,j,c_0,C_0,\ldots,C_{k_0}$.
nodes.proof_html: Define $b_{0,0}=b_t$ and recursively $b_{j+1,l}=\partial_yb_{j,l}+i(\partial_y\phi_t)b_{j,l-1}$, taking absent indices as zero. Then $\partial_y^j(e^{i\phi_t}b_t)=e^{i\phi_t}\sum_{l=0}^j b_{j,l}$. Mixed derivatives of $b_{j,l}$ have symbol order $K+l$, size $B\Lambda^lY^{-j}$, by the two preceding lemmas. Choose an integer $L>K+j-p$ and use homogeneous IBP for every $l$; the factors $\Lambda^l$ cancel the gain $\Lambda^{-l}$. For fixed $t>0$ the support stays compact locally in $y$, and the integrable near-zero powers have order at least $K>p$, which justifies parameter differentiation even for $\eta=0$. Finally $2\ell+q_1\le2N-1$ gives $\ell\le N-1$; since $t\le1$ and $Y\Lambda\ge1$, $B\Lambda^{p-K}\le AY^{-N}\Lambda^{p-N}$. The chosen $L$ fixes a finite sufficient $k_0$.

nodes.title: Bound for one remainder summand
nodes.statement_html: In the setting of lem:c03_mult_expansion, assume moreover $c_0^{-1}\Lambda\le\lambda\le c_0\Lambda$, $|\lambda^{(k)}|\le C_k\Lambda Y^{-k}$, $|a^{(k)}|\le C_kAY^{-k}$ on $(Y/4,4Y)$, $k\ge0$. Fix a summand $(r,q)$ of eqn:appendix_oscillatory_multiplier_taylor_remainder, $\ell=\sum_{j\ge2}q_j$, $K=2N-1+q_1$, $B=A\Lambda^{q_1+\ell}Y^{-2N+1+\ell}t^{q_1}$, and for $0<t\le1$ $\phi_t(z)=\lambda(y)z+\Theta_y(tz)$, $b_t(z)=z^{2N-1}a^{(r)}(y+tz)\prod_j(\Theta_y^{(j)}(tz))^{q_j}$. Then for $s\ge0$, uniformly in $t\in(0,1]$, $Y\le y\le2Y$: \begin{equation} |\partial_z^sb_t(z)|\le C B|z|^{K-s}, \end{equation} \begin{equation} \phi_t'(z)=(1-t)\lambda(y)+t\lambda(y+tz),\quad c_0^{-1}\Lambda\le\phi_t'\le c_0\Lambda,\quad |\partial_z^s(1/\phi_t')|\le C\Lambda^{-1}(t/Y)^s\le C\Lambda^{-1}|z|^{-s} \end{equation} on $\operatorname{supp}b_t$, and, for $\eta\ge0$ and $Y\Lambda\ge1$, \begin{equation} \Bigl|\int e^{i\phi_t(z)-\eta z^2}\frac{b_t(z)}{|z|^{1+p}}dz\Bigr|\le CB\Lambda^{p-K}=CAt^{q_1}(Y\Lambda)^{-2N+1+\ell}\Lambda^{p}\le CAY^{-N}\Lambda^{p-N}. \end{equation} The same bounds hold for $\partial_y^j$ of the integral ($j=0,1$, indeed any $j$) with an extra factor $Y^{-j}$. Constants depend on $p,N,s,j,c_0$ and finitely many $C_k$.
nodes.proof_html: On $\operatorname{supp}b_t$, $y+tz\in(Y/4,4Y)$, so $t|z|\le4Y$. $\Theta_y'(w)=\lambda(y+w)-\lambda(y)$ gives $|\Theta'_y(tz)|\le C\Lambda Y^{-1}t|z|$; $|\Theta^{(j)}_y|\le C\Lambda Y^{1-j}$ for $j\ge2$. Multiply: $|b_t|\le CAY^{-r}(\Lambda Y^{-1}t|z|)^{q_1}\prod_{j\ge2}(\Lambda Y^{1-j})^{q_j}|z|^{2N-1}=CB|z|^K$, using $r+\sum jq_j=2N-1$. Each $\partial_z$ costs a factor $tY^{-1}\le4|z|^{-1}$ (on the $a$, $\Theta^{(j)}$, $j\ge2$ factors) or $|z|^{-1}$ (on $z^{2N-1}$, and on $\Theta'_y(tz)$ which is $\le Ct\Lambda Y^{-1}|z|$ with derivative $\le Ct\Lambda Y^{-1}$). This is eqn:appendix_oscillatory_multiplier_remainder_symbols. eqn:appendix_oscillatory_multiplier_phase_derivative_bounds: $\phi_t'$ is a convex combination of values of $\lambda$; derivatives of $1/\phi'_t$ by Fa\`a di Bruno with $|\partial_z^s\phi_t'|\le Ct^{s}\Lambda Y^{-s}$. eqn:appendix_oscillatory_multiplier_remainder_summand: lem:c03_ibp_homogeneous ($K\ge2N-1\ge1>p$). Last inequality: $\sum_jjq_j\le2N-1$ forces $2\ell+q_1\le2N-1$, so $\ell\le N-1$; $t\le1$; $Y\Lambda\ge1$ so $(Y\Lambda)^{-2N+1+\ell}\le(Y\Lambda)^{-N}$. $y$-derivatives: $\partial_y\Theta_y(w)=\lambda(y+w)-\lambda(y)-\lambda'(y)w$, so $|\partial_y\phi_t|\le C\Lambda Y^{-1}|z|$ with matching $z$-derivative bounds, and $|\partial_y\partial_z^sb_t|\le CBY^{-1}|z|^{K-s}$. $\partial_y[e^{i\phi_t}b_t]=e^{i\phi_t}(\partial_yb_t+i\partial_y\phi_t\,b_t)$: amplitudes of type $(BY^{-1},K)$ and $(B\Lambda Y^{-1},K+1)$; lem:c03_ibp_homogeneous gives $CBY^{-1}\Lambda^{p-K}$ for both. Differentiation under the integral is legitimate for $\eta>0$ and $t>0$ (compact support). Iterate for higher $j$.

nodes.title: Difference symbols on the controlled phase domain
nodes.statement_html: Let two data sets satisfy $\mathsf H$ with the same $Y,\Lambda,A,c_0,C_k$, $Y,\Lambda\ge1$, $A>0$, and assume $\delta\ge0$ and $|\partial^k(a_1-a_0)|\le C_k\delta A Y^{-k}$, $|\partial^k(\Psi_1-\Psi_0)|\le C_k\delta Y^{-k}$ on $(Y/4,4Y)$. For a fixed index $(r,q)$, each $j,s\in\N$, and symbol hypotheses through order $2N+j+s+3$, there is $C$ depending only on $N,j,s,c_0$ and those finitely many $C_k$ such that \[ |\partial_y^j\partial_z^s(b_{1,t}-b_{0,t})|\le C\delta B Y^{-j}|z|^{K-s} \] for all $y\in[Y,2Y]$, $0<t\le1$, $z\ne0$; and \[ |\partial_y^j\partial_z^s(\phi_{1,t}-\phi_{0,t})| \le C\delta Y^{-j-1}|z|^{1-s} \] when additionally $y+tz\in(Y/4,4Y)$. All amplitudes are extended by zero as in their definitions.
nodes.proof_html: Telescope each finite product defining $b_t$, differentiating its factors with the finite Leibniz rule. A difference of amplitudes supplies $\delta$, while a difference of phase derivatives supplies $\delta/Y$ in place of $\Lambda$; use $(Y\Lambda)^{-1}\le1$. For the second estimate write $\Delta\phi_t=(1-t)\Delta\Psi'(y)z+\Delta\Psi(y+tz)-\Delta\Psi(y)$ and integrate along the segment in the phase domain. Higher derivatives use the corresponding finite derivative bounds. No statement is made about the arbitrary extensions of the phases outside that domain.

nodes.title: Absolutely integrable phase-interpolation identity
nodes.statement_html: Let $0<p<1$, $Y>0$, $N\ge1$, and $r+\sum lq_l=2N-1$. Let $a_0,a_1\in C_c^\infty((Y/4,4Y);\C)$ and $\Psi_0,\Psi_1\in C^\infty((Y/4,4Y);\R)$. For $y\in[Y,2Y]$, $0<t\le1$, and $\eta\ge0$, all integrals below converge absolutely, including the double integral with respect to $(\sigma,z)$, and \[ I_{1,\eta}-I_{0,\eta} =\int e^{i\phi_{1,t}-\eta z^2}(b_{1,t}-b_{0,t})|z|^{-1-p}dz +i\int_0^1\!\int e^{i((1-\sigma)\phi_{0,t}+\sigma\phi_{1,t})-\eta z^2} (\phi_{1,t}-\phi_{0,t})b_{0,t}|z|^{-1-p}dz\,d\sigma. \] The identity may be differentiated any fixed number of times in $y$ on $(Y/2,3Y)$.
nodes.proof_html: Apply $e^{iu}-e^{iv}=i(u-v)\int_0^1e^{i((1-\sigma)v+\sigma u)}d\sigma$ pointwise. For fixed $t>0$, the union of the two amplitude supports is compact and varies within a common compact set on compact $y$ intervals. At zero the amplitudes vanish to order at least $2N-1\ge1>p$, and $\Delta\phi_t=O(|z|)$. These bounds persist under any fixed number of $y$ derivatives. They give integrable majorants uniform in $\sigma\in[0,1]$, justifying Fubini and differentiation.

nodes.title: Uniform estimate for the two interpolated difference contributions
nodes.statement_html: Fix $0<p<1$ and $\delta\ge0$. Under the hypotheses of lem:c03_mult_difference_symbols, for every $j\in\N$ there is a finite $k_0=k_0(p,N,j)$ such that the corresponding finite symbol and difference bounds give \[ |\partial_y^j(I_{1,\eta}-I_{0,\eta})| \le C\delta BY^{-j}\Lambda^{p-K} +C\delta BY^{-j-1}\Lambda^{p-K-1} \le 2C\delta AY^{-N-j}\Lambda^{p-N} \] for $y\in[Y,2Y]$, $0<t\le1$, $\eta\ge0$. Here $C=C(p,N,j,c_0,C_0,\ldots,C_{k_0})>0$ is independent of $\delta,Y,\Lambda,A,y,t,\eta$.
nodes.proof_html: In the first interpolation term the amplitude has size $\delta B$ and order $K$. In the second it has size $\delta B/Y$ and order $K+1$. The convexly interpolated phase has the same reciprocal derivative bounds, uniformly in $\sigma$. Repeat the explicit differentiated-amplitude recursion of the parameter-IBP lemma for each term, apply the homogeneous estimate, and integrate $\sigma\in[0,1]$. Each of the two final terms is at most $C\delta AY^{-N-j}\Lambda^{p-N}$; retain the factor $2$. Lean route: instead of differentiating the $\sigma$-integral of the interpolation identity, interpolate both phase and amplitude, $\Phi_\sigma=(1-\sigma)\phi_0+\sigma\phi_1$, $H_\sigma=(1-\sigma)b_0+\sigma b_1$, write $\partial_y^j(I_1-I_0)=\mc R(1)-\mc R(0)$ with $\mc R(\sigma)=\int e^{-\eta z^2}|z|^{-1-p}\partial_y^j(e^{i\Phi_\sigma}H_\sigma)\,dz$, and bound $\mc R'(\sigma)$ (differentiation under the $z$-integral) uniformly in $\sigma\in[0,1]$ by the two homogeneous-IBP estimates above; the interpolation identity of the preceding lemma is not used.

nodes.title: Difference of remainders
nodes.statement_html: Let $(a_\nu,\Psi_\nu)$, $\nu=0,1$, satisfy the hypotheses of lem:c03_mult_summand with the same $Y,\Lambda,A$ and constants, and suppose for some $\delta\in[0,1]$: $|\partial^k(a_1-a_0)|\le C_k\delta AY^{-k}$, $|\partial^k(\Psi_1-\Psi_0)|\le C_k\delta Y^{-k}$ on $(Y/4,4Y)$, $k\ge0$. Let $I_\nu(y,t)$ be the integral in eqn:appendix_oscillatory_multiplier_remainder_summand for $(a_\nu,\Psi_\nu)$ (same summand). Then For $z\ne0$, the amplitude bound below holds globally; the phase bound is asserted only when $y+tz\in(Y/4,4Y)$. \begin{equation} |\partial_y^j\partial_z^s(b_{1,t}-b_{0,t})|\le C\delta BY^{-j}|z|^{K-s},\qquad |\partial_y^j\partial_z^s(\phi_{1,t}-\phi_{0,t})|\le C\delta Y^{-j-1}|z|^{1-s}, \end{equation} \begin{equation} I_1-I_0=\int e^{i\phi_{1,t}}\frac{b_{1,t}-b_{0,t}}{|z|^{1+p}}dz+i\int_0^1\!\!\int e^{i((1-\sigma)\phi_{0,t}+\sigma\phi_{1,t})}\frac{(\phi_{1,t}-\phi_{0,t})b_{0,t}}{|z|^{1+p}}dz\,d\sigma \end{equation} (with $e^{-\eta z^2}$ inserted throughout), and \begin{equation} |\partial_y^j(I_1-I_0)|\le C\delta BY^{-j}\Lambda^{p-K}+C\delta BY^{-j-1}\Lambda^{p-K-1}\le 2C\delta AY^{-N-j}\Lambda^{p-N}. \end{equation}
nodes.proof_html: Telescoping the products defining $b_{\nu,t}$: each difference of factors gains $\delta$, since $|\Theta'_{1,y}(tz)-\Theta'_{0,y}(tz)|\le C\delta Y^{-2}t|z|\le C\delta\Lambda Y^{-1}t|z|$ (as $Y^{-2}\le\Lambda Y^{-1}$ by $Y\Lambda\ge1$) and $|\Theta^{(k)}_{1,y}-\Theta^{(k)}_{0,y}|\le C\delta Y^{-k}\le C\delta\Lambda Y^{1-k}$. $\phi_{1,t}-\phi_{0,t}=(1-t)\Delta\Psi'(y)z+\Delta\Psi(y+tz)-\Delta\Psi(y)$ with $\Delta\Psi=\Psi_1-\Psi_0$; its size is $\le C\delta Y^{-1}|z|$. eqn:appendix_oscillatory_multiplier_difference_integrals: $e^{iu}-e^{iv}=i(u-v)\int_0^1e^{i((1-\sigma)v+\sigma u)}d\sigma$ and Fubini. Each interpolated phase $(1-\sigma)\phi_{0,t}+\sigma\phi_{1,t}$ satisfies eqn:appendix_oscillatory_multiplier_phase_derivative_bounds: its derivative is a convex combination of $\phi'_{0,t},\phi'_{1,t}\in[c_0^{-1}\Lambda,c_0\Lambda]$, and the inverse-derivative bounds follow by Fa\`a di Bruno as before. Apply lem:c03_ibp_homogeneous (and its $y$-differentiated version as in lem:c03_mult_summand): the first integral with $(\delta B,K)$, the second with $(\delta BY^{-1},K+1)$, giving eqn:appendix_oscillatory_multiplier_difference_summand; finally $Y^{-1}\Lambda^{-1}\le1$ and the last step of eqn:appendix_oscillatory_multiplier_remainder_summand.

nodes.title: Parameter integral representation of the multiplier remainder
nodes.statement_html: Fix $0<p<1$, $N\ge1$, and $j\in\N$. There is an integer $k_0=k_0(p,N,j)$ such that phase data satisfying $\mathsf H$ through order $k_0$, with $Y,\Lambda\ge1$, $A>0$, $c_0>0$, have the following properties. Put $n=2N-1$. For $y\in[Y,2Y]$, \[ \mc R_{\rm mult,N}(y)=-c_p n\sum_{r+\sum lq_l=n}d_{r,q} \int_0^1(1-t)^{n-1}I_0(y,t)\,dt. \] The $t$ integrals converge absolutely; their value at the single point $t=0$ is immaterial. The remainder is $C^j$ on $(Y/2,3Y)$ and its derivatives through order $j$ are the same finite sums with the corresponding $y$ derivatives of $I_0$ under the $t$ integral. The sufficient finite order $k_0$ is chosen before the symbol constants, amplitude and phase. If the data satisfy such bounds at every finite order, this also gives smoothness.
nodes.proof_html: First insert $\eta>0$. Taylor's integral formula, the Gaussian factor and the near-zero vanishing give absolute double-integrability, so Fubini gives the parameter formula with $I_\eta$. The summand bound is uniform in $t\in(0,1]$ and $\eta\ge0$; for fixed $t>0$, compact-support dominated convergence removes $\eta$. Apply dominated convergence in $t$ and the regularized-limit identity. The all-order parameter bounds on a neighbourhood of $[Y,2Y]$ justify repeated differentiation in $y$ under the $t$ integral and show smoothness.

nodes.title: All-order remainder bounds and their difference estimate
nodes.statement_html: Fix $0<p<1$, $N\ge1$, $j\in\N$, $c_0>0$. There is an integer $k_0=k_0(p,N,j)$ such that for every finite nonnegative list $C_0,\ldots,C_{k_0}$ there is $C>0$, independent of $Y,\Lambda,A$ and of the data, with \[ |\partial_y^j\mc R_{\rm mult,N}(y)|\le CAY^{-N-j}\Lambda^{p-N} \] whenever $Y,\Lambda\ge1$, $A>0$, $\mathsf H$ holds through order $k_0$, and $y\in[Y,2Y]$. For two such data with difference bounds $|\partial^k(a_1-a_0)|\le C_k\delta AY^{-k}$ and $|\partial^k(\Psi_1-\Psi_0)|\le C_k\delta Y^{-k}$ on $(Y/4,4Y)$, $k\le k_0$, $\delta\ge0$, the same conclusion holds for their remainder difference with right-hand side $C\min\{1,\delta\}AY^{-N-j}\Lambda^{p-N}$, after enlarging $C$.
nodes.proof_html: Bound the finite sum and integrate $(1-t)^{2N-2}$, whose integral is $1/(2N-1)$. For $\delta\le1$ use the difference-integral bound with its factor $2$. For $\delta\ge1$ use the individual remainder estimates at the same derivative order $j$. This all-order individual statement is needed for that last argument even though the expansion theorem only requests individual bounds for $j=0,1$.

nodes.title: First three coefficients and the two-term remainder
nodes.statement_html: Under the multiplier phase hypotheses, for $y\in[Y,2Y]$, \[ B_0=\lambda^pa,\quad B_1=-ip\lambda^{p-1}a',\quad B_2=-\frac{p(p-1)}2\lambda^{p-2}(a''+i\lambda'a). \] For $j=0,1$ there is $C=C(p,c_0,C_0,\ldots,C_4)>0$, independent of $Y,\Lambda,A$, such that \[ \left|\partial_y^j\left(\frac{p(p-1)}2\lambda^{p-2}a''\right)\right| \le CAY^{-2-j}\Lambda^{p-2}. \]
nodes.proof_html: At $z=0$, $\Theta_y'=0$ and $\Theta_y''=\lambda'(y)$. Thus $F_y(0)=a$, $F_y'(0)=a'$, and $F_y''(0)=a''+i\lambda'a$. Substitute in the coefficient definition. The last bound is the product rule, $\lambda\asymp\Lambda$, $|\lambda'|\le C_1\Lambda/Y$, and the bounds for $a''$ and $a'''$.

nodes.title: Oscillatory multiplier expansion
nodes.statement_html: Let $0<p<1$, $A>0$, $Y,\Lambda\ge1$, $a\in C_c^\infty((Y/4,4Y);\C)$, $\Psi\in C^\infty((Y/4,4Y);\R)$, $\lambda=\Psi'$, and suppose that on $(Y/4,4Y)$, for all $k\ge0$, \[ c_0^{-1}\Lambda\le\lambda\le c_0\Lambda,\qquad|\partial_y^k\lambda|\le C_k\Lambda Y^{-k},\qquad|\partial_y^ka|\le C_kAY^{-k}. \] Let $m(\xi)=\xi^p$, $\Theta_y(z)=\Psi(y+z)-\Psi(y)-\lambda(y)z$. For $N\ge1$ and $Y\le y\le2Y$ define $\mc R_{\textup{mult},N}$ by \begin{equation} |D|^p(ae^{i\Psi})(y)=e^{i\Psi(y)}\Bigl[\sum_{k=0}^{2N-2}B_k(y)+\mc R_{\textup{mult},N}(y)\Bigr], \end{equation} \begin{equation} B_k(y)=\frac{(-i)^k}{k!}m^{(k)}(\lambda(y))\,\partial_z^k\bigl[a(y+z)e^{i\Theta_y(z)}\bigr]\big|_{z=0}. \end{equation} Then there is $C=C(p,N,j,c_0,(C_k)_{k\le k_0(N,j)})$ such that for $j=0,1$ and $Y\le y\le2Y$: \begin{equation} |\partial_y^j\mc R_{\textup{mult},N}(y)|\le CAY^{-N-j}\Lambda^{p-N}. \end{equation} In particular \begin{equation} |D|^p(ae^{i\Psi})=e^{i\Psi}\Bigl[\lambda^pa-ip\lambda^{p-1}a'-\frac{ip(p-1)}2\lambda^{p-2}\lambda'a+\sq{\mc R}_{\textup{mult},2}\Bigr], \end{equation} with $\sq{\mc R}_{\textup{mult},2}=\mc R_{\textup{mult},2}-\frac{p(p-1)}2\lambda^{p-2}a''$ and $|\partial_y^j\sq{\mc R}_{\textup{mult},2}|\le CAY^{-2-j}\Lambda^{p-2}$, $j=0,1$. Moreover, if $(a_\nu,\Psi_\nu)$, $\nu=0,1$, satisfy these hypotheses with the same $Y,\Lambda,A,c_0,C_k$ and, for some $\delta\ge0$, $|\partial^k(a_1-a_0)|\le C_k\delta AY^{-k}$, $|\partial^k(\Psi_1-\Psi_0)|\le C_k\delta Y^{-k}$ ($k\ge0$) on $(Y/4,4Y)$, then for every $j\ge0$ \begin{equation} |\partial_y^j(\mc R_{\textup{mult},N,1}-\mc R_{\textup{mult},N,0})(y)|\le C\min\{1,\delta\}AY^{-N-j}\Lambda^{p-N},\qquad Y\le y\le2Y . \end{equation}
nodes.proof_html: Step 1. By lem:c03_mult_expansion, $\mc R_{\textup{mult},N}(y)=-c_p\lim_{\eta\downarrow0}\int e^{i\lambda z-\eta z^2}R_{2N-1}(z)|z|^{-1-p}dz$. Insert eqn:appendix_oscillatory_multiplier_taylor_remainder; for fixed $\eta>0$ Fubini in $(z,t)$ is justified since the $t$-integrand in the Taylor remainder is bounded by $\|F_y^{(2N-1)}\|_{L^\infty}|z|^{2N-1}$, and $|z|^{2N-2-p}e^{-\eta z^2}\in L^1$. Note $e^{i\lambda z}e^{i\Theta_y(tz)}=e^{i\phi_t(z)}$. So $\mc R_{\textup{mult},N}$ is a finite sum of $c\int_0^1(1-t)^{2N-2}I_\eta(y,t)dt$ with $I_\eta$ as in lem:c03_mult_summand; $|I_\eta(y,t)|\le CAY^{-N}\Lambda^{p-N}$ uniformly in $\eta,t$ and $I_\eta(y,t)\to I_0(y,t)$, so by dominated convergence the bound passes to $\mc R_{\textup{mult},N}$. The $y$-derivative ($j=1$) is handled identically using the $y$-differentiated bounds of lem:c03_mult_summand (differentiate under the $t$-integral for $\eta>0$; the $\eta\to0$ limit of the derivatives is locally uniform in $y$, so it equals the derivative of the limit). Step 2 (two-term form). With $N=2$, $\Theta'_y(0)=0$, $\Theta''_y(0)=\lambda'(y)$: $B_0=\lambda^pa$, $B_1=-ip\lambda^{p-1}a'$, $B_2=-\frac{p(p-1)}2\lambda^{p-2}(a''+i\lambda'a)$. And $|\partial_y^j(\lambda^{p-2}a'')|\le CAY^{-2-j}\Lambda^{p-2}$. Step 3 (differences). For $\delta\le1$ sum lem:c03_mult_difference over summands and integrate in $t$ (same limiting argument). For $\delta>1$ use the triangle inequality and Step 1 for each $\nu$ (for all $j$, by the any-$j$ version of lem:c03_mult_summand).

nodes.title: Differentiating the fractional integral
nodes.statement_html: Let $g\in C^2(\R;\C)$ with $g,g'$ bounded and $g''$ locally bounded. Then $|D|^pg\in C^1(\R)$ and $(|D|^pg)'=|D|^p(g')$ pointwise.
nodes.proof_html: Write $|D|^pg(y)=c_\alpha\int_\R(g(y)-g(y-h))|h|^{-\alpha}dh$. For $|y|\le Y_1$ the $y$-derivative of the integrand is $(g'(y)-g'(y-h))|h|^{-\alpha}$, bounded by $\sup_{|w|\le Y_1+1}|g''|\,|h|^{1-\alpha}\mathbf 1_{|h|\le1}+2\|g'\|_\infty|h|^{-\alpha}\mathbf 1_{|h|>1}$, which is integrable ($1-\alpha=-p>-1$, $\alpha>1$) and independent of $y$. Dominated differentiation (Mathlib hasDerivAt\_integral\_of\_dominated\_loc\_of\_deriv\_le) gives the derivative; continuity of $|D|^pg'$ follows from lem:c01_frac_well_defined and dominated convergence with the same majorant.

nodes.title: Weak Fourier computation of $\mc L_0$ and of $|D|^p-y$
nodes.statement_html:
• Let $m\in C^1(\R;\C)\cap L^1(\R)$ vanish on a neighbourhood of $0$, with $|m(\xi)|+|m'(\xi)|\le K\ang\xi^{N}$ for some $K,N$, and put $n:=\xi m'+(2+i\xi|\xi|^p)m$. Assume $n\in L^1(\R)$ and that $g:=\widecheck m$ is $C^2$ with $g,g'$ bounded and $|g''(y)|\le K\ang y^N$. Then $\mc L_0g=\widecheck n$ pointwise on $\R$.
  • Let $m\in C^1_c(\R;\C)$ and suppose $g:=\widecheck m$ is $C^1$ with $g$ bounded and $|g'(y)|\le K\ang y^N$. Then $|D|^pg(y)-yg(y)=\widecheck{n_b}(y)$ for all $y$, where $n_b:=|\xi|^pm-im'$.
nodes.proof_html:
Both sides are continuous in each case ($|D|^pg'$, $|D|^pg$ by lem:c01_frac_duality; $\widecheck n$, $\widecheck{n_b}$ since $n,n_b\in L^1$), so it suffices to show $\int(\text{LHS})\varphi=\int(\text{RHS})\varphi$ for all $\varphi\in\mathcal S(\R)$ (fundamental lemma; Mathlib ae\_eq\_zero\_of\_integral\_contDiff\_smul\_eq\_zero plus continuity). Write $\Phi(\xi):=\widehat\varphi(-\xi)$. For $\psi\in L^1$, Fubini ($m\in L^1$) gives $\int g\psi\,dy=\frac1{2\pi}\int m(\xi)\widehat\psi(-\xi)\,d\xi$.

(1) By lem:c01_frac_duality applied to $g'$ (bounded, $g''$ polynomially bounded), $\int(|D|^pg')\varphi=\int g'|D|^p\varphi=-\int g\,(|D|^p\varphi)'$; the boundary terms vanish because $g$ is bounded and $|D|^p\varphi$ decays like $\ang y^{-\alpha}$; moreover $(|D|^p\varphi)'=|D|^p\varphi'$ is $(i\xi|\xi|^p\widehat\varphi)^\vee$ by lem:c01_frac_singular_integral, an $L^1$ function with $L^1$ Fourier transform. Also $\int yg'\varphi=-\int g(\varphi+y\varphi')$ (boundary terms vanish, $g$ bounded, $\varphi$ Schwartz). Hence $\int(\mc L_0g)\varphi=\int g\psi$ with $\psi=-|D|^p\varphi'+2\varphi+y\varphi'$, and $\widehat\psi(\eta)=(1-i\eta|\eta|^p)\widehat\varphi(\eta)-\eta\widehat\varphi'(\eta)$ (using $\widehat{y\varphi'}=i\p_\eta(i\eta\widehat\varphi)=-\widehat\varphi-\eta\widehat\varphi'$ and Fourier inversion for $|D|^p\varphi'$). At $\eta=-\xi$: $\widehat\psi(-\xi)=(1+i\xi|\xi|^p)\Phi(\xi)-\xi\Phi'(\xi)$. Integrating by parts on $(-\infty,0)$ and $(0,\infty)$ separately, $-\int m\xi\Phi'=\int(\xi m)'\Phi$: the boundary terms vanish at $0$ ($m=0$ near $0$) and at $\pm\infty$ ($\xi m\Phi\to0$ since $m$ has polynomial growth and $\Phi$ is Schwartz). Thus $\int(\mc L_0g)\varphi=\frac1{2\pi}\int n(\xi)\Phi(\xi)d\xi=\int\widecheck n\,\varphi$ (Fubini, $n\in L^1$).

(2) By lem:c01_frac_duality, $\int(|D|^pg)\varphi=\int g|D|^p\varphi=\frac1{2\pi}\int m|\xi|^p\Phi\,d\xi$ (since $\widehat{|D|^p\varphi}=|\eta|^p\widehat\varphi$, an even weight). Also $\widehat{y\varphi}(\eta)=i\widehat\varphi'(\eta)$, so $\widehat{y\varphi}(-\xi)=-i\Phi'(\xi)$ and $\int yg\varphi=\frac1{2\pi}\int m(-i\Phi')=\frac1{2\pi}\int im'\Phi$ (no boundary terms: $m$ has compact support). Subtract.

nodes.title: A Dirichlet-type integral
nodes.statement_html: For every $y\in\R$, $\int_0^\infty\frac{1-\cos(y\xi)}{\xi^2}d\xi=\frac\pi2|y|$ (absolutely convergent). Consequently $W(y)=-\frac y2+\frac1\pi\int_0^\infty\frac{1-\cos(y\xi)}{\xi^2}d\xi$.

nodes.title: Oscillatory integrals with the dispersive phase
nodes.statement_html: For $m\in\R$ let $S^m_+$ be the set of $a\in C^\infty(\R;\C)$ with $a=0$ on $(-\infty,1]$ and $|\p^l_\xi a(\xi)|\le C_l\xi^{m-l}$ for $\xi\ge1$, $l\ge0$. Fix $\rho\in C^\infty_c(\R;[0,1])$ with $\rho=1$ on $[-1,1]$ and $\operatorname{supp}\rho\subset[-2,2]$. For $a\in S^m_+$ and $y\in\R$ set \[ \operatorname{Osc}[a](y):=\lim_{M\to\infty}\int_0^\infty\rho(\xi/M)\,a(\xi)\,e^{i(y\xi-\Phi_0(\xi))}\,d\xi . \]

nodes.title: Symbol bounds under truncation and multiplication by frequency
nodes.statement_html: Let $m\in\R$, $a\in S^m_+$, and let nonnegative numbers $C_l$ satisfy $|a^{(l)}(\xi)|\le C_l\xi^{m-l}$ for $\xi\ge1$ and $l\in\N$. For every $j\in\N$, $a_j(\xi):=(i\xi)^ja(\xi)$ belongs to $S^{m+j}_+$; for each $l$, its symbol constant depends only on $j,l,m,C_0,\ldots,C_l$. Let $\rho$ be any truncation of def:c04_osc_integral. For $M\ge1$ put $a_M(\xi)=\rho(\xi/M)a(\xi)$. Then $a_M\in C_c^\infty(\R;\C)$, $a_M=0$ on $(-\infty,1]$, and for each $l\in\N$ there is $B_l=B_l(m,\rho,C_0,\ldots,C_l)>0$, independent of $M$, such that \[ |a_M^{(l)}(\xi)|\le B_l\xi^{m-l}\qquad(\xi\ge1). \] Also $a_M^{(l)}(\xi)=a^{(l)}(\xi)$ for $0<\xi<M$. If $L\ge1$ and $\theta\in C_c^\infty(\R;[0,1])$ equals $1$ on $[0,L]$ and vanishes for $\xi\ge2L$, the same conclusions, with vanishing on $(-\infty,L]$, hold for $b_M=\rho(\cdot/M)(1-\theta)a$ and $b_\infty=(1-\theta)a$, except that compact support is asserted only for $b_M$. Their constants may additionally depend on $L$ and finitely many derivatives of $\theta$.
nodes.proof_html:
Expand every derivative by the finite Leibniz formula. On the support of a derivative
  of $\rho(\xi/M)$, $\xi\le2M$, hence $M^{-r}\le2^r\xi^{-r}$.
  Derivatives of $\theta$ are supported in a fixed compact interval bounded away from zero.
  For $(i\xi)^j$, use its explicit polynomial derivatives. Flatness at the endpoints of
  the constant regions gives smoothness and the asserted equality for $\xi<M$.
  Keep the finite sums of products of derivative bounds explicit; no constant may depend on $M$.

nodes.title: Reciprocal derivatives of the nonstationary phase
nodes.statement_html: Let $0<p<1$ and $\phi_y(\xi)=y\xi-\xi^{p+1}/(p+1)$ for $\xi>0$. For every $l\in\N$ there is $D_l=D_l(p)>0$ with the following properties. If $Y\ge1$, $|y|\le Y$, and $\xi\ge(2Y)^{1/p}+2$, then \[ |\phi_y'(\xi)|\ge\tfrac12\xi^p,\qquad \left|\p_\xi^l\frac1{y-\xi^p}\right|\le D_l\xi^{-p-l}. \] If $y\le-1$ and $\xi\ge1$, then \[ |\phi_y'(\xi)|=|y|+\xi^p,\qquad \left|\p_\xi^l\frac1{y-\xi^p}\right| \le D_l(|y|+\xi^p)^{-1}\xi^{-l} \le D_l|y|^{-1}\xi^{-l}. \] The reciprocal is smooth on each of these nonstationary regions.
nodes.proof_html:
Use $\p_\xi^r\xi^p=p(p-1)\cdots(p-r+1)\xi^{p-r}$.
  Inductively differentiate $(y-\xi^p)q_y=1$ to express $q_y^{(l)}$ through lower
  derivatives and one additional factor $(y-\xi^p)^{-1}$. In the first region use
  $|y-\xi^p|\ge\xi^p/2$; in the second use
  $\xi^p/(|y|+\xi^p)\le1$. This proves the bounds with $D_l$ depending only on $p,l$.

nodes.title: One integration-by-parts step: flat extension and symbol bound
nodes.statement_html: Let $L\ge1$, $m,\sigma\in\R$, $A,H>0$, $b\in C^\infty(\R;\C)$ with $b=0$ on $(-\infty,L]$, and $q\in C^\infty((L/2,\infty);\R)$. Set $T_qb=-\p_\xi(bq/i)$ on $(L,\infty)$ and $T_qb=0$ on $(-\infty,L]$. Then $T_qb\in C^\infty(\R;\C)$, every derivative of $T_qb$ vanishes on $(-\infty,L]$, and $\operatorname{supp}T_qb\subset\operatorname{supp}b$. For every $k\in\N$ and $\xi\ge L$, \[ \p_\xi^kT_qb(\xi) =i\sum_{r=0}^{k+1}\binom{k+1}{r}b^{(r)}(\xi)q^{(k+1-r)}(\xi). \] If nonnegative numbers $B_0,\ldots,B_{k+1}$ and $D_0,\ldots,D_{k+1}$ satisfy \[ |b^{(r)}(\xi)|\le B_rA\xi^{m-r},\qquad |q^{(r)}(\xi)|\le D_rH\xi^{-\sigma-r} \quad(\xi\ge L,\ 0\le r\le k+1), \] then \[ |\p_\xi^kT_qb(\xi)|\le \left(\sum_{r=0}^{k+1}\binom{k+1}{r}B_rD_{k+1-r}\right) AH\xi^{m-1-\sigma-k}\qquad(\xi\ge L). \] Thus this one-step constant involves only the displayed finite lists and $k$, and is independent of $L,A,H,b,q$ once those bounds are fixed.
nodes.proof_html:
Glue $bq$ on $(L/2,\infty)$ to zero on $(-\infty,L)$; the two definitions agree
  on their overlap because $b$ vanishes there. The resulting global function is smooth.
  Since all derivatives of $b$ vanish at $L$, its derivative multiplied by $i=-1/i$
  equals the stated zero extension $T_qb$, including at $L$.
  Differentiation and multiplication do not enlarge the closed support of $b$.
  Apply the ordinary finite Leibniz formula at order $k+1$.
  Each product of bounds has exponent
  $(m-r)+(-\sigma-(k+1-r))=m-1-\sigma-k$; summing gives the explicit constant.

nodes.title: Iterated symbol bounds from a finite recurrence
nodes.statement_html: Let $L,m,\sigma,A,H,b,q$ satisfy the regularity and support hypotheses of lem:c04_osc_ibp_step, and let nonnegative sequences $(B_r),(D_r)$ satisfy its derivative bounds for every $r\in\N$. Define nonnegative coefficients by the finite recurrence \[ E_{0,k}=B_k,\qquad E_{n+1,k}=\sum_{r=0}^{k+1}\binom{k+1}{r}E_{n,r}D_{k+1-r}. \] For all $N,k\in\N$, $T_q^Nb$ is smooth, vanishes on $(-\infty,L]$, has support contained in $\operatorname{supp}b$, and \[ |\p_\xi^kT_q^Nb(\xi)| \le E_{N,k}AH^N\xi^{m-N(1+\sigma)-k}\qquad(\xi\ge L). \] The coefficient $E_{N,k}$ depends only on $N,k$ and $B_0,\ldots,B_{N+k},D_0,\ldots,D_{N+k}$. If $d:=m-N(1+\sigma)<-1$, then $T_q^Nb\in L^1((0,\infty))$ and \[ \int_0^\infty|T_q^Nb(\xi)|d\xi \le E_{N,0}AH^N\frac{L^{d+1}}{-d-1}. \] No compact-support hypothesis is imposed on $b$ in this lemma.
nodes.proof_html: Induct on $N$, simultaneously for all derivative orders $k$. At step $N+1$ apply the one-step lemma with symbol order $m-N(1+\sigma)$, amplitude scale $AH^N$, and derivative constants $E_{N,r}$. The resulting finite Leibniz sum is exactly the recurrence for $E_{N+1,k}$. The same induction proves smoothness, zero extension, support preservation, nonnegativity of the coefficients, and their dependence on the stated finite lists. For the last assertion, the function vanishes below $L$ and is dominated above $L$ by $E_{N,0}AH^N\xi^d$; integrate that power using $d<-1$.

nodes.title: Repeated integration by parts with quantified symbol loss
nodes.statement_html: Let $L\ge1$, $m,\sigma\in\R$, and $A,H>0$. Let $b\in C^\infty(\R;\C)$ vanish on $(-\infty,L]$, and let $q\in C^\infty((L/2,\infty);\R)$ satisfy, for every $r\in\N$ and $\xi\ge L$, \[ |b^{(r)}(\xi)|\le B_r A\xi^{m-r},\qquad |q^{(r)}(\xi)|\le D_r H\xi^{-\sigma-r}, \] where $B_r,D_r\ge0$ are fixed. Define $T_qb=-\p_\xi(bq/i)$ on $(L,\infty)$, extended by zero to $(-\infty,L]$, and iterate this operator. Every $T_q^Nb$ is smooth and vanishes on $(-\infty,L]$. For all $N,k\in\N$ there is $C_{N,k}>0$, depending only on $N,k,m,\sigma$ and $B_0,\ldots,B_{N+k},D_0,\ldots,D_{N+k}$, such that \[ |\p_\xi^kT_q^Nb(\xi)| \le C_{N,k} A H^N\xi^{m-N(1+\sigma)-k}\qquad(\xi\ge L). \] Suppose in addition that $b$ has compact support, $\phi\in C^\infty((0,\infty);\R)$, and $q(\xi)\phi'(\xi)=1$ for $\xi>L$. Then all the following integrals converge absolutely and \[ \int_0^\infty b(\xi)e^{i\phi(\xi)}d\xi =\int_0^\infty T_q^Nb(\xi)e^{i\phi(\xi)}d\xi\qquad(N\in\N). \] Compact support of $b$ is not needed for the symbol bound; if $m-N(1+\sigma)<-1$, that bound makes $T_q^Nb$ integrable on $(0,\infty)$.
nodes.proof_html: Smoothness, support preservation, the symbol estimate, and the integrability assertion are lem:c04_osc_ibp_iteration; take $C_{N,k}=1+E_{N,k}$ to obtain a positive constant. For the compact-support integral identity, continuity extends $q\phi'=1$ from $(L,\infty)$ to $L$, so $\phi'(L)\ne0$. Consequently the compact support of $b$ is contained in the nonstationary open set $U=(L/2,\infty)\cap\{\xi:\phi'(\xi)\ne0\}$, even when that support contains $L$. Integrate by parts $N$ times on $U$ (compactly supported amplitudes, no boundary terms), with the operator $L_\phi a=(a/(i\phi'))'$, which has the opposite sign of ours. On $(L,\infty)$, $q=1/\phi'$; below $L$, all derivatives of $b$ and of its iterates vanish by lem:c04_osc_ibp_step. Thus $T_q^Nb=(-1)^NL_\phi^Nb$ by induction. The factor $(-1)^N$ in the generic integration-by-parts identity cancels this sign. Finally, all amplitudes vanish outside $(0,\infty)$, so its whole-line integrals equal the half-line integrals displayed here. Lean route: the identity is proved by direct interval integration by parts, without the generic compact-support iteration lemma of the analysis chapter.

nodes.title: Locally uniform cutoff limit and independence of truncation
nodes.statement_html: Let $a\in S^m_+$ and, for an admissible truncation $\rho$, write $F_M^\rho(a;y)=\int_0^\infty\rho(\xi/M)a(\xi)e^{i\phi_y(\xi)}d\xi$ for $M>0$. These integrals converge absolutely. There is a continuous function $F:\R\to\C$ such that $F_M^\rho(a;\cdot)\to F$ locally uniformly as $M\to\infty$ for every admissible $\rho$, with the same $F$ for all $\rho$. Thus $F=\operatorname{Osc}[a]$ for the fixed truncation of def:c04_osc_integral. More precisely, fix $Y\ge1$, $L\ge(2Y)^{1/p}+2$, and a cutoff $\theta$ as in lem:c04_osc_cutoff_symbols. Put $b_\infty=(1-\theta)a$ and $q_y(\xi)=(y-\xi^p)^{-1}$ on $(L/2,\infty)$; this interval is nonstationary because $p<1$ and $L/2>Y^{1/p}$. If $N\in\N$ and $m-N(1+p)<-1$, then for $|y|\le Y$, \[ F(y)=\int_0^\infty\theta a e^{i\phi_y}d\xi+ \int_0^\infty T_{q_y}^Nb_\infty e^{i\phi_y}d\xi, \] with both integrals absolutely convergent. For each fixed $\rho$ there is $C=C(p,m,N,Y,L,\theta,\rho,C_0,\ldots,C_N)>0$ such that \[ \sup_{|y|\le Y}|F_M^\rho(a;y)-F(y)| \le C M^{m-N(1+p)+1}\qquad(M\ge2L). \]
nodes.proof_html: The compact part $\theta a$ is unaffected by $\rho(\xi/M)$ once $M\ge2L$. Apply the integration-by-parts lemma with $\sigma=p$, $A=H=1$ to $b_M=\rho(\cdot/M)b_\infty$. Its $N$-fold transform equals that of $b_\infty$ on $(0,M)$. Bound the difference on $(M,\infty)$ by $2C\xi^{m-N(1+p)}$ and integrate this explicit power. This proves the displayed error and a common limit independent of $\rho$. The same formula gives consistency on overlapping compact intervals. Each $F_M^\rho$ is continuous by compact-support dominated convergence, hence the limit is continuous.

nodes.title: Agreement with Lebesgue and improper integrals
nodes.statement_html: Let $a\in S^m_+$. If $a\in L^1((0,\infty))$, then for every $y\in\R$ the function $\xi\mapsto a(\xi)e^{i\phi_y(\xi)}$ is integrable and \[ \operatorname{Osc}[a](y)=\int_0^\infty a(\xi)e^{i\phi_y(\xi)}d\xi. \] If $m<p$, then for every $y\in\R$, \[ \lim_{M\to\infty}\int_0^M a(\xi)e^{i\phi_y(\xi)}d\xi=\operatorname{Osc}[a](y). \] The second assertion does not claim absolute convergence of the untruncated integral.
nodes.proof_html: For the first assertion use $|\rho(\xi/M)ae^{i\phi_y}|\le|a|$ and dominated convergence. For the second choose a fixed large $L$ beyond the stationary point and use the compact/tail splitting from lem:c04_osc_cutoff_limit with one integration by parts. The boundary term at $M$ is bounded by $CM^{m-p}$ and tends to zero. The transformed tail has bound $C\xi^{m-p-1}$, which is integrable because $m<p$. The resulting limit is the same absolutely convergent representation as the cutoff limit.

nodes.title: Differentiating the cutoff integrals and their limit
nodes.statement_html: Let $a\in S^m_+$ and let $F_M^\rho(a;y)$ have the meaning of lem:c04_osc_cutoff_limit. For every $M>0$, every $j\in\N$, and every $y\in\R$, its differentiated integrand is absolutely integrable, $F_M^\rho(a;\cdot)$ is smooth, and \[ \p_y^jF_M^\rho(a;y)=F_M^\rho((i\xi)^ja;y). \] The function $\operatorname{Osc}[a]$ is smooth on $\R$, and for all $j\in\N$, \[ \p_y^j\operatorname{Osc}[a]=\operatorname{Osc}[(i\xi)^ja]. \] In particular $i\xi a\in S^{m+1}_+$ and $\p_y\operatorname{Osc}[a]=\operatorname{Osc}[i\xi a]$.
nodes.proof_html: For fixed $M$, all $\xi$-moments of $\rho(\xi/M)a(\xi)$ have compact support, so dominated differentiation gives the displayed derivative at every order. The symbol-closure lemma permits applying locally uniform convergence to both $(i\xi)^ja$ and $(i\xi)^{j+1}a$. Use the theorem that locally uniform limits of differentiable functions and of their derivatives preserve the derivative, first for $j=0$ and then inductively. Continuity of every limit supplied by lem:c04_osc_cutoff_limit yields $C^\infty$ regularity.

nodes.title: Rapid decay of the oscillatory integral on the negative half-line
nodes.statement_html: Let $a\in S^m_+$ with symbol constants $C_l$. For every real $N\ge0$ there are $K\in\N$ and $C=C(p,m,N,\rho,C_0,\ldots,C_K)>0$ such that \[ |F_M^\rho(a;y)|\le C|y|^{-N}\quad(M\ge1,\ y\le-1),\qquad |\operatorname{Osc}[a](y)|\le C|y|^{-N}\quad(y\le-1). \] One may choose any integer $K\ge N$ with $K>m+1$.
nodes.proof_html: Here no stationary point or auxiliary tail cutoff is needed. Apply the transfer lemma with $L=1$, $\sigma=0$, $A=1$, $H=|y|^{-1}$, and $b=\rho(\cdot/M)a$. The reciprocal-phase lemma supplies derivative constants independent of $y\le-1$. After $K$ integrations by parts the absolute value of the integrand is bounded by $C|y|^{-K}\xi^{m-K}$ on $[1,\infty)$, uniformly in $M$. Integrate this power, use $|y|^{-K}\le|y|^{-N}$, and pass to the cutoff limit.

nodes.title: Properties of $\operatorname{Osc}$
nodes.statement_html:
Let $a\in S^m_+$.
  • The limit defining $\operatorname{Osc}[a](y)$ exists, locally uniformly in $y\in\R$, and does not depend on $\rho$. If $a\in L^1$ it equals the Lebesgue integral $\int_0^\infty ae^{i(y\xi-\Phi_0)}d\xi$; if $m<p$ it equals the improper Riemann integral $\lim_{M\to\infty}\int_0^M ae^{i(y\xi-\Phi_0)}d\xi$.
  • $\operatorname{Osc}[a]\in C^\infty(\R)$ and $\p_y\operatorname{Osc}[a]=\operatorname{Osc}[i\xi a]$ (note $i\xi a\in S^{m+1}_+$).
  • For all $N\ge0$ there is $C$ (depending on $N,m,p$ and finitely many $C_l$) with $|\operatorname{Osc}[a](y)|\le C|y|^{-N}$ for $y\le-1$.
nodes.proof_html: The locally uniform limit and independence of the truncation are exactly lem:c04_osc_cutoff_limit. Its compatibility with the two ordinary integration conventions is lem:c04_osc_ordinary_integrals. The frequency-shift and differentiation statements follow from lem:c04_osc_parameter_derivatives. The negative-half-line estimate is lem:c04_osc_negative_tail. Their proofs isolate the cutoff, reciprocal-phase, and repeated-integration-by-parts interfaces needed for these conclusions.

nodes.title: The constant $\mu_*$
nodes.statement_html: $\mu_*:=-\dfrac{i}{\sqrt{2\pi p}}\in\C\setminus\{0\}$.

nodes.title: Linear seed and its pieces
nodes.statement_html: For $y\in\R$ define \begin{equation} f_0(y)=-\frac y2+\frac1\pi\int_0^\infty\frac{1-\cos(y\xi-\Phi_0(\xi))}{\xi^2}\,d\xi, \qquad f_{0,+}(y)=-\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^\infty\frac{\chi_+(\xi)}{\xi^2}e^{i(y\xi-\Phi_0(\xi))}\,d\xi, \end{equation} $f_{0,\textup{high}}:=2\operatorname{Re}f_{0,+}$, $f_{0,\textup{low}}:=f_0-f_{0,\textup{high}}$, and $\Gamma_+(y):=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^\infty\frac{\chi_+'(\xi)}{\xi}e^{i(y\xi-\Phi_0(\xi))}d\xi$ (a Schwartz function, the integrand being smooth with compact support in $[1,2]$). For $y>0$ let \[ \lambda_0(y)=y^{1/p},\qquad \Psi_0(y)=\frac p{p+1}y^{1+1/p},\qquad a_*(y)=\frac{e^{-i(\Psi_0(y)-\pi/4)}}{\mu_*\lambda_0(y)^{-(p+1)/2}}\,f_{0,+}'(y), \] so that, identically for $y>0$, $f_{0,+}'(y)=\mu_*\lambda_0(y)^{-(p+1)/2}a_*(y)e^{i(\Psi_0(y)-\pi/4)}$ (note $\lambda_0^{-(p+1)/2}=y^{-\beta}$, $\Psi_0'=\lambda_0$). Finally for $\mu\in\C$ put \begin{equation} f_{0,\mu}=f_0+2\operatorname{Re}\Bigl[\Bigl(\frac\mu{\mu_*}-1\Bigr)f_{0,+}\Bigr]. \end{equation}

nodes.title: Absolute convergence and the high-frequency seed symbol
nodes.statement_html: Let $\frac34<p<1$. For every $y\in\R$, both integrands \[ \xi\longmapsto\frac{1-\cos(y\xi-\Phi_0(\xi))}{\xi^2},\qquad \xi\longmapsto\frac{\chi_+(\xi)}{\xi^2}e^{i(y\xi-\Phi_0(\xi))} \] belong to $L^1((0,\infty))$. The function $a_{-2}(\xi)=\chi_+(\xi)/\xi^2$, extended by zero for $\xi\le0$, belongs to $L^1(\R)\cap S^{-2}_+$. For each $l\in\N$ there is $C_l=C_l(l,\chi_+)>0$ with $|a_{-2}^{(l)}(\xi)|\le C_l\xi^{-2-l}$ for $\xi\ge1$. For every $Y\ge1$, the first integrand is dominated uniformly in $|y|\le Y$ by \[ \tfrac12(Y+1)^2\mathbf1_{(0,1]}(\xi)+2\xi^{-2}\mathbf1_{(1,\infty)}(\xi), \] and the absolute value of the second is dominated by $\xi^{-2}\mathbf1_{(1,\infty)}(\xi)$.
nodes.proof_html:
Use $0\le1-\cos u\le u^2/2$ and
  $|y\xi-\Phi_0(\xi)|\le(Y+1)\xi$ on $(0,1]$; outside that interval use
  $|1-\cos u|\le2$. The high-frequency cutoff removes the origin and the
  exponential has modulus one. On $[2,\infty)$ the derivatives of $a_{-2}$ are
  explicit derivatives of $\xi^{-2}$. On $[1,2]$, compactness bounds each derivative.
  Near $\xi=1$ and on $(-\infty,1]$, the cutoff is flat, which justifies the zero extension.

nodes.title: Oscillatory representation and regularity of the positive seed
nodes.statement_html: For $\frac34<p<1$, write $a_{-2}(\xi)=\chi_+(\xi)/\xi^2$, extended by zero for $\xi\le0$. Then $f_{0,+}\in C^\infty(\R;\C)$, and for all $j\in\N$ and $y\in\R$, \[ f_{0,+}(y)=-\frac1{2\pi}\operatorname{Osc}[a_{-2}](y),\qquad \p_y^jf_{0,+}(y)=-\frac1{2\pi}\operatorname{Osc}[(i\xi)^ja_{-2}](y). \] Furthermore $f_{0,+}(y)\to0$ as $|y|\to\infty$ (equivalently, along the cocompact filter on $\R$).
nodes.proof_html: The first equality uses the absolutely convergent case of the oscillatory-integral compatibility lemma. Differentiate it using the all-order derivative formula. For decay, the function $\mathbf1_{\xi>0}a_{-2}(\xi)e^{-i\Phi_0(\xi)}$ is in $L^1(\R)$; apply the Riemann--Lebesgue lemma to its inverse Fourier transform with the fixed $1/(2\pi)$ normalization. No differentiation of an untruncated, nonabsolute integral is needed.

nodes.title: An absolutely convergent representation of the low-frequency seed
nodes.statement_html: Let $\frac34<p<1$ and \[ H_0(y,\xi)=\frac{\operatorname{Re}[1-(1-\chi_+(\xi))e^{i(y\xi-\Phi_0(\xi))}]}{\xi^2} \qquad(\xi>0). \] For every $y\in\R$, $H_0(y,\cdot)\in L^1((0,\infty))$, and \[ f_{0,\textup{low}}(y)=-\frac y2+\frac1\pi\int_0^\infty H_0(y,\xi)d\xi, \qquad f_0(y)=f_{0,\textup{low}}(y)+2\operatorname{Re}f_{0,+}(y). \] For every $Y\ge1$ there is an integrable function $B_Y:(0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$, depending only on $p,Y,\chi_+$, with $|H_0(y,\xi)|\le B_Y(\xi)$ for $|y|\le Y$.
nodes.proof_html: Write the numerator as $1-\cos(y\xi-\Phi_0(\xi))+\chi_+(\xi)\cos(y\xi-\Phi_0(\xi))$. The previous lemma bounds both resulting integrands and their sum uniformly on compact $y$-intervals. Split the absolutely convergent integral and use $f_{0,\textup{low}}=f_0-2\operatorname{Re}f_{0,+}$.

nodes.title: Derivative formulas for the low-frequency seed
nodes.statement_html: For $\frac34<p<1$, $f_{0,\textup{low}}\in C^\infty(\R)$ and \[ f_{0,\textup{low}}'(y)=-\frac12+ \frac1\pi\int_0^\infty(1-\chi_+(\xi))\frac{\sin(y\xi-\Phi_0(\xi))}{\xi}d\xi. \] For all integers $k\ge2$, \[ f_{0,\textup{low}}^{(k)}(y)=-\frac1\pi\int_0^\infty (1-\chi_+(\xi))\operatorname{Re}[(i\xi)^ke^{i(y\xi-\Phi_0(\xi))}]\xi^{-2}d\xi. \] Every displayed integrand belongs to $L^1((0,\infty))$ for every $y$. The first is dominated uniformly in $|y|\le Y$ by $(Y+\xi^p)\mathbf1_{(0,2]}(\xi)$; the $k$th one, $k\ge2$, by $\xi^{k-2}\mathbf1_{(0,2]}(\xi)$. In particular, for every $k\ge2$ there is $C_k=C_k(k,\chi_+)>0$ with $|f_{0,\textup{low}}^{(k)}(y)|\le C_k$ for all $y\in\R$.
nodes.proof_html: Differentiate $H_0$ first on a fixed compact $y$-interval. Since $|\sin(y\xi-\Phi_0)|/\xi\le|y|+\xi^p$, its first derivative has the stated majorant. Every subsequent derivative is a compactly supported power moment; its majorant is integrable even at $\xi=0$ because $k-2\ge0$. Apply dominated differentiation successively, retaining continuity at each stage. Integrating the majorant for $k\ge2$ gives a bound independent of $y$.

nodes.title: Fourier symbol of the second low-frequency derivative
nodes.statement_html: For $\frac34<p<1$, define $m_{\textup{low}}(\xi)=(1-\chi_+(|\xi|))e^{-i\Phi_0(\xi)}$ on $\R$. Then $m_{\textup{low}}\in C^1_c(\R;\C)$, its support lies in $[-2,2]$, $m_{\textup{low}}(-\xi)=\overline{m_{\textup{low}}(\xi)}$, and \[ f_{0,\textup{low}}''(y)=\widecheck{m_{\textup{low}}}(y)\qquad(y\in\R). \] The inverse transform is absolutely convergent for every $y$, and is real-valued.
nodes.proof_html: The even cutoff is constant near zero and smooth away from zero; the phase is odd and $C^1$ with derivative $|\xi|^p$. Thus the symbol is $C^1$ and compactly supported. Use the $k=2$ formula from the preceding lemma. Split the whole-line inverse transform into its positive and negative halves, substitute $\xi\mapsto-\xi$ in the latter, and use Hermitian symmetry to obtain $\pi^{-1}$ times the real positive-half integral. The factor $(i\xi)^2=-\xi^2$ cancels the minus sign in that derivative formula.

nodes.title: Corner comparison as two absolutely convergent integrals
nodes.statement_html: Let $\frac34<p<1$ and, on $(0,\infty)$, put \[ b(\xi)=(1-\chi_+(\xi))\frac{1-e^{-i\Phi_0(\xi)}}{\xi^2},\qquad a_{-2}(\xi)=\frac{\chi_+(\xi)}{\xi^2}. \] Both $b$ and $a_{-2}$ are integrable on $(0,\infty)$, and $|b(\xi)|\le\xi^{p-1}\mathbf1_{(0,2]}(\xi)$. Define the absolutely convergent integrals \[ \mc I_1(y)=\frac1\pi\operatorname{Re}\int_0^\infty e^{iy\xi}b(\xi)d\xi, \qquad \mc I_2(y)=\frac1\pi\operatorname{Re}\int_0^\infty e^{iy\xi}a_{-2}(\xi)d\xi. \] Then $f_{0,\textup{low}}(y)-W(y)=\mc I_1(y)+\mc I_2(y)$ for every $y\in\R$.
nodes.proof_html: The bound $|1-e^{-it}|\le|t|$ gives the claimed bound for $b$ because $\Phi_0(\xi)=\xi^{p+1}/(p+1)$ on $\xi>0$ and $p>0$. Subtract the Dirichlet integral formula for $W$ from the low-frequency representation. All integrals involved are absolutely convergent. Use $e^{iy\xi}-(1-\chi_+)e^{iy\xi-i\Phi_0} =e^{iy\xi}[(1-\chi_+)(1-e^{-i\Phi_0})+\chi_+]$ and distribute the integral and real part.

nodes.title: Well-posedness and smoothness of the seed
nodes.statement_html:
• The integrals defining $f_0$ and $f_{0,+}$ converge absolutely for every $y$; $f_{0,+}=-\frac1{2\pi}\operatorname{Osc}[\chi_+\xi^{-2}]$ is $C^\infty$ with $\p_y^jf_{0,+}=-\frac1{2\pi}\operatorname{Osc}[(i\xi)^j\chi_+\xi^{-2}]$, and $f_{0,+}(y)\to0$ as $|y|\to\infty$.
  • $f_{0,\textup{low}}(y)=-\frac y2+\frac1\pi\int_0^\infty\operatorname{Re}\bigl[1-(1-\chi_+(\xi))e^{i(y\xi-\Phi_0(\xi))}\bigr]\xi^{-2}d\xi$; $f_{0,\textup{low}}\in C^\infty(\R)$ with $f_{0,\textup{low}}'(y)=-\frac12+\frac1\pi\int_0^\infty(1-\chi_+)\frac{\sin(y\xi-\Phi_0)}{\xi}d\xi$ and $f_{0,\textup{low}}^{(k)}(y)=-\frac1\pi\int_0^\infty(1-\chi_+)\operatorname{Re}[(i\xi)^ke^{i(y\xi-\Phi_0)}]\xi^{-2}d\xi$ for $k\ge2$, all absolutely convergent. In particular $f_{0,\textup{low}}''=\widecheck{m_{\textup{low}}}$ with $m_{\textup{low}}(\xi):=(1-\chi_+(|\xi|))e^{-i\Phi_0(\xi)}\in C^1_c(\R)$, and $f_{0,\textup{low}}^{(k)}$ is bounded for $k\ge2$.
  • For all $y\in\R$: $f_{0,\textup{low}}(y)-W(y)=\mc I_1(y)+\mc I_2(y)$, where $\mc I_1(y)=\frac1\pi\operatorname{Re}\int_0^\infty e^{iy\xi}b(\xi)d\xi$, $b(\xi)=(1-\chi_+(\xi))\frac{1-e^{-i\Phi_0(\xi)}}{\xi^2}$, and $\mc I_2(y)=\frac1\pi\operatorname{Re}\int_0^\infty e^{iy\xi}\chi_+(\xi)\xi^{-2}d\xi$, both absolutely convergent.
  • $f_0=f_{0,\textup{low}}+2\operatorname{Re}f_{0,+}\in C^\infty(\R;\R)$.
nodes.proof_html: Item (1) combines lem:c04_seed_integrable and lem:c04_seed_high_regular. Item (2) combines the low-frequency representation, derivative, and Fourier-symbol lemmas lem:c04_seed_low_representation, lem:c04_seed_low_derivatives, lem:c04_seed_low_fourier. Item (3) is lem:c04_seed_corner_decomposition. Finally the defining identity $f_0=f_{0,\textup{low}}+2\operatorname{Re}f_{0,+}$ and the smoothness of both summands prove item (4).

nodes.title: Low-frequency remainder $\mc I_1$
nodes.statement_html: $\mc I_1\in C^\infty(\R)$ and for every $j\ge0$ there is $C_j=C_j(p,\chi_+)$ with $|\p_y^j\mc I_1(y)|\le C_j|y|^{-p-j}$ for $|y|\ge1$.
nodes.proof_html:
First, $|\p^k_\xi b(\xi)|\le C_k\xi^{p-1-k}$ on $(0,2]$ and $b=0$ on $[2,\infty)$: $1-e^{-i\Phi_0}=F(\Phi_0)$ with $F(s)=1-e^{-is}$, $F(0)=0$, and by
  Faà di Bruno $\p^k[F(\Phi_0)]$ is a sum of terms $F^{(r)}(\Phi_0)\prod_{i\le r}\Phi_0^{(l_i)}$, $r\ge1$, $\sum l_i=k$, each bounded by
  $C\xi^{r(p+1)-k}\le C\xi^{p+1-k}$ for $\xi\le2$; then use Leibniz with $(1-\chi_+)\xi^{-2}$. Hence
  $|\p^k(\xi^jb)|\le C\xi^{p-1+j-k}$. Since $\xi^jb\in L^1$ with compact support, $\p_y^j\mc I_1=\frac1\pi\operatorname{Re}\int_0^\infty(i\xi)^je^{iy\xi}b\,d\xi$.
  Let $|y|\ge1$, $\rho_y=|y|^{-1}\le1$. Then $|\int_0^{\rho_y}|\le C\int_0^{\rho_y}\xi^{p+j-1}=C|y|^{-p-j}$. On $[\rho_y,2]$ integrate by parts $j+1$ times
  with $e^{iy\xi}=(iy)^{-1}\p_\xi e^{iy\xi}$: the boundary terms at $2$ vanish (all derivatives of $b$ vanish there), those at $\rho_y$ are
  $\le C|y|^{-k-1}\rho_y^{p+j-1-k}=C|y|^{-p-j}$ ($0\le k\le j$), and the final integral is
  $\le C|y|^{-j-1}\int_{\rho_y}^2\xi^{p-2}d\xi\le\frac{C}{1-p}|y|^{-j-1}\rho_y^{p-1}=C'|y|^{-p-j}$ (using $p<1$).

nodes.title: High-frequency remainder $\mc I_2$
nodes.statement_html: $\mc I_2\in C^\infty(\R\setminus\{0\})$ and for all $j,N\ge0$ there is $C_{j,N}$ with $|\p_y^j\mc I_2(y)|\le C_{j,N}|y|^{-N}$ for $|y|\ge1$.
nodes.proof_html:
Let $c=\chi_+\xi^{-2}$; $|c^{(l)}(\xi)|\le C_l\xi^{-2-l}$, $c=0$ on $(-\infty,1]$. For $y\ne0$ and $L\ge0$, integrating by parts $L$ times
  (boundary terms vanish: $c^{(k)}=0$ near $1$ and $c^{(k)}(\xi)\to0$ as $\xi\to\infty$) gives
  $\int_0^\infty e^{iy\xi}c\,d\xi=(-iy)^{-L}\int_0^\infty e^{iy\xi}c^{(L)}d\xi=:(-iy)^{-L}G_L(y)$. Since $\xi^lc^{(L)}\in L^1$ for $l\le L$,
  $G_L\in C^L$ with $|G_L^{(l)}|\le\int\xi^l|c^{(L)}|<\infty$. Take $L\ge\max(j,N)$ and apply Leibniz to $y^{-L}G_L$ for $|y|\ge1$.

nodes.title: Rapid decay of $f_{0,+}$ on the left
nodes.statement_html: For all $j,N\ge0$ there is $C_{j,N}$ with $|\p_y^jf_{0,+}(y)|\le C_{j,N}|y|^{-N}$ for $y\le-1$.
nodes.proof_html: $\p^j_yf_{0,+}=-\frac1{2\pi}\operatorname{Osc}[(i\xi)^j\chi_+\xi^{-2}]$ with $(i\xi)^j\chi_+\xi^{-2}\in S^{j-2}_+$; apply lem:c04_osc_integral(3).

nodes.title: The slowly varying amplitude $a_*$
nodes.statement_html: There are $y_0\ge2$ (depending only on $p,\chi_+$) and constants $C_j$ such that for $y\ge y_0$ and $j\ge0$: $|\p_y^j(a_*-1)(y)|\le C_jy^{-2\beta-j}$. In particular $|a_*|\le2$ and $|\p_y^ja_*|\le C_jy^{-j}$ on $[y_0,\infty)$, and $|\p^j_yf_{0,+}'(y)|\le C_jy^{-\beta+j/p}$ for $y\ge y_0$.
nodes.proof_html: By lem:c04_seed_decomposition(1), $f_{0,+}'=-\frac i{2\pi}\operatorname{Osc}[a]$ with $a=\chi_+/\xi\in S^{-1}_+$; since $-1<p$ this is the improper integral $\int_0^\infty a(\xi)e^{i(y\xi-\xi^{p+1}/(p+1))}d\xi$ of lem:appendix_homogeneous_stationary_phase (with $m=-1$; $a$ vanishes for $\xi\le1$, $|\p^ka|\le C_k\xi^{-1-k}$). That lemma gives $y_1$ with, for $y\ge y_1$, \[f_{0,+}'(y)=-\frac i{2\pi}\Bigl(\frac{2\pi}p\Bigr)^{1/2}\lambda_0^{(1-p)/2}e^{i(\Psi_0-\pi/4)}\bigl(a(\lambda_0)+r\bigr) =\mu_*\lambda_0^{(1-p)/2}e^{i(\Psi_0-\pi/4)}\bigl(a(\lambda_0)+r\bigr),\] $|\p^jr|\le C_j\lambda_0^{-1-(p+1)}y^{-j}$. Hence $a_*=\lambda_0^{(1-p)/2+(p+1)/2}(a(\lambda_0)+r)=\lambda_0(a(\lambda_0)+r)$. For $y\ge2^p$, $\lambda_0\ge2$ so $a(\lambda_0)=\lambda_0^{-1}$ and $a_*-1=\lambda_0r$. Leibniz with $|\p^i\lambda_0|\le C_iy^{1/p-i}$: $|\p^j(\lambda_0r)|\le C\sum_iy^{1/p-i}y^{-(p+2)/p-(j-i)}=Cy^{-(p+1)/p-j}=Cy^{-2\beta-j}$. Take $y_0\ge\max(y_1,2^p,2)$ so large that $C_0y_0^{-2\beta}\le1$. For the last claim, $f_{0,+}'=\mu_*a_*y^{-\beta}e^{i(\Psi_0-\pi/4)}$ and $|\p^ke^{i\Psi_0}|\le C_ky^{k/p}$ (Faà di Bruno, $|\p^l\Psi_0|\le Cy^{1+1/p-l}$, and $1/p-(l-1)\le l/p$); Leibniz.

nodes.title: Global bounds for the high-frequency part
nodes.statement_html: There is $C$ with $|f_{0,+}(y)|+|f_{0,+}'(y)|\le C$ and $|f_{0,+}''(y)|+|f_{0,+}'''(y)|\le C\ang y^{2/p}$ for all $y\in\R$.
nodes.proof_html: By lem:c04_seed_decomposition, $f_{0,+}$ is continuous and tends to zero as $|y|\to\infty$, hence is globally bounded. For derivatives, combine the positive-tail estimates of lem:c04_seed_amplitude with the negative-tail estimates of lem:c04_f0plus_negative and continuity on the intervening compact interval. The first derivative has exponent $-\beta<0$; the second and third derivatives have exponents $-\beta+1/p$ and $-\beta+2/p$, both at most $2/p$. Since $\ang y\ge1$, enlarge the constant to combine the bounds.

nodes.title: $\mc L_0$ applied to $f_{0,+}$
nodes.statement_html: $\mc L_0f_{0,+}=-\Gamma_+$ pointwise on $\R$.
nodes.proof_html: Apply lem:c04_weak_L0(1) with $m(\xi)=-\chi_+(\xi)\xi^{-2}e^{-i\Phi_0(\xi)}$ ($\xi>0$), $m=0$ ($\xi\le0$): $m\in C^\infty\cap L^1$, $m=0$ on $(-\infty,1]$, $|m|+|m'|\le C$, $f_{0,+}=\widecheck m$, and the regularity of $g=f_{0,+}$ is lem:c04_f0plus_global. With $E=e^{-i\Phi_0}$, $E'=-i\xi^pE$ for $\xi>0$: $\xi m'=-\chi_+'\xi^{-1}E+2\chi_+\xi^{-2}E+i\chi_+\xi^{p-1}E$ and $(2+i\xi^{1+p})m=-2\chi_+\xi^{-2}E-i\chi_+\xi^{p-1}E$, so $n=-\chi_+'\xi^{-1}E\,\mathbf 1_{\xi>0}\in C_c^\infty$ and $\widecheck n=-\Gamma_+$.

nodes.title: $\mc L_0f_0$ is constant
nodes.statement_html: $f_0\in\mathcal A$, $\mc L_0f_0\in C^1(\R)$ and $(\mc L_0f_0)'\equiv0$.
nodes.proof_html: $f_{0,\textup{low}}'$ is bounded: for $|y|\ge1$ it equals $W'+\mc I_1'+\mc I_2'$, bounded by lem:c04_I1_bound, lem:c04_I2_bound, and it is continuous on $[-1,1]$; $f_{0,\textup{low}}^{(k)}$, $k\ge2$, are bounded by lem:c04_seed_decomposition(2). With lem:c04_f0plus_global, $f_0'$ is bounded and $C^1$, so $f_0\in\mathcal A$. By $\R$-linearity and since $|D|^p$ commutes with $\operatorname{Re}$, $\mc L_0f_0=\mc L_0f_{0,\textup{low}}+2\operatorname{Re}\mc L_0f_{0,+}=\mc L_0f_{0,\textup{low}}-2\operatorname{Re}\Gamma_+$ (lem:c04_L0_f0plus). By lem:c04_frac_derivative with $g=f_{0,\textup{low}}'$, $(\mc L_0f_{0,\textup{low}})'=|D|^pf_{0,\textup{low}}''+f_{0,\textup{low}}'-f_{0,\textup{low}}'-yf_{0,\textup{low}}''=(|D|^p-y)f_{0,\textup{low}}''$. Apply lem:c04_weak_L0(2) with $m=m_{\textup{low}}$: for $\xi>0$, $m_{\textup{low}}'=-\chi_+'E-i\xi^p(1-\chi_+)E$, so $n_b=|\xi|^pm_{\textup{low}}-im_{\textup{low}}'=i\chi_+'(\xi)E$; for $\xi<0$, $n_b(\xi)=-i\chi_+'(-\xi)e^{-i\Phi_0(\xi)}=\ov{n_b(-\xi)}$. Hence $(|D|^p-y)f_{0,\textup{low}}''=\frac1\pi\operatorname{Re}\int_0^\infty i\chi_+'(\xi)e^{i(y\xi-\Phi_0)}d\xi=2\operatorname{Re}\Gamma_+'$ (differentiate $\Gamma_+$ under the integral). Thus $(\mc L_0f_0)'=2\operatorname{Re}\Gamma_+'-2\operatorname{Re}\Gamma_+'=0$.

nodes.title: Tails of the seed
nodes.statement_html: For every $j\ge0$ there is $C_j$ such that $|\p_y^j(f_{0,\textup{low}}-W)(y)|\le C_j|y|^{-p-j}$ for $|y|\ge1$, and $|\p^j_y(f_0(y)+y)|\le C_j|y|^{-p-j}$ for $y\le-1$.
nodes.proof_html: The first claim is lem:c04_seed_decomposition(3) with lem:c04_I1_bound, lem:c04_I2_bound ($N=p+j$). For $y\le-1$, $W(y)=-y$, so $f_0+y=(f_{0,\textup{low}}-W)+2\operatorname{Re}f_{0,+}$; use lem:c04_f0plus_negative with $N=p+j$.

nodes.title: $f_0$ solves the linearized equation
nodes.statement_html: $\mc L_0f_0\equiv0$ on $\R$.
nodes.proof_html: By lem:c04_L0_f0_constant, $\mc L_0f_0\equiv\kappa$; we show $\mc L_0f_0(y)\to0$ as $y\to-\infty$. Write $\mc L_0f_0=|D|^pf_0'+(f_0+y)-y(f_0'+1)$. For $y\le-2$, lem:c04_seed_tails gives $|f_0+y|\le C|y|^{-p}$, $|y(f_0'+1)|\le C|y|^{-p}$. In $|D|^pf_0'(y)=c_\alpha\int(f_0'(y)-f_0'(y-h))|h|^{-\alpha}dh$: for $|h|\le|y|/2$ both $y,y-h\le y/2\le-1$, so $|f_0'(y)-f_0'(y-h)|\le|h|\sup_{w\le y/2}|f_0''(w)|\le C|h||y|^{-p-2}$, contributing $\le C|y|^{-p-2}|y|^{1-p}$; for $|h|>|y|/2$ the integrand is $\le2\|f_0'\|_\infty|h|^{-\alpha}$, contributing $\le C|y|^{-p}$. All terms tend to $0$, so $\kappa=0$.

nodes.title: The linear solution
nodes.statement_html:
$f_0\in C^\infty(\R;\R)\cap\mathcal A$, $\mc L_0(f_0)=0$, $\lim_{y\to-\infty}f_0'(y)=-1$, $\lim_{y\to\infty}f_0'(y)=0$, and, with $y_0$ from lem:c04_seed_amplitude, for every $j\ge0$ there is $C_j$ (depending only on $p,\chi_+,j$) with:
  • $|\p_y^j(a_*-1)(y)|\le C_jy^{-2\beta-j}$ for $y\ge y_0$;
  • $|\p_y^j(f_{0,\textup{low}}-W)(y)|\le C_j|y|^{-p-j}$ for $|y|\ge1$, and $|\p_y^j(f_0(y)+y)|\le C_j|y|^{-p-j}$ for $y\le-1$;
  • for every $\mu\in\C$, $f_{0,\mu}\in C^\infty(\R;\R)\cap\mathcal A$ and $\mc L_0(f_{0,\mu})=G_\mu$.
nodes.proof_html: Smoothness: lem:c04_seed_decomposition(4); $\mc L_0f_0=0$: lem:c04_L0_f0; (1): lem:c04_seed_amplitude; (2): lem:c04_seed_tails. Limits of $f_0'$: at $-\infty$ from (2); at $+\infty$, $f_0'=f_{0,\textup{low}}'+2\operatorname{Re}f_{0,+}'$ with $|f_{0,\textup{low}}'|\le Cy^{-p-1}$ ((2), $W'=0$) and $|f_{0,+}'|\le Cy^{-\beta}$ (lem:c04_seed_amplitude). (3) $f_{0,\mu}$ is real, smooth, in $\mathcal A$ by lem:c04_f0plus_global. By linearity and lem:c04_L0_f0plus, $\mc L_0f_{0,\mu}=0+2\operatorname{Re}[(\mu/\mu_*-1)(-\Gamma_+)]=2\operatorname{Re}[(1-\mu/\mu_*)\Gamma_+]$. By def:G_mu and the conjugate symmetry of $\widehat{G_\mu}$, $G_\mu(y)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_\R\widehat{G_\mu}e^{iy\xi}d\xi=\frac1\pi\operatorname{Re}\int_0^\infty(1-\frac\mu{\mu_*})\frac{\chi_+'}\xi e^{i(y\xi-\Phi_0)}d\xi=2\operatorname{Re}[(1-\frac\mu{\mu_*})\Gamma_+(y)]$.

nodes.title: Cubic part of the nonlinearity
nodes.statement_html: For $\epsilon\ge0$ and $v\in\mathcal A$ (real or complex valued) let \begin{equation} \mc Q_{\epsilon,3}(v)(y)=-\frac{(p+1)\epsilon c_\alpha}2\int_\R\frac{v'(y)-v'(z)}{|y-z|^\alpha}\,S_v(y,z)^2\,dz , \end{equation} and more generally the trilinear form $T(u,v,w)(y)=\int_\R\frac{u'(y)-u'(z)}{|y-z|^\alpha}S_v(y,z)S_w(y,z)\,dz$, so that $\mc Q_{\epsilon,3}(v)=\kappa_\epsilon T(v,v,v)$ with $\kappa_\epsilon:=-\frac{(p+1)\epsilon c_\alpha}2$. The integrals converge absolutely since $|S_v|\le\|v'\|_\infty$ and by lem:c01_frac_well_defined.

nodes.title: Cubic response to a sine
nodes.statement_html: The coefficients $c_1(\epsilon),c_2(\epsilon)$ defined by the integral formulas in def:c04_correction_constants are the unique real numbers with $\mc Q_{\epsilon,3}(\sin)(y)=c_1\cos y+c_2\cos(3y)$ for all $y\in\R$. There is $C_3=C_3(p)$ such that, for every $\epsilon\ge0$, $c_i(\epsilon)=\epsilon c_i(1)$ and $|c_1|,|c_2|\le C_3\epsilon$.
nodes.proof_html: Let $e_\sigma(y)=e^{i\sigma y}$, $\sigma\in\{\pm1\}$. Substituting $z=y-h$: $e_\sigma'(y)-e_\sigma'(y-h)=i\sigma e^{i\sigma y}(1-e^{-i\sigma h})$, $S_{e_\sigma}(y,y-h)=e^{i\sigma y}(1-e^{-i\sigma h})/h$. Hence $T(e_{\sigma_1},e_{\sigma_2},e_{\sigma_3})(y)=e^{i(\sigma_1+\sigma_2+\sigma_3)y}\tau(\sigma)$ with $\tau(\sigma)=i\sigma_1\int_\R\prod_{k=1}^3(1-e^{-i\sigma_kh})\,|h|^{-\alpha}h^{-2}dh$, and $|\tau(\sigma)|\le C_\tau:=\int_\R\min(2,|h|)^3|h|^{-\alpha-2}dh<\infty$ ($3-\alpha-2=-p>-1$ near $0$, $-\alpha-2<-1$ at $\infty$). Since $\sin=\frac1{2i}\sum_\sigma\sigma e_\sigma$ and $T$ is $\C$-trilinear on bounded $C^2$ functions with bounded derivatives (absolute convergence), $\mc Q_{\epsilon,3}(\sin)(y)=\sum_{k\in\{\pm1,\pm3\}}d_ke^{iky}$ with $|d_k|\le|\kappa_\epsilon|C_\tau$. The function $F=\mc Q_{\epsilon,3}(\sin)$ is real ($\sin$ real) and even: for odd $v$, $v'$ is even and $S_v(-y,-z)=S_v(y,z)$, so substituting $z\mapsto-z$ shows $\mc Q_{\epsilon,3}(v)(-y)=\mc Q_{\epsilon,3}(v)(y)$. The odd part $i\sum d_k\sin(ky)$ of $F$ vanishes, so $F=(d_1+d_{-1})\cos y+(d_3+d_{-3})\cos3y$; taking real parts, $c_1=\operatorname{Re}(d_1+d_{-1})$, $c_2=\operatorname{Re}(d_3+d_{-3})$, $|c_i|\le2|\kappa_\epsilon|C_\tau$. Uniqueness: $\cos y,\cos3y$ are linearly independent. Linearity in $\epsilon$: $\mc Q_{\epsilon,3}=\epsilon\mc Q_{1,3}$.

nodes.title: Correction constants
nodes.statement_html: For $\epsilon\ge0$ define the coefficients directly by \[ c_1(\epsilon):=\frac1\pi\int_0^{2\pi}\mc Q_{\epsilon,3}(\sin)(y)\cos y\,dy, \qquad c_2(\epsilon):=\frac1\pi\int_0^{2\pi}\mc Q_{\epsilon,3}(\sin)(y)\cos(3y)\,dy. \] Set $n_\epsilon:=4c_1(\epsilon)$ and $c_{\textup{cubic}}:=-4c_2(\epsilon)/(3^p-1)$ ($3^p>1$). The sine-response lemma then identifies these explicit coefficients with the paper's coefficients; its normalization reads \begin{equation} \mc Q_{\epsilon,3}(2\sin(\cdot))(y)=2n_\epsilon\cos y-2(3^p-1)c_{\textup{cubic}}\cos(3y) \end{equation} (since $\mc Q_{\epsilon,3}$ is $3$-homogeneous). For $\mu\in\C$ set \begin{equation} c_{\textup{log}}(\mu)=-\frac{n_\epsilon|\mu|^2}p,\quad c_{\textup{power}}=-\frac{c_\epsilon}{1-p^2},\quad c_+=-\frac{c_\epsilon}{p+1},\quad c_-=\frac{c_\alpha}{p+1}\int_0^1[A_\epsilon(t)-1]t^{p-1}dt , \end{equation} with $c_\epsilon$ from lem:analysis_coefficient, and $\sq\lambda_{\epsilon,\mu}(y):=-\frac{c_\epsilon}py^{-p-1}+c_{\textup{log}}(\mu)y^{-1-1/p}$ for $y>0$.

nodes.title: Size of the constants
nodes.statement_html: Let $K_\mu>0$. There is $C$ (depending on $p,K_\mu$) such that for $\epsilon\in[0,1]$, $|\mu|\le K_\mu$: $|c_\epsilon|,|n_\epsilon|,|c_{\textup{cubic}}|,|c_{\textup{log}}(\mu)|,|c_{\textup{power}}|,|c_\pm|\le C\epsilon$; all vanish at $\epsilon=0$; $c_{\textup{log}}$ is continuous in $\mu$. Moreover for $y\ge1$, $k\ge0$: $|\p^k_y\sq\lambda_{\epsilon,\mu}(y)|\le C_k\epsilon y^{-p-1-k}$.
nodes.proof_html: $|c_\epsilon|\le C\epsilon$, $c_0=0$: lem:analysis_coefficient ($A_0\equiv1$). $n_\epsilon,c_{\textup{cubic}}$: lem:c04_cubic_sine_response. $|A_\epsilon(t)-1|\le\frac\alpha2\epsilon t^2$ gives $|c_-|\le C\epsilon$. For $\sq\lambda$: $1+1/p>p+1$, so $y^{-1-1/p-k}\le y^{-p-1-k}$ for $y\ge1$.

nodes.title: Approximate solution family
nodes.statement_html: Fix $\delta\in(0,|\mu_*|/2]$, $\ov B=\ov B(\mu_*,\delta)=\{\mu\in\C:|\mu-\mu_*|\le\delta\}$ (so $|\mu|\le2|\mu_*|$). Let $C_\lambda$ be the constant of lem:c04_constants_small for $k=0$, $K_\mu=2|\mu_*|$, and fix $\epsilon_0:=\min\{1,(2C_\lambda)^{-1}\}$ (so $|\sq\lambda_{\epsilon,\mu}(y)|\le\frac12$ for $y\ge1$; later chapters may decrease $\epsilon_0$). Let $R_0:=\max\{y_0,2\}$ with $y_0$ from lem:c04_seed_amplitude, and fix $R\ge R_0$ (in particular $R\ge2$; later chapters may enlarge $R_0$). Let $\chi_R(y):=\chi_+(y/R)$ (so $\chi_R=0$ on $(-\infty,R]$, $\chi_R=1$ on $[2R,\infty)$, $|\p^j\chi_R|\le\|\chi_+^{(j)}\|_\infty R^{-j}$). For $\epsilon\in[0,\epsilon_0]$, $\mu\in\ov B$ and $y>R/2$ define \begin{equation} \lambda_{\epsilon,\mu}(y):=\Psi_{\epsilon,\mu}'(y)=y^{1/p}+c_{\textup{power}}\Bigl(\frac{1-p^2}p\Bigr)y^{1/p-p-1}+\frac{c_{\textup{log}}(\mu)}y,\qquad\Psi_{\epsilon,\mu}(R)=\Psi_0(R), \end{equation} \begin{equation} Z_{\epsilon,\mu}(y)=\mu\,a_*(y)\,\lambda_{\epsilon,\mu}(y)^{-(p+1)/2}e^{i(\Psi_{\epsilon,\mu}(y)-\pi/4)} . \end{equation} We abbreviate $f=\ov f_{\epsilon,\mu}$, $Z=Z_{\epsilon,\mu}$, $\lambda=\lambda_{\epsilon,\mu}$, $\Psi=\Psi_{\epsilon,\mu}$, and write $Z_0:=Z_{0,\mu_*}$ (also $\lambda_0,\Psi_0$ agree with $\lambda_{0,\mu},\Psi_{0,\mu}$, see lem:c04_phase_basic). Define \begin{equation} f_{\textup{slow}}(y)=c_+y^{-p}\chi_R(y)+c_-|y|^{-p}\chi_R(-y), \end{equation} \begin{equation} f_{\textup{osc}}(y)=-2\chi_R(y)\operatorname{Re}\int_y^\infty\Bigl(Z_{\epsilon,\mu}(t)+c_{\textup{cubic}}Z_{\epsilon,\mu}(t)^3-\frac\mu{\mu_*}Z_0(t)\Bigr)dt \quad(y>R),\qquad f_{\textup{osc}}(y)=0\quad(y\le R), \end{equation} (absolutely convergent, see lem:c04_Z_bounds) and \begin{equation} \ov f_{\epsilon,\mu}=f_{0,\mu}+f_{\textup{slow}}+f_{\textup{osc}} . \end{equation} By lem:c04_family_regions, for $y\ge2R$ \begin{equation} \ov f_{\epsilon,\mu}(y)=f_{0,\textup{low}}(y)+c_+y^{-p}-2\operatorname{Re}\int_y^\infty\bigl(Z(t)+c_{\textup{cubic}}Z(t)^3\bigr)dt, \end{equation} and for $y\le-2R$ \begin{equation} \ov f_{\epsilon,\mu}(y)=f_0(y)+2\operatorname{Re}\Bigl[\Bigl(\frac\mu{\mu_*}-1\Bigr)f_{0,+}(y)\Bigr]+c_-|y|^{-p}. \end{equation}

nodes.title: Basic properties of the modified phase
nodes.statement_html:
For $\epsilon\in[0,\epsilon_0]$, $\mu\in\ov B$, $y>R/2$ (so $y\ge1$):
  • $\lambda=\lambda_0(1+\sq\lambda_{\epsilon,\mu})$, hence $\frac12y^{1/p}\le\lambda(y)\le\frac32y^{1/p}$, and $|\p^k\lambda|\le C_ky^{1/p-k}$, $|\p^k(\lambda^{-q})|\le C_{k,q}y^{-q/p-k}$ for every $q>0$;
  • $\Psi_{\epsilon,\mu}(y)=\Psi_0(y)+c_{\textup{power}}(y^{1/p-p}-R^{1/p-p})+c_{\textup{log}}(\mu)\log(y/R)$, and $|\p^k e^{i\Psi}|\le C_ky^{k/p}$;
  • at $\epsilon=0$: $\lambda_{0,\mu}=\lambda_0$, $\Psi_{0,\mu}=\Psi_0$, $Z_{0,\mu}=\frac\mu{\mu_*}Z_0$, $c_{\textup{cubic}}=c_\pm=0$; and $Z_0=f_{0,+}'$ on $(R/2,\infty)$.
Constants are admissible.
nodes.proof_html: (1) $c_{\textup{power}}\frac{1-p^2}p=-\frac{c_\epsilon}p$ and $\frac{c_{\textup{log}}}y=\lambda_0c_{\textup{log}}y^{-1-1/p}$; $|\sq\lambda|\le\frac12$ by the choice of $\epsilon_0$. Derivatives by Leibniz/Faà di Bruno using lem:c04_constants_small and $|\p^k\lambda_0|\le C_ky^{1/p-k}$, $1+\sq\lambda\in[\frac12,\frac32]$. (2) Differentiate the right side: $c_{\textup{power}}(\frac1p-p)y^{1/p-p-1}+\frac{c_{\textup{log}}}y$ matches eqn:approx_modified_frequency, and the value at $R$ is $\Psi_0(R)$. For $e^{i\Psi}$: Faà di Bruno, each factor $\p^l\Psi=\p^{l-1}\lambda$ is $\le Cy^{1/p-l+1}\le Cy^{l/p}$ ($1/p\ge1$). (3) $c_0=0$ and $n_0=4c_1(0)=0$; the identity $Z_0=f_{0,+}'$ is the definition of $a_*$.

nodes.title: Bounds for $Z$
nodes.statement_html: For $j\ge0$ there are admissible $C_j$ with, for $y\ge R$, $\epsilon\in[0,\epsilon_0]$, $\mu\in\ov B$: $|\p^jZ(y)|\le C_jy^{-\beta+j/p}$, $|\p^j(Z^3)(y)|\le C_jy^{-3\beta+j/p}$, $|\p^j(Z/\lambda)(y)|\le C_jy^{-\beta-1/p+j/p}$, and $|\p^j_y(a_*\lambda^{-q})(y)|\le C_{j,q}y^{-q/p-j}$ ($q>0$). In particular $\int_y^\infty|Z|\le C y^{1-\beta}$ ($\beta>1$).
nodes.proof_html: Leibniz with $|\p^ka_*|\le C_ky^{-k}$ (lem:c04_seed_amplitude, $R\ge y_0$), lem:c04_phase_basic(1),(2), $|\mu|\le2|\mu_*|$ and $\lambda^{-(p+1)/2}\approx y^{-\beta}$; for $Z^3$ use $Z^3=\mu^3a_*^3\lambda^{-3(p+1)/2}e^{3i(\Psi-\pi/4)}$ and $|\p^ke^{3i\Psi}|\le C_ky^{k/p}$; $y^{-k}\le y^{k/p}$.

nodes.title: Regional forms and smoothness of the family
nodes.statement_html: For $\epsilon\in[0,\epsilon_0]$, $\mu\in\ov B$: $\ov f_{\epsilon,\mu}\in C^\infty(\R;\R)\cap\mathcal A$; $f_{\textup{slow}}=0$ on $[-R,R]$, $f_{\textup{osc}}=0$ on $(-\infty,R]$; eqn:approx_family_positive holds for $y\ge2R$ and eqn:approx_family_negative for $y\le-2R$; $\ov f_{0,\mu_*}=f_0$. For $y\ge2R$, $\ov f'=f_{0,\textup{low}}'-pc_+y^{-p-1}+2\operatorname{Re}(Z+c_{\textup{cubic}}Z^3)$.
nodes.proof_html: The integrand of $f_{\textup{osc}}$ is smooth on $(R/2,\infty)$ and $O(t^{-\beta})$, so $F(y):=\int_y^\infty(\cdots)$ is smooth on $(R/2,\infty)$ with $F'=-(\cdots)$; since $\chi_R$ vanishes on $(-\infty,R]$, $\chi_RF$ extended by $0$ is smooth on $\R$. $f_{\textup{slow}}$ is smooth since $\chi_R(\pm y)$ vanish near $0$. Bounded derivative: lem:c04_Z_bounds, lem:c04_f0plus_global, $f_0\in\mathcal A$. For $y\ge2R$: $\chi_R(y)=1$, $\chi_R(-y)=0$, and $f_{0,\mu}=f_0-2\operatorname{Re}f_{0,+}+2\operatorname{Re}[\frac\mu{\mu_*}f_{0,+}]$ with $f_{0,+}(y)=-\int_y^\infty f_{0,+}'=-\int_y^\infty Z_0$ (lem:c04_seed_decomposition(1): $f_{0,+}\to0$; lem:c04_phase_basic(3)); the $\frac\mu{\mu_*}Z_0$ terms cancel and $f_0-2\operatorname{Re}f_{0,+}=f_{0,\textup{low}}$. For $y\le-2R$: $f_{\textup{osc}}=0$, $f_{\textup{slow}}=c_-|y|^{-p}$. At $(0,\mu_*)$: $c_\pm=c_{\textup{cubic}}=0$ and $Z_{0,\mu_*}=Z_0$. The derivative formula follows from the fundamental theorem of calculus.

nodes.title: Frequency and phase differences
nodes.statement_html: For $j\ge0$ there are admissible $C_j$ with, for $y\ge R$, $\epsilon\in[0,\epsilon_0]$, $\mu\in\ov B$, \begin{equation} |\p^j_y(\lambda_{\epsilon,\mu}-\lambda_0)(y)|\le C_j\epsilon y^{\frac1p-p-1-j}, \end{equation} \begin{equation} |\p^j_y(\Psi_{\epsilon,\mu}-\Psi_0)(y)|\le C_j\epsilon y^{\frac1p-p-j}. \end{equation}
nodes.proof_html: $\lambda-\lambda_0=-\frac{c_\epsilon}py^{1/p-p-1}+c_{\textup{log}}y^{-1}$ and $-1<\frac1p-p-1$, so for $y\ge1$ both terms are $\le C\epsilon y^{1/p-p-1-j}$ after $j$ derivatives. For $j\ge1$, $\p^j(\Psi-\Psi_0)=\p^{j-1}(\lambda-\lambda_0)$. For $j=0$, by lem:c04_phase_basic(2), $|\Psi-\Psi_0|\le|c_{\textup{power}}|y^{1/p-p}+|c_{\textup{log}}|\log y\le C\epsilon y^{1/p-p}$ (as $\log y\le\frac{1}{1/p-p}y^{1/p-p}$ for $y\ge1$).

nodes.title: Reciprocal-frequency amplitudes and their differences
nodes.statement_html: Fix $\frac34<p<1$ and $0<\delta\le|\mu_*|/2$. There are $\epsilon_0\in(0,1]$ and $R_0\ge2$, depending only on $p,\delta$ and the fixed cutoffs, with the following property. For every $q>0$ and $j\in\N$ there is $C_{j,q}>0$, depending only on those fixed data and $j,q$, such that for all $R\ge R_0$, $\epsilon\in[0,\epsilon_0]$, $\mu\in\ov B$, and $y\ge R$, \[ F_q=a_*\lambda^{-q},\qquad F_{q,0}=a_*\lambda_0^{-q} \] are smooth on $(R/2,\infty)$ and satisfy \[ |\p_y^jF_q(y)|+|\p_y^jF_{q,0}(y)|\le C_{j,q}y^{-q/p-j},\qquad |\p_y^j(F_q-F_{q,0})(y)|\le C_{j,q}\epsilon y^{-q/p-p-1-j}. \] The thresholds $\epsilon_0,R_0$ are chosen before $j,q$; the constants are independent of $R,\epsilon,\mu,y$.
nodes.proof_html: Use $\lambda=\lambda_0(1+\sq\lambda)$ with $|\sq\lambda|\le1/2$ and $|\p^k\sq\lambda|\le C_k\epsilon y^{-p-1-k}$. The smooth functions $(1+t)^{-q}$ and $[(1+t)^{-q}-1]/t$, the latter extended at zero, have bounded derivatives of every fixed order on $[-1/2,1/2]$. Apply the finite chain-rule expansion to obtain $|\p^k[(1+\sq\lambda)^{-q}-1]|\le C_{k,q}\epsilon y^{-p-1-k}$: every term contains at least one derivative of $\sq\lambda$, and additional factors $\epsilon y^{-p-1}$ are bounded by one after a fixed threshold choice. Multiply by $a_*y^{-q/p}$ and use the Leibniz formula and the symbol bounds on $a_*$. Smoothness follows from the positive frequency and the smooth positive seed. This is the place to reuse an all-order product/composition API for symbol bounds.

nodes.title: Interpolated phases and exponential differences
nodes.statement_html: Fix $\frac34<p<1$ and $0<\delta\le|\mu_*|/2$. There are $\epsilon_0\in(0,1]$ and $R_0\ge2$, depending only on $p,\delta$ and the fixed cutoffs, such that for every $j\in\N$ there is $C_j>0$ with the following bounds, uniformly for $R\ge R_0$, $\epsilon\in[0,\epsilon_0]$, $\mu\in\ov B$, and $y\ge R$. Put $d=1/p-p>0$, $\Delta\Psi=\Psi-\Psi_0$, and $\Psi_s=\Psi_0+s\Delta\Psi$ for $s\in[0,1]$. Then \[ \sup_{0\le s\le1}|\p_y^je^{i\Psi_s(y)}|\le C_jy^{j/p},\qquad |\p_y^j(e^{i\Psi(y)}-e^{i\Psi_0(y)})|\le C_j\epsilon y^{d+j/p}. \] These functions are smooth in $y\in(R/2,\infty)$, and on that interval \[ e^{i\Psi(y)}-e^{i\Psi_0(y)} =i\int_0^1\Delta\Psi(y)e^{i\Psi_s(y)}ds. \] Every $y$-derivative can be passed through this integral on $[0,1]$; on compact $y$-intervals its derivative integrands have a common finite majorant independent of $s$. All constants in the displayed bounds are independent of $s,R,\epsilon,\mu,y$.
nodes.proof_html: The derivative $\Psi_s'=\lambda_0+s(\lambda-\lambda_0)$ has uniform symbol bounds $|\p_y^k\Psi_s'|\le C_ky^{1/p-k}$. Induct on $j$ in $\p_y e^{i\Psi_s}=i\Psi_s'e^{i\Psi_s}$ to prove the first bound, retaining the finite polynomial in phase derivatives. The identity follows from the fundamental theorem of calculus in $s$. Joint smoothness on a neighbourhood of each compact subset of $(R/2,\infty)\times[0,1]$ permits differentiation under that proper integral. Use Leibniz and $|\p_y^k\Delta\Psi|\le C_k\epsilon y^{d-k}$: the term with $k$ derivatives on $\Delta\Psi$ has exponent $d-k+(j-k)/p\le d+j/p$ because $y\ge R\ge2$.

nodes.title: The two product terms in the amplitude-phase difference
nodes.statement_html: Fix $\frac34<p<1$ and $0<\delta\le|\mu_*|/2$. There are thresholds $\epsilon_0\in(0,1]$, $R_0\ge2$, chosen before derivative orders and powers, such that for every $q>0$, $j\in\N$ there is $C_{j,q}>0$ satisfying the following for every $R\ge R_0$, $\epsilon\in[0,\epsilon_0]$, $\mu\in\ov B$, and $y\ge R$. With $F_q=a_*\lambda^{-q}$, $F_{q,0}=a_*\lambda_0^{-q}$, put \[ B_q=\mu(F_q-F_{q,0})e^{i\Psi},\qquad P_q=\mu F_{q,0}(e^{i\Psi}-e^{i\Psi_0}). \] Both terms are smooth on $(R/2,\infty)$ and \[ |\p_y^jB_q(y)|\le C_{j,q}\epsilon y^{-q/p-p-1+j/p},\qquad |\p_y^jP_q(y)|\le C_{j,q}\epsilon y^{1/p-p-q/p+j/p}. \] These constants depend only on $p,\delta,j,q$ and the fixed cutoffs. Defining $D_q=\mu a_*[\lambda^{-q}e^{i\Psi}-\lambda_0^{-q}e^{i\Psi_0}]$, one has $D_q=B_q+P_q$ and, on $(R/2,\infty)$, \[ Z_{\epsilon,\mu}-\frac\mu{\mu_*}Z_0=e^{-i\pi/4}D_{(p+1)/2}. \]
nodes.proof_html: Take the minimum of the two epsilon thresholds and the maximum of the two radius thresholds from the preceding lemmas. Bound $|\mu|$ by $|\mu_*|+\delta$. In the Leibniz sum for $B_q$, the term with $k$ derivatives on its amplitude has exponent $-q/p-p-1-k+(j-k)/p\le-q/p-p-1+j/p$. For $P_q$, the corresponding exponent is $-q/p-k+(1/p-p)+(j-k)/p\le1/p-p-q/p+j/p$. Sum the finite binomial coefficients. The first identity is algebraic; the second uses $\lambda_{0,\mu_*}=\lambda_0$, $\Psi_{0,\mu_*}=\Psi_0$, and $\mu_*\ne0$.

nodes.title: Amplitude-phase differences
nodes.statement_html: For $q>0$ let $D_q:=\mu a_*\bigl[\lambda^{-q}e^{i\Psi}-\lambda_0^{-q}e^{i\Psi_0}\bigr]$. For $j\ge0$ there are admissible $C_{j,q}$ with $|\p_y^jD_q(y)|\le C_{j,q}\epsilon y^{\frac1p-p-\frac qp+\frac jp}$ for $y\ge R$. Moreover $|\p_y^j\p_y[a_*\lambda^{-q}-a_*\lambda_0^{-q}]|\le C\epsilon y^{-q/p-p-2-j}$. In particular ($q=\frac{p+1}2$, $q/p=\beta$) \begin{equation} \Bigl|\p^j_y\Bigl(Z_{\epsilon,\mu}-\frac\mu{\mu_*}Z_0\Bigr)(y)\Bigr|\le C_j\epsilon y^{\frac1p-p-\beta+\frac jp}. \end{equation}
nodes.proof_html: Use common thresholds obtained by a finite minimum in $\epsilon_0$ and maximum in $R_0$. By lem:c04_Z_difference_products, $D_q=B_q+P_q$ with both summands smooth. Differentiate the sum and add their bounds. The exponent of $B_q$ is smaller than the stated exponent by $1+1/p$, so $y\ge R\ge2$ gives the first estimate after enlarging the constant. The second estimate is the reciprocal-amplitude difference bound of lem:c04_reciprocal_amplitude_difference at order $j+1$. For the last assertion take $q=(p+1)/2$ in the exact identity for $Z$ from lem:c04_Z_difference_products; multiplication by $e^{-i\pi/4}$ preserves norms, and $q/p=\beta$.

nodes.title: Primitive of $Z$ by integration by parts
nodes.statement_html: For $y\ge R$, with $q_1=\frac{p+3}2$ (so $q_1/p=\beta+\frac1p$), \[ \int_y^\infty Z(t)dt=\frac{iZ(y)}{\lambda(y)}+i\mu e^{-i\pi/4}\int_y^\infty\p_t\bigl(a_*\lambda^{-q_1}\bigr)(t)e^{i\Psi(t)}dt, \] the last integral converging absolutely. Hence, with admissible $C$: (a) $|\int_y^\infty Z|\le Cy^{-\beta-1/p}$; (b) $|\int_y^\infty(Z-\frac\mu{\mu_*}Z_0)|\le C\epsilon y^{-p-\beta}$; (c) $|c_{\textup{cubic}}\int_y^\infty Z^3|\le C\epsilon y^{1-3\beta}\le C\epsilon\min\{y^{-p-\beta},y^{-\beta-1/p}\}$.
nodes.proof_html: On $[y,M]$ write $Z=\mu e^{-i\pi/4}(a_*\lambda^{-(p+1)/2})\frac{\p_te^{i\Psi}}{i\lambda}$ and integrate by parts; the boundary term at $M$ is $O(M^{-\beta-1/p})\to0$ and $|\p_t(a_*\lambda^{-q_1})|\le Ct^{-\beta-1/p-1}$ (lem:c04_Z_bounds), integrable. Since $-1/i=i$, the formula follows. (a): $|Z/\lambda|\le Cy^{-\beta-1/p}$ and $\int_y^\infty t^{-\beta-1/p-1}dt\le Cy^{-\beta-1/p}$. (b): apply the formula to $Z$ and to $\frac\mu{\mu_*}Z_0$ (the latter is the formula at $\epsilon=0$ multiplied by $\mu/\mu_*$) and subtract: the boundary terms give $e^{-i\pi/4}iD_{q_1}(y)$, bounded by $C\epsilon y^{1/p-p-\beta-1/p}=C\epsilon y^{-p-\beta}$ (lem:c04_Z_difference); the integrands differ by $\p_t(a_*\lambda^{-q_1})(e^{i\Psi}-e^{i\Psi_0})+\p_t(a_*\lambda^{-q_1}-a_*\lambda_0^{-q_1})e^{i\Psi_0}$, bounded by $Ct^{-\beta-1/p-1}\cdot\epsilon t^{1/p-p}+C\epsilon t^{-\beta-1/p-p-2}\le C\epsilon t^{-p-\beta-1}$; integrate. (c): $|c_{\textup{cubic}}|\le C\epsilon$, $|Z|^3\le Ct^{-3\beta}$, $3\beta>1$; and $1-3\beta\le-p-\beta\iff p+1\le2\beta$ (true, $2\beta=1+1/p$), $1-3\beta=-\beta-1/p$.

nodes.title: Approximate phase differences
