Hence $\mc V_\epsilon$ restricts to a linear bijection of $Y_\gamma$ with $\|\mc V_\epsilon\|,\|\mc V_\epsilon^{-1}\|\le C$.
nodes.proof_html: $\mc V_\epsilon G=G$ on $(-\infty,1]$. For $y>1$: $(\mc V_\epsilon G)'=(p+1)(\phi_\epsilon')^p\phi_\epsilon''\,(G\circ\phi_\epsilon)+(\phi_\epsilon')^{p+2}(G'\circ\phi_\epsilon)$ a.e.; with $\phi_\epsilon'\in[\frac12,\frac32]$, $|\phi_\epsilon''|\le C\ang{y}^{-p-2}$, $\ang{\phi_\epsilon(y)}\approx\ang{y}$ we get $|\p^j\mc V_\epsilon G(y)|\le C\|G\|_{Y_\gamma}\ang{y}^{-\gamma+j/p}$, $j=0,1$. Same for $\mc V_\epsilon^{-1}G=(\psi_\epsilon')^{p+1}G\circ\psi_\epsilon$ with eqn:linear_inverse_phi_bounds.

nodes.title: $\mc V_\epsilon^{-1}-I$ is small on smooth forcings
nodes.statement_html: Let $\gamma\in\R$. There is $C=C(p,\gamma,\chi_+,C_0)$ such that for $0\le\epsilon\le\epsilon_c$ and every $G\in Y_\gamma$ with $G\in C^2((1,\infty))$ and $M(G):=\sup_{y>1}\ang{y}^\gamma(|G(y)|+|G'(y)|+|G''(y)|)<\infty$: \[ \|(\mc V_\epsilon^{-1}-I)G\|_{Y_\gamma}\le C\,\epsilon\,M(G). \]
nodes.proof_html: On $y\le1$ the function vanishes. For $y>1$, with $\psi=\psi_\epsilon$ (so $y,\psi(y)\in(1,\infty)$, and the segment between them lies in $(1,\infty)$, where $\ang{\cdot}\approx\ang{y}$): $(\mc V_\epsilon^{-1}-I)G=[(\psi')^{p+1}-1]G\circ\psi+(G\circ\psi-G)$, so by the mean value theorem and lem:c08_psi_bounds, $|\cdot|\le C|c_\epsilon|M(G)(\ang{y}^{-p-1-\gamma}+\ang{y}^{-p-\gamma})$. Its derivative is $(p+1)(\psi')^p\psi''\,G\circ\psi+[(\psi')^{p+2}-1]G'\circ\psi+(G'\circ\psi-G')$, bounded by $C|c_\epsilon|M(G)(\ang{y}^{-\gamma-p-2}+\ang{y}^{-\gamma-p-1}+\ang{y}^{-\gamma-p})\le C|c_\epsilon|M(G)\ang{y}^{-\gamma+1/p}$. Conclude with $|c_\epsilon|\le C_0\epsilon$.

nodes.title: Transport of $G_\mu$
nodes.statement_html: Let $\gamma\in\R$. There is $C=C(p,\gamma,\chi_+,C_0)$ such that for $0\le\epsilon\le\epsilon_c$ and all $\mu\in\C$, \[ \|(\mc V_\epsilon^{-1}-I)G_\mu\|_{Y_\gamma}\le C\,\epsilon\,\Bigl|1-\frac{\mu}{\mu_*}\Bigr| . \] In particular, for any closed disc $\ov B=\ov B(\mu_*,\delta)$, $\sup_{\mu\in\ov B}\|(\mc V_\epsilon^{-1}-I)G_\mu\|_{Y_\gamma}\le C\,\epsilon\,\delta/|\mu_*|$.
nodes.proof_html: $\widehat{G_\pm}$ are smooth and compactly supported (in $1\le|\xi|\le2$; $\chi_+'$ is supported in $[1,2]$), so $G_\pm$ are Schwartz; they are real-valued by the Hermitian extension. With $z=1-\mu/\mu_*$, comparing Fourier transforms on $\xi>0$ and using Hermitian symmetry, $G_\mu=(\operatorname{Re}z)G_++(\operatorname{Im}z)G_-$. Apply lem:c08_V_inverse_minus_identity to $G_\pm$ ($M(G_\pm)<\infty$, $G_\pm\in Y_\gamma$) and linearity.

nodes.title: $\mc R_{1,\epsilon}$
nodes.statement_html: Let $\gamma\in\R$. There is $C$ such that for $0\le\epsilon\le\epsilon_c$, $r\in X_\gamma$: \begin{equation} \|\mc R_{1,\epsilon}r\|_{Y_\gamma}\le C\epsilon\|r\|_{X_\gamma}. \end{equation}
nodes.proof_html: $\mc R_{1,\epsilon}r=0$ on $y\le1$. For $y>1$, by lem:c08_phi_bounds and the product rule, $|\mc R_{1,\epsilon}r|\le C|c_\epsilon|\ang{y}^{-p-1-\gamma}\|r\|$ and $|\p_y\mc R_{1,\epsilon}r|\le C|c_\epsilon|(\ang{y}^{-p-2}|r|+\ang{y}^{-p-1}|r'|)\le C|c_\epsilon|\|r\|\ang{y}^{-\gamma+1/p}$.

nodes.title: Kernel bounds, near region
nodes.statement_html:
There is $C=C(p,\chi_+)$ such that for $0\le\epsilon\le\epsilon_c$, $y\in\R$ and $0<|y-z|\le\frac14\ang{y}$:
  • $K_\epsilon(y,z)=0$ and $(\p_y+\p_z)K_\epsilon(y,z)=0$ whenever $\max(y,z)<1$; in particular for all $y\le0$ (then $z\le y+\frac14\ang{y}\le\frac14$).
  • $|K_\epsilon(y,z)|\le C|c_\epsilon|\ang{y}^{-p-2}|y-z|^{-p}$.
  • $(\p_y+\p_z)K_\epsilon(y,z)=-c_\alpha(p+1)|y-z|^{-1-p}\bigl(\frac{\phi'(y)}{S_\phi}\bigr)^{p+1} \bigl(\frac{\phi''(y)}{\phi'(y)}-\frac{S_{\phi'}(y,z)}{S_\phi(y,z)}\bigr)$ ($\phi=\phi_\epsilon$), and $|(\p_y+\p_z)K_\epsilon(y,z)|\le C|c_\epsilon|\ang{y}^{-p-3}|y-z|^{-p}$.
Moreover, for all $y\neq z$: $|K_\epsilon(y,z)|+|(\p_y+\p_z)K_\epsilon(y,z)|\le C\min(|y-z|^{-p},|y-z|^{-1-p})$.
nodes.proof_html: (1) $\phi=\mathrm{id}$ on $(-\infty,1)$. For $y\le0$: $\ang{y}\le1-y$ gives $y+\frac14\ang{y}\le\frac{3y+1}4\le\frac14$. For (2),(3): every $\zeta$ between $y$ and $z$ satisfies $\frac34\ang{y}\le\ang{\zeta}\le\frac54\ang{y}$ ($\ang{\cdot}$ is 1-Lipschitz). Since $S_\phi(y,z)=\int_0^1\phi'(z+s(y-z))ds$ and $S_{\phi'}(y,z)=\int_0^1\phi''(z+s(y-z))ds$, eqn:linear_phi_bounds gives $|\phi'(y)-S_\phi|\le C|c_\epsilon|\ang{y}^{-p-2}|y-z|$ and $|\phi''(y)-S_{\phi'}|\le C|c_\epsilon|\ang{y}^{-p-3}|y-z|$. As $a:=\phi'(y)/S_\phi\in[\frac13,3]$, $|1-a^{p+1}|\le C|1-a|\le C|\phi'(y)-S_\phi|$, giving (2). The formula in (3) follows from $(\p_y+\p_z)|y-z|^{-1-p}=0$, $(\p_y+\p_z)S_\phi(y,z)=S_{\phi'}(y,z)$, and $\frac{\phi''}{\phi'}-\frac{S_{\phi'}}{S_\phi}=\frac{\phi''(S_\phi-\phi')+\phi'(\phi''-S_{\phi'})}{\phi'S_\phi}$, whose modulus is $\le C|c_\epsilon|\ang{y}^{-p-3}|y-z|$ (using also $|\phi''|\le C\ang{y}^{-p-2}$). The global bound: $\phi''$ is bounded, so $|S_\phi-\phi'(y)|\le C\min(1,|y-z|)$ and $|S_{\phi'}|\le C$.

nodes.title: Kernel bounds, far region
nodes.statement_html: There is $C=C(p,\chi_+)$ such that for $0\le\epsilon\le\epsilon_c$ and $|y-z|\ge\frac18\ang{y}$: \[ |K_\epsilon(y,z)|\le C|c_\epsilon|\Bigl(\frac{\ang{y}^{-p-1}}{|y-z|^{p+1}}+\frac{\ang{z}^{-p}}{|y-z|^{p+2}}\Bigr),\qquad |\p_yK_\epsilon(y,z)|\le C|c_\epsilon|\Bigl(\frac{\ang{y}^{-p-2}}{|y-z|^{p+1}}+\frac{\ang{z}^{-p}}{|y-z|^{p+3}}\Bigr). \]
nodes.proof_html: $\phi'(y)-S_\phi(y,z)=(\phi'(y)-1)-\frac{(\phi-\mathrm{id})(y)-(\phi-\mathrm{id})(z)}{y-z}$, so by eqn:linear_phi_bounds $|\phi'(y)-S_\phi|\le C|c_\epsilon|(\ang{y}^{-p-1}+\frac{\ang{y}^{-p}+\ang{z}^{-p}}{|y-z|})\le C|c_\epsilon|(\ang{y}^{-p-1}+\frac{\ang{z}^{-p}}{|y-z|})$ using $|y-z|\ge\ang{y}/8$. This and $|1-a^{p+1}|\le C|1-a|$ give the first bound. For fixed $z$, $\p_yS_\phi(y,z)=\frac{\phi'(y)-S_\phi}{y-z}$, hence $|\p_yK_\epsilon|\le C\bigl(|\phi''(y)||y-z|^{-1-p}+|\phi'(y)-S_\phi||y-z|^{-2-p}\bigr)$ \begin{equation} \le C|c_\epsilon|\Bigl(\frac{\ang{y}^{-p-2}}{|y-z|^{p+1}}+\frac{\ang{y}^{-p-1}}{|y-z|^{p+2}}+\frac{\ang{z}^{-p}}{|y-z|^{p+3}}\Bigr), \end{equation} and the middle term is $\le8\ang{y}^{-p-2}|y-z|^{-p-1}$.

nodes.title: Derivative of $\mc R_{2,\epsilon}r$
nodes.statement_html: Let $\gamma$ be admissible, $0\le\epsilon\le\epsilon_c$, $r\in X_\gamma$. Then $\mc R_{2,\epsilon}r$ is locally Lipschitz and for a.e.\ $y$ \[ \p_y(\mc R_{2,\epsilon}r)(y)=\int_\R\bigl[(\p_y+\p_z)K_\epsilon(y,z)\,r'(z)+K_\epsilon(y,z)\,r''(z)\bigr]dz, \] the integral being absolutely convergent, locally uniformly in $y$.
nodes.proof_html: Write $\mc R_{2,\epsilon}r(y)=\int k(y,u)r'(y-u)du$ with $k(y,u)=K_\epsilon(y,y-u)$; then $\p_yk(y,u)=[(\p_y+\p_z)K_\epsilon](y,y-u)$. By the global bound of lem:c08_R2_kernel_near, $|k|+|\p_yk|\le C\min(|u|^{-p},|u|^{-1-p})\in L^1(du)$. Also $|r''(y-u)|\le\|r\|w_2(y-u)\le\|r\|\ang{y-u}^{s}$ with $s=\max(0,\frac2p-\gamma)<\frac1p-\beta=\frac{1-p}{2p}<p$ (since $\gamma>\beta+\frac1p$ and $2p^2+p-1>0$), so $\int\min(|u|^{-p},|u|^{-1-p})\ang{y-u}^{s}du<\infty$ locally uniformly in $y$. For $y_0<y_1$, $u\mapsto$ fixed, $y\mapsto k(y,u)r'(y-u)$ is absolutely continuous with derivative $\p_yk\,r'+k\,r''$ a.e.; integrate in $y\in[y_0,y_1]$ and use Fubini to get $\mc R_{2,\epsilon}r(y_1)-\mc R_{2,\epsilon}r(y_0)=\int_{y_0}^{y_1}(\text{RHS})\,dy$. Change back $z=y-u$. Lean route (Lipschitz domination, no Fubini over $[y_0,y_1]\times\R$): at every $x_0$ apply differentiation under the integral in the variable $u=y-z$ with a Lipschitz majorant: for a.e.\ $u$, $x\mapsto K_\epsilon(x,x-u)r'(x-u)$ is Lipschitz on $B(x_0,1)$ with constant $C\|r\|\ang{x_0}G(u)$, $G(u)=\mathbf 1_{|u|\le1}|u|^{-p}+4\ang u^{-1-p+s}\in L^1$, and differentiable at $x_0$ whenever $r'$ is differentiable at $x_0-u$; hence $\mc R_{2,\epsilon}r$ is differentiable everywhere with the stated derivative, and local Lipschitz continuity follows by the mean value theorem.

nodes.title: $\mc R_{2,\epsilon}$, near contributions
nodes.statement_html:
Let $\gamma$ be admissible and fix $\vartheta\in C_c^\infty(\R;[0,1])$ with $\vartheta=1$ on $[-\frac18,\frac18]$, $\operatorname{supp}\vartheta\subset[-\frac14,\frac14]$. There is $C=C(p,\gamma,\chi_+,\vartheta)$ such that for $0\le\epsilon\le\epsilon_c$, $r\in X_\gamma$ and $y\in\R$ (a.e.\ $y$ in (2)):
  • $\bigl|\int_{|y-z|\le\ang{y}/4}K_\epsilon(y,z)r'(z)dz\bigr|\le C|c_\epsilon|\|r\|_{X_\gamma}\ang{y}^{-\gamma}$;
  • $\bigl|\int\vartheta(\frac{y-z}{\ang{y}})\bigl[(\p_y+\p_z)K_\epsilon\,r'(z)+K_\epsilon\,r''(z)\bigr]dz\bigr|\le C|c_\epsilon|\|r\|_{X_\gamma}\ang{y}^{-\gamma+1/p}$;
and both integrals vanish for $y\le0$.
nodes.proof_html: Vanishing for $y\le0$: lem:c08_R2_kernel_near(1). For $y>0$: in the region $\ang{z}\approx\ang{y}$, so $|r'(z)|\le C\|r\|\ang{y}^{-\gamma+1/p}$, $|r''(z)|\le C\|r\|\ang{y}^{-\gamma+2/p}$; and $\int_{|y-z|\le\ang{y}/4}|y-z|^{-p}dz=\frac{2}{1-p}(\ang{y}/4)^{1-p}$. Then (1) is bounded by $C|c_\epsilon|\|r\|\ang{y}^{-p-2+1-p-\gamma+1/p}=C|c_\epsilon|\|r\|\ang{y}^{-\gamma+(1/p-2p-1)}\le C|c_\epsilon|\|r\|\ang{y}^{-\gamma}$ since $\frac1p<2p+1$. In (2) (support of $\vartheta$ inside $|y-z|\le\ang{y}/4$), $|\ldots|\le C|c_\epsilon|\ang{y}^{-p-2}\int|y-z|^{-p}(\ang{y}^{-1}|r'|+|r''|)\le C|c_\epsilon|\|r\|\ang{y}^{-\gamma+2/p-2p-1}\le C|c_\epsilon|\|r\|\ang{y}^{-\gamma+1/p}$.

nodes.title: $\mc R_{2,\epsilon}$, far contributions
nodes.statement_html:
Let $\gamma$ be admissible and $\vartheta$ as in lem:c08_R2_near. There is $C$ such that for $0\le\epsilon\le\epsilon_c$, $r\in X_\gamma$ and (a.e.) $y\in\R$:
  • $\bigl|\int_{|y-z|>\ang{y}/4}K_\epsilon(y,z)r'(z)dz\bigr|\le C|c_\epsilon|\|r\|_{X_\gamma}\ang{y}^{-p-2}$;
  • the identity (boundary terms vanish) \begin{equation} \int\Bigl[1-\vartheta\Bigl(\tfrac{y-z}{\ang{y}}\Bigr)\Bigr]\bigl[(\p_y+\p_z)K_\epsilon\,r'+K_\epsilon\,r''\bigr]dz =\int\Bigl[1-\vartheta\Bigl(\tfrac{y-z}{\ang{y}}\Bigr)\Bigr]\p_yK_\epsilon\,r'\,dz-\frac1{\ang{y}}\int\vartheta'\Bigl(\tfrac{y-z}{\ang{y}}\Bigr)K_\epsilon\,r'\,dz \end{equation} holds, and the left side is bounded by $C|c_\epsilon|\|r\|_{X_\gamma}\ang{y}^{-p-3}$.
nodes.proof_html: (1) By lem:c08_R2_kernel_far and $|y-z|>\ang{y}/4$, $\ang{z}^{-p}\le1$: $|K_\epsilon|\le C|c_\epsilon|(\ang{y}^{-2p-2}+\ang{y}^{-p-2})$; multiply by $|r'|$ and integrate, using $\|r'\|_{L^1}\le C\|r\|_{X_\gamma}$ (lem:c08_L1_embedding, $\gamma-\frac1p>1$). (2) On the support of $1-\vartheta(\frac{y-z}{\ang{y}})$, $|y-z|\ge\ang{y}/8>0$, so $z\mapsto K_\epsilon(y,z)r'(z)$ is locally absolutely continuous there with derivative $\p_zK_\epsilon r'+K_\epsilon r''$. Split $(\p_y+\p_z)K_\epsilon=\p_yK_\epsilon+\p_zK_\epsilon$ and integrate by parts on $[-R,R]$; the boundary terms $(1-\vartheta)K_\epsilon r'$ at $\pm R$ tend to $0$ ($|K_\epsilon|\le C|y-z|^{-1-p}$, $r'$ bounded), and $\p_z[1-\vartheta(\frac{y-z}{\ang{y}})]=\ang{y}^{-1}\vartheta'(\frac{y-z}{\ang{y}})$. All integrals converge absolutely (lem:c08_R2_derivative). First term on the right: by lem:c08_R2_kernel_far and $|y-z|\ge\ang{y}/8$, it is $\le C|c_\epsilon|(\ang{y}^{-2p-3}+\ang{y}^{-p-3})\|r'\|_{L^1}$. Second term: $\vartheta'$ is supported in $\frac18\ang{y}\le|y-z|\le\frac14\ang{y}$, where lem:c08_R2_kernel_near(2) gives $|K_\epsilon|\le C|c_\epsilon|\ang{y}^{-2p-2}$; so it is $\le C|c_\epsilon|\ang{y}^{-2p-3}\|r'\|_{L^1}$.

nodes.title: $\mc R_{2,\epsilon}$ is small from $X_\gamma$ to $Y_\gamma$
nodes.statement_html: Let $\gamma$ be admissible. There is $C=C(p,\gamma,\chi_+,C_0)$ such that for $0\le\epsilon\le\epsilon_c$ and $r\in X_\gamma$: $\mc R_{2,\epsilon}r\in Y_\gamma$ and $\|\mc R_{2,\epsilon}r\|_{Y_\gamma}\le C\epsilon\|r\|_{X_\gamma}$.
nodes.proof_html: $\mc R_{2,\epsilon}r$ is locally Lipschitz (lem:c08_R2_derivative), so in $W^{1,\infty}_{\rm loc}$. Value: split at $|y-z|=\ang{y}/4$: $|\mc R_{2,\epsilon}r(y)|\le C|c_\epsilon|\|r\|(\ang{y}^{-\gamma}+\ang{y}^{-p-2})\le C|c_\epsilon|\|r\|\ang{y}^{-\gamma}$ because $\gamma<2p+1<p+2$. Derivative: split the integrand of lem:c08_R2_derivative with $\vartheta+(1-\vartheta)$: for $y\ge0$, $|\p_y\mc R_{2,\epsilon}r|\le C|c_\epsilon|\|r\|(\ang{y}^{-\gamma+1/p}+\ang{y}^{-p-3})\le C|c_\epsilon|\|r\|\ang{y}^{-\gamma+1/p}$; for $y\le0$ only the far part survives: $\le C|c_\epsilon|\|r\|\ang{y}^{-p-3}\le C|c_\epsilon|\|r\|\ang{y}^{-\gamma-1}$ since $\gamma+1<p+3$. Finally $|c_\epsilon|\le C_0\epsilon$.

nodes.title: Conjugation of the linear operator
nodes.statement_html:
There are $\epsilon_c>0$ (depending only on $p,\chi_+$ and the constant $C_0$ of lem:analysis_coefficient) and, for every admissible $\gamma$, a constant $C(\gamma)$ such that for all $0\le\epsilon\le\epsilon_c$:
  • $\mc U_\epsilon,\mc V_\epsilon$ (def:U_eps, def:V_eps) are $\R$-linear bijections of the space of all functions $\R\to\R$, independent of $\gamma$; they restrict to bijections $X_\gamma\to X_\gamma$, resp.\ $Y_\gamma\to Y_\gamma$, and $\|\mc U_\epsilon\|_{X_\gamma\to X_\gamma},\|\mc U_\epsilon^{-1}\|_{X_\gamma\to X_\gamma},\|\mc V_\epsilon\|_{Y_\gamma\to Y_\gamma},\|\mc V_\epsilon^{-1}\|_{Y_\gamma\to Y_\gamma}\le C(\gamma)$;
  • $\mc R_\epsilon$ maps $X_\gamma$ into $Y_\gamma$ with $\|\mc R_\epsilon r\|_{Y_\gamma}\le C(\gamma)\epsilon\|r\|_{X_\gamma}$;
  • $\mc V_\epsilon\bigl(\mc L_0(\mc U_\epsilon r)\bigr)=\mc L_\epsilon r$ pointwise on $\R$, for all $r\in X_\gamma$;
  • $\|(\mc V_\epsilon^{-1}-I)G\|_{Y_\gamma}\le C(\gamma)\epsilon\sup_{y>1}\ang{y}^\gamma(|G|+|G'|+|G''|)$ for $G\in Y_\gamma\cap C^2((1,\infty))$;
  • for every $\delta>0$: $\sup_{\mu\in\ov B(\mu_*,\delta)}\|(\mc V_\epsilon^{-1}-I)G_\mu\|_{Y_\gamma}\le C(\gamma)\,\epsilon\,\delta/|\mu_*|$.
nodes.proof_html: (1): def:U_eps, def:V_eps, lem:c08_U_bounded, lem:c08_V_bounded. (2): lem:c08_R1_bound, lem:c08_R2_bound. (3): lem:c08_conjugation_identity. (4): lem:c08_V_inverse_minus_identity. (5): lem:c08_V_inverse_G_mu.

nodes.title: Shifted fractional kernel: domination and continuity
nodes.statement_html: Let $0<p<1$, $A,M,N\ge0$, and let $w:\R\to\C$ be locally Lipschitz with $|w(x)|\le M$ for every $x$ and $|w'(x)|\le A\ang{x}^N$ for a.e.\ $x$. For every $B\ge1$, $|x|\le B$ and $h\ne0$, \[ \frac{|w(x)-w(x-h)|}{|h|^{1+p}}\le A\ang{B+1}^N|h|^{-p}\mathbf1_{\{0<|h|\le1\}} +2M|h|^{-1-p}\mathbf1_{\{|h|>1\}}. \] The right side is integrable in $h$. Consequently the integral defining $|D|^pw(x)$ is absolutely convergent for every $x$, $|D|^pw$ is continuous, and there is $C_{p,N}>0$, independent of $A,M,w,x$, such that $|\,|D|^pw(x)|\le C_{p,N}(A+M)\ang{x}^N$ for every $x$.
nodes.proof_html:
On the segment between $x-h$ and $x$, for $|h|\le1$ and $|x|\le B$, the a.e.\ derivative bound is
  $A\ang{B+1}^N$. Local Lipschitz regularity implies absolute continuity there, so the fundamental
  theorem of calculus bounds the increment by $A\ang{B+1}^N|h|$. Outside $[-1,1]$ use $2M$.
  Integrate the powers separately; they are integrable because $p<1$ near zero and $p>0$ at infinity.
  For continuity, use this common majorant on a compact neighborhood of $x$ in the shifted formula.
  For growth, apply the same argument with the local derivative bound
  $A\ang{|x|+1}^N\le C_NA\ang{x}^N$, and use $\ang{x}^N\ge1$ for the far part.

nodes.title: Fractional integration by parts against Schwartz functions
nodes.statement_html: Let $0<p<1$, let $w\in L^1(\R;\C)$ be bounded and locally Lipschitz, and suppose $|w'(x)|\le A\ang{x}^N$ a.e.\ for some $A,N\ge0$. For every $\varphi\in\mathcal S(\R;\C)$, \[ \int_{\R^2}\frac{|w(x)-w(x-h)|\,|\varphi(x)|}{|h|^{1+p}}\,dx\,dh<\infty, \] and both pairings below converge absolutely and satisfy the bilinear identity \[ \int_\R (|D|^pw)(x)\varphi(x)\,dx =\int_\R w(x)(|D|^p\varphi)(x)\,dx . \] No complex conjugation is used in these pairings.
nodes.proof_html: Integrate the near/far majorants of lem:c08_frac_shift_majorant against $|\varphi(x)|$; polynomial weights times a Schwartz function are integrable. To exchange the differences, first restrict the $h$ integral to $\delta<|h|<L$ with $0<\delta<L$. Each separated term is then absolutely integrable, so translation in $x$ and symmetry $h\mapsto-h$ transfer the difference from $w$ to $\varphi$. Let $\delta\downarrow0$ and $L\to\infty$ using the established domination. On the transferred side, the bound $|\varphi(x)-\varphi(x+h)|\le\min\{|h|\|\varphi'\|_\infty,2\|\varphi\|_\infty\}$, together with $w\in L^1$, supplies the corresponding integrable majorant. Lean route: no truncation $\delta<|h|<L$; Fubini is applied directly to the two absolutely integrable double integrals, splitting the $x$-integral for each fixed $h$.

nodes.title: The fractional multiplier in Schwartz-test form
nodes.statement_html: Let $0<p<1$ and let $w\in L^1(\R;\C)$ be bounded and locally Lipschitz with $|w'(x)|\le A\ang{x}^N$ a.e.\ for some $A,N\ge0$. For every $\varphi\in\mathcal S(\R;\C)$, \[ \int_\R(|D|^pw)(x)\widehat\varphi(x)\,dx =\int_\R |\xi|^p\widehat w(\xi)\varphi(\xi)\,d\xi, \] and both integrals are absolutely convergent. This is $\operatorname{HasDistFourier}(|D|^pw,\xi\mapsto|\xi|^p\widehat w(\xi))$ in the Fourier convention of def:fourier_convention.
nodes.proof_html: Apply lem:c08_frac_pairing_fubini with $\widehat\varphi$, which is Schwartz. The Schwartz multiplier identity in lem:c01_frac_singular_integral, applied to real and imaginary parts and converted to the present Fourier normalization, gives $|D|^p\widehat\varphi=\widehat{(|\cdot|^p\varphi)}$. Fubini then gives $\int w\,\widehat{(|\cdot|^p\varphi)}=\int\widehat w\,|\xi|^p\varphi$: its absolute majorant is $|w(x)|\,|\xi|^p|\varphi(\xi)|\in L^1(\R^2)$. The left pairing is integrable by the polynomial bound from lem:c08_frac_shift_majorant. Lean route: the multiplier identity $|D|^p\hat\varphi=\widehat{|\xi|^p\varphi}$ is re-derived for complex Schwartz $\varphi$ (the chapter-1 singular-integral lemma is stated only for real $\varphi$), from the integral $\int(1-\cos(az))|z|^{-1-p}dz=c\,|a|^p$.

nodes.title: Fourier transform of the singular integral on $L^1$ functions
nodes.statement_html: Let $w\in L^1(\R;\C)$ be bounded and locally Lipschitz with $|w'(x)|\le A\ang{x}^N$ a.e.\ for some $A,N\ge0$. Then $|D|^pw$ (def:frac_multiplier) is continuous with $|\,|D|^pw(x)|\le C\ang{x}^N$, and its distributional Fourier transform is the bounded-times-$|\xi|^p$ function $|\xi|^p\widehat w(\xi)$.
nodes.proof_html: Choose a nonnegative bound $M$ for $|w|$. Continuity and polynomial growth follow from lem:c08_frac_shift_majorant; lem:c08_frac_test_transform is precisely the required distributional Fourier identity, with absolute convergence of every test pairing.

nodes.title: Fourier transform of an integrable weak derivative
nodes.statement_html: Let $u:\R\to\C$ be locally Lipschitz, with $u,u'\in L^1(\R)$ and $u(x)\to0$ as $x\to\pm\infty$. Here $u'$ is the a.e.\ derivative, represented by Lean's total derivative. For every $\xi\in\R$, \[ \widehat{u'}(\xi)=i\xi\widehat u(\xi). \] Both Fourier integrals are absolutely convergent; $\widehat u$ is continuous and $|\widehat u(\xi)|\le\|u\|_{L^1}$ for every $\xi$.
nodes.proof_html:
Integrate by parts on $[-R,R]$, using absolute continuity of $u$ on compact intervals.
  The endpoint terms $u(\pm R)e^{\mp iR\xi}$ tend to zero. The two integral terms converge by the
  $L^1$ assumptions, proving the identity also at $\xi=0$. Dominated convergence proves continuity
  of $\widehat u$, and the integral triangle inequality gives its bound.

nodes.title: Fourier-test identity for the dilation term
nodes.statement_html: Let $u:\R\to\C$ be locally Lipschitz with $u,u'\in L^1(\R)$ and $u(x)\to0$ as $x\to\pm\infty$. For every $\varphi\in\mathcal S(\R;\C)$, \[ \int_\R -x u'(x)\widehat\varphi(x)\,dx =-\int_\R \xi\widehat u(\xi)\varphi'(\xi)\,d\xi, \] with both integrals absolutely convergent. In particular the distributional transform of $-xu'$ is $\partial_\xi(\xi\widehat u)$, in this tested sense.
nodes.proof_html: Since $\widehat{\varphi'}(x)=ix\widehat\varphi(x)$, the left integral equals $i\int u'(x)\widehat{\varphi'}(x)dx$. Fubini is justified by $u'\in L^1$ and $\varphi'\in L^1$, and gives $i\int\widehat{u'}\varphi'$. Substitute lem:c08_fourier_deriv_L1 and use $i^2=-1$. The original left integrand is integrable because $x\widehat\varphi(x)$ is bounded; the right one is integrable because $\widehat u$ is bounded and $\xi\varphi'(\xi)$ is integrable.

nodes.title: $\mc L_0$ on the Fourier side
nodes.statement_html: Let $\gamma>1+\frac1p$ and $r\in X_\gamma$. Then $\widehat r$ is bounded and continuous, $\mc L_0r$ is continuous and polynomially bounded, and in $\mathcal S'(\R)$ \[ \widehat{\mc L_0r}(\xi)=i\xi|\xi|^p\,\widehat r(\xi)+\widehat r(\xi)+\p_\xi\bigl(\xi\,\widehat r(\xi)\bigr), \] where $\p_\xi$ is the distributional derivative.
nodes.proof_html: The weighted bounds and lem:c08_L1_embedding imply $r,r'\in L^1$, boundedness of $r'$, and $r\to0$ at both infinities. Apply lem:c08_fourier_deriv_L1 to $u=r$. The function $r'$ is locally Lipschitz and its a.e.\ derivative satisfies $|r''(x)|\le\|r\|_{X_\gamma}\ang{x}^{2/p}$, so lem:c08_frac_kernel_fourier applies to $r'$. It gives continuity, polynomial growth and transform $i\xi|\xi|^p\widehat r$ for the fractional term. The local terms $r-xr'$ are continuous and polynomially bounded directly from the weighted bounds; their test identities are Fubini for $r\in L^1$ and lem:c08_drift_test_transform. Adding the three absolutely convergent pairings gives the displayed identity.

nodes.title: The free inverse $\mc T_0$ and the subspace $\sq Y_\gamma$
nodes.statement_html: For $\gamma>1$ and $G\in Y_\gamma$ (so $G\in L^1$ and $\widehat G$ is bounded and continuous) define $m_G:\R\to\C$, \begin{equation} m_G(\xi):=\int_0^1t\,e^{-i(1-t^{p+1})\Phi_0(\xi)}\,\widehat G(t\xi)\,dt \;=\;\frac{e^{-i\Phi_0(\xi)}}{\xi^2}\int_0^\xi\eta\,e^{i\Phi_0(\eta)}\widehat G(\eta)\,d\eta\quad(\xi\neq0), \end{equation} (for $\xi<0$, $\int_0^\xi$ is the oriented integral) and $\mc T_0G:=\widecheck{m_G}\in\mathcal S'(\R)$, i.e.\ the tempered distribution with $\widehat{\mc T_0G}=m_G$. $\mc T_0$ is $\R$-linear and its definition does not involve $\gamma$. For admissible $\gamma$, $\sq Y_\gamma:=\{G\in Y_\gamma:\ell(G)=0\}$ (as in def:ell). We say $\mc T_0G\in X_\gamma$ if there is $r\in X_\gamma$ with $\widehat r=m_G$; this $r$ is unique and is identified with $\mc T_0G$.

nodes.title: Properties of the symbol $m_G$; the ODE in $\xi$
nodes.statement_html:
Let $\gamma>1$ and $G\in Y_\gamma$. Then:
  • the two expressions in eqn:linear_free_inverse agree for $\xi\neq0$; $m_G$ is continuous on $\R$, $|m_G|\le\frac12\|G\|_{L^1}$, $m_G(0)=\frac12\widehat G(0)$;
  • $m_G(-\xi)=\ov{m_G(\xi)}$; hence $\mc T_0G$ is real (as a distribution);
  • $m_G\in C^1(\R\setminus\{0\})$ and $\xi\,m_G'(\xi)+\bigl(2+i\xi|\xi|^p\bigr)m_G(\xi)=\widehat G(\xi)$ for $\xi\neq0$; equivalently $\p_\xi\bigl(\xi^2e^{i\Phi_0(\xi)}m_G(\xi)\bigr)=\xi e^{i\Phi_0(\xi)}\widehat G(\xi)$;
  • $\xi\mapsto\xi m_G(\xi)$ is locally Lipschitz on $\R$ and $\p_\xi(\xi m_G)+m_G+i\xi|\xi|^pm_G=\widehat G$ a.e.\ and in $\mathcal D'(\R)$.
nodes.proof_html:
(1) Substitute $\eta=t\xi$ and use $\Phi_0(t\xi)=t^{p+1}\Phi_0(\xi)$ ($t>0$, both signs of $\xi$). Continuity: dominated
  convergence in the $t$-form ($|\widehat G|\le\|G\|_{L^1}$, $\int_0^1t\,dt=\frac12$). (2) $\widehat G(-\eta)=\ov{\widehat G(\eta)}$ ($G$ real),
  $\Phi_0$ odd. (3) FTC applied to the second expression ($\widehat G$ continuous), using $\Phi_0'=|\xi|^p$:
  $m_G'=-i|\xi|^pm_G-\frac2\xi m_G+\frac{\widehat G}{\xi}$. (4) For $\xi\ne0$, $(\xi m_G)'=m_G+\xi m_G'=\widehat G-m_G-i\xi|\xi|^pm_G$,
  bounded on compacts; $\xi m_G$ is continuous at $0$ (value $0$); a continuous function, $C^1$ off $0$ with locally
  bounded derivative, is locally Lipschitz, and its distributional derivative is the a.e.\ derivative.

nodes.title: Uniqueness: $\mc L_0$ is injective on $X_\gamma$
nodes.statement_html: Let $\gamma>1+\frac1p$, $r\in X_\gamma$, $G\in Y_\gamma$ with $\mc L_0r=G$ pointwise. Then $\widehat r=m_G$, i.e.\ $r=\mc T_0G$. In particular $\mc L_0r=0$, $r\in X_\gamma$ implies $r=0$.
nodes.proof_html: By lem:c08_L0_fourier, $\p_\xi(\xi\widehat r)+\widehat r+i\xi|\xi|^p\widehat r=\widehat G$ in $\mathcal D'(\R)$. On $(0,\infty)$ multiply by the smooth function $\xi e^{i\Phi_0}$ (Leibniz rule for distributions): $\p_\xi(\xi^2e^{i\Phi_0}\widehat r)=\xi e^{i\Phi_0}\widehat G$ in $\mathcal D'((0,\infty))$. Hence $\xi^2e^{i\Phi_0}\widehat r-\int_0^\xi\eta e^{i\Phi_0}\widehat G\,d\eta$ has zero distributional derivative on $(0,\infty)$, so equals a constant $\kappa_+$ a.e., hence everywhere (both continuous). Let $\xi\to0^+$: the left side tends to $0$ since $\widehat r$ is bounded; so $\kappa_+=0$. Same on $(-\infty,0)$. Thus $\widehat r=m_G$ off $0$, and at $0$ by continuity.

nodes.title: $\mc T_0$ is a right inverse whenever $\mc T_0G\in X_\gamma$
nodes.statement_html: Let $\gamma>1+\frac1p$ and $G\in Y_\gamma$, and suppose $r\in X_\gamma$ satisfies $\widehat r=m_G$. Then $\mc L_0r=G$ pointwise on $\R$. (No condition $\ell(G)=0$ is assumed here; it is needed only to have $\mc T_0G\in X_\gamma$.)
nodes.proof_html: By lem:c08_L0_fourier and lem:c08_free_ode(4), $\widehat{\mc L_0r}=\widehat G$ in $\mathcal S'$. By injectivity of the Fourier transform on $\mathcal S'$, $\mc L_0r=G$ as distributions, hence a.e.; both are continuous, so everywhere.

nodes.title: Truncated kernel of $\ell$
nodes.statement_html: For $R>0$, $y\in\R$ put $K_R(y):=-i\int_0^Re^{i(\Phi_0(\xi)-y\xi)}d\xi$. Then for each $y$ the limit $K(y):=\lim_{R\to\infty}K_R(y)$ exists, and there is $C=C(p)$ with \[ \sup_{R>0}|K_R(y)|\le C\,\varpi(y),\qquad \varpi(y)=\ang{y}^{-1}\ (y\le0),\quad \varpi(y)=\ang{y}^{\frac{1-p}{2p}}\ (y\ge0). \]
nodes.proof_html: Write $F_y(\xi)=e^{i(\Phi_0(\xi)-y\xi)}$ and $L_y=\int_0^1F_y(\xi)d\xi+E_y(1)$, where $E_y$ is the tail integral of lem:appendix_stationary. Splitting the proper integral at $1$ shows $\int_0^R F_y\to L_y$, hence $K_R(y)\to-iL_y$. For $\eta>0$, $E_y(\eta)=\int_\eta^1 F_y+E_y(1)$; continuity of the proper integral at $\eta=0$ gives $E_y(\eta)\to L_y$, so the same tail estimate bounds $|L_y|$ by $C\varpi(y)$. Finally $\int_0^R F_y=L_y-E_y(R)$, hence $|K_R(y)|\le2C\varpi(y)$ uniformly in $R>0$.

nodes.title: Continuity of $\ell$
nodes.statement_html: Let $\gamma>\beta+\frac1p$ (in particular every admissible $\gamma$). For every $G\in Y_\gamma$ the limit $\ell(G)=\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_0^R\xi e^{i\Phi_0(\xi)}\widehat G(\xi)d\xi$ of def:ell exists, \[ \ell(G)=\int_\R G'(y)K(y)\,dy\qquad(K\text{ from lem:c08_ell_kernel, the integral absolutely convergent}), \] and there is $C=C(p,\gamma)$ with $|\ell(G)|\le C\|G\|_{Y_\gamma}$. Thus $\ell:Y_\gamma\to\C$ is a continuous $\R$-linear functional and $\sq Y_\gamma$ is a closed subspace.
nodes.proof_html: By lem:c08_L1_embedding, $\xi\widehat G(\xi)=-i\widehat{G'}(\xi)$, so by Fubini on $[0,R]\times\R$ ($G'\in L^1$), $\int_0^R\xi e^{i\Phi_0}\widehat G\,d\xi=\int_\R G'(y)K_R(y)\,dy$. Now $|G'(y)K_R(y)|\le C\|G\|_{Y_\gamma}v(y)$ with $v(y)=\ang{y}^{-\gamma-2}$ for $y\le0$ and $v(y)=\ang{y}^{-\gamma+\frac1p+\frac{1-p}{2p}}=\ang{y}^{-\gamma+\frac{3-p}{2p}}$ for $y\ge0$; $v\in L^1$ iff $\gamma>\frac{3-p}{2p}+1=\frac{p+3}{2p}=\beta+\frac1p$. Dominated convergence gives existence of the limit, the formula, and $|\ell(G)|\le C\|G\|_{Y_\gamma}\|v\|_{L^1}$.

nodes.title: Tail form of $m_G$ on $\sq Y_\gamma$
nodes.statement_html: Let $\gamma>\beta+\frac1p$ and $G\in Y_\gamma$ with $\ell(G)=0$. Then, with improper integrals $\int_\xi^\infty:=\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_\xi^R$ and $\int_{-\infty}^\xi:=\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_{-R}^\xi$ (which exist), \begin{equation} m_G(\xi)=-\frac{e^{-i\Phi_0(\xi)}}{\xi^2}\int_\xi^\infty\eta e^{i\Phi_0(\eta)}\widehat G(\eta)\,d\eta\quad(\xi>0),\qquad m_G(\xi)=\frac{e^{-i\Phi_0(\xi)}}{\xi^2}\int_{-\infty}^\xi\eta e^{i\Phi_0(\eta)}\widehat G(\eta)\,d\eta\quad(\xi<0). \end{equation}
nodes.proof_html: $\xi>0$: $\int_0^\xi=\ell(G)-\lim_R\int_\xi^R=-\int_\xi^\infty$ (limit exists by prop:linear_ell_continuity). $\xi<0$: substituting $\eta=-s$ and using $\widehat G(-s)=\ov{\widehat G(s)}$, $\Phi_0$ odd: $\int_{-R}^0\eta e^{i\Phi_0}\widehat G\,d\eta=-\ov{\int_0^R s e^{i\Phi_0}\widehat G\,ds}\to-\ov{\ell(G)}=0$. Hence $\int_0^\xi=-\int_\xi^0=\lim_R\int_{-R}^\xi$.

nodes.title: Low/high frequency splitting of $\mc T_0$
nodes.statement_html: Fix $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\R;[0,1])$ even, with $\chi=1$ on $[-1,1]$ and $\operatorname{supp}\chi\subset[-2,2]$ (the same $\chi$ as in prop:appendix_nonsmooth_fourier_inverse and as in chapter 09). For $\gamma>1$, $G\in Y_\gamma$: \begin{equation} \widehat{\mc T_{\rm l}G}:=\chi\,m_G,\qquad \widehat{\mc T_{\rm h}G}:=(1-\chi)\,m_G, \end{equation} i.e.\ $\mc T_{\rm l}G(y)=\frac1{2\pi}\int\chi(\xi)m_G(\xi)e^{iy\xi}d\xi$ (a bounded $C^\infty$ real function, as $\chi m_G$ is bounded, compactly supported and Hermitian), and $\mc T_{\rm h}G=\widecheck{((1-\chi)m_G)}\in\mathcal S'$. In Lean, the high-frequency operator is the continuous, polynomially bounded real representative with this transform when one exists, and is $0$ otherwise, as for $\mc T_0$ in def:T_0. Membership in $X_\gamma$ alone therefore does not establish its Fourier transform; the reconstruction statement and its norm bound are recorded separately in lem:c08_frequency_split_sum.

nodes.title: Intermediate space $Z_\gamma$
nodes.statement_html: For $\gamma\in\R$ let $Z_\gamma$ be the space of continuous $H:\R\to\C$ with $H|_{(-\infty,-1)}\in W^{2,\infty}_{\rm loc}((-\infty,-1))$ and \[ \|H\|_{Z_\gamma}:=\sup_{y\in\R}\ang{y}^\gamma|H(y)|+\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{y\le-1}\ang{y}^\gamma\bigl(\ang{y}|H'(y)|+\ang{y}^2|H''(y)|\bigr)<\infty. \]

nodes.title: Averaging operators and low-frequency multipliers
nodes.statement_html: For $k\in\N_0$, $\gamma>1$, $G\in Y_\gamma$: \begin{equation} \mc A_kG(y):=\int_0^1(1-t^\alpha)^kG(y/t)\,dt . \end{equation} Let \begin{equation} m_k(\xi):=\chi(\xi)\Phi_0(\xi)^k,\qquad H_k:=\widecheck{m_k},\ \ H_k(y)=\frac1{2\pi}\int m_k(\xi)e^{iy\xi}d\xi,\qquad \mc M_kH:=H_k*H . \end{equation}

nodes.title: Kernel bounds for $H_k$
nodes.statement_html: There are $C_1,C_2$ (depending on $p,\chi$) such that for all $k\ge0$, $j\in\{0,1,2\}$, $y\in\R$: \begin{equation} |\p^jH_k(y)|\le C_1C_2^k\ang{y}^{-p-2-j}, \end{equation} hence $\|\p^jH_k\|_{L^1}\le C_1'C_2^k$. Moreover $H_k\in C^\infty$, $H_k$ is real for even $k$ and purely imaginary for odd $k$, so $(-i)^kH_k$ is real.
nodes.proof_html: The bound is prop:appendix_nonsmooth_fourier_inverse (same normalisation of $\widecheck{\ }$ up to the factor $\frac1{2\pi}$). Smoothness: $m_k$ is bounded with compact support. Parity: $m_k$ is real with $m_k(-\xi)=(-1)^km_k(\xi)$.

nodes.title: Weighted convolution
nodes.statement_html: Let $a\ge b>1$. Then $\int_\R\ang{y-z}^{-a}\ang{z}^{-b}dz\le C_{a,b}\ang{y}^{-b}$ for all $y$.
nodes.proof_html:
On $|z|\ge|y|/2$: $\ang{z}\ge\ang{y}/2$, so the contribution is $\le2^b\ang{y}^{-b}\int\ang{u}^{-a}du$. On $|z|<|y|/2$:
  $|y-z|\ge|y|/2$, $\ang{y-z}^{-a}\le2^a\ang{y}^{-a}\le2^a\ang{y}^{-b}$, times $\int\ang{z}^{-b}dz$.

nodes.title: Integrability and Fourier transform of the averaging operator
nodes.statement_html: Let $\frac34<p<1$, $\gamma>1$, and $G\in Y_\gamma$. For every integer $k\ge0$, $\mc A_kG\in L^1(\R)$ with $\|\mc A_kG\|_{L^1}\le\frac12\|G\|_{L^1}$, and for every $\xi\in\R$, \[ \widehat{\mc A_kG}(\xi)=\int_0^1t(1-t^{p+1})^k\widehat G(t\xi)\,dt . \] The double integrals used to exchange the $y$ and $t$ integrations converge absolutely.
nodes.proof_html:
From the value part of the $Y_\gamma$ norm and $\gamma>1$, $G\in L^1$.
  For $t>0$, substitution $y=tu$ gives $\int|G(y/t)|dy=t\|G\|_1$.
  Since $0\le(1-t^{p+1})^k\le1$ on $[0,1]$, Tonelli bounds the absolute double integral by
  $\|G\|_1\int_0^1t\,dt=\frac12\|G\|_1$. Fubini is therefore valid, also after multiplication by
  $e^{-iy\xi}$; the same substitution gives the Fourier identity. The value assigned at $t=0$ is irrelevant.

nodes.title: Fourier transform of a low-frequency convolution
nodes.statement_html: Let $\frac34<p<1$ and $k\ge0$. Then $H_k\in L^1(\R;\C)$ and $\widehat H_k=m_k$ pointwise. For every $H\in L^1(\R;\C)$, the defining convolution $\mc M_kH(y)$ is absolutely convergent for every $y$, belongs to $L^1(\R;\C)$, and \[ \|\mc M_kH\|_{L^1}\le\|H_k\|_{L^1}\|H\|_{L^1},\qquad \widehat{\mc M_kH}(\xi)=m_k(\xi)\widehat H(\xi)\quad(\xi\in\R). \]
nodes.proof_html: The kernel lemma supplies $H_k\in L^1\cap L^\infty$. The symbol $m_k$ is continuous with compact support, so Fourier inversion with both $m_k$ and its inverse transform integrable gives $\widehat H_k=m_k$ everywhere. Boundedness of $H_k$ gives pointwise absolute convergence. Tonelli bounds the absolute integral of the convolution by the product of the $L^1$ norms. Fubini, followed by $u=y-z$, proves the Fourier product identity with the stated $2\pi$ convention.

nodes.title: Uniform Fourier-side Taylor series
nodes.statement_html: Let $\frac34<p<1$, $\gamma>1$, and $G\in Y_\gamma$. Put $M_p=2^{p+1}/(p+1)$ and, for $n\in\N$, \[ Q_n(\xi)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\frac{(-i)^k}{k!}m_k(\xi)\widehat{\mc A_kG}(\xi),\qquad e_n=\sum_{k=n}^{\infty}\frac{M_p^k}{k!}. \] The scalar series defining $e_n$ converges and $e_n\to0$. For every $n\in\N$ and $\xi\in\R$, \[ |\chi(\xi)m_G(\xi)-Q_n(\xi)|\le\tfrac12\|G\|_{L^1}e_n. \] Thus $Q_n\to\chi m_G$ uniformly on $\R$; no upper restriction on $\gamma$ is needed.
nodes.proof_html: Substitute the Fourier formula for $\mc A_kG$ and move the finite sum into the $t$ integral. On $\operatorname{supp}\chi$, $|(1-t^{p+1})\Phi_0(\xi)|\le M_p$ for $0\le t\le1$. The exponential series remainder is bounded by $e_n$, uniformly in $(t,\xi)$ there. Multiply by $t|\widehat G(t\xi)|\le t\|G\|_1$, integrate $t$, and use $|\chi|\le1$. Outside the support both sides of the Fourier-series difference are zero. Summability of the scalar exponential series proves $e_n\to0$ and the claimed uniform convergence.

nodes.title: Identification of a convergent series in the weighted space
nodes.statement_html: Let $\frac34<p<1$, $\gamma>1$, $G\in Y_\gamma$, and put $S_n=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(-i)^k\mc M_k\mc A_kG/k!$. Suppose $S_n\in X^\C_\gamma$ for every $n$, $S\in X^\C_\gamma$, and $\|S_n-S\|_{X^\C_\gamma}\to0$ as $n\to\infty$. Then $\widehat S=\chi m_G$ pointwise and $S(y)=\mc T_{\rm l}G(y)$ for every $y\in\R$. This is a conditional assertion for every $\gamma>1$; convergence in $X^\C_\gamma$ is not a conclusion.
nodes.proof_html: Since $\gamma>1$, the weighted value bound gives $\|S_n-S\|_{L^1}\le C_\gamma\|S_n-S\|_{X^\C_\gamma}$, with all norms finite by the membership hypotheses. The Fourier transforms therefore converge uniformly to $\widehat S$. The first two lemmas identify these transforms with $Q_n$, and the third gives their uniform limit $\chi m_G$. This symbol is continuous, integrable and Hermitian by lem:c08_free_ode. Fourier inversion for the continuous $L^1$ function $S$ gives $S=(\chi m_G)^\vee$ everywhere; Hermitian symmetry makes this inverse real, so it equals the real-part definition of $\mc T_{\rm l}G$.

nodes.title: Series representation of $\mc T_{\rm l}$
nodes.statement_html: Let $\gamma>1$, $G\in Y_\gamma$. Then $\widehat{\mc A_kG}(\xi)=\int_0^1t(1-t^\alpha)^k\widehat G(t\xi)dt$, $\widehat{\mc M_kH}=m_k\widehat H$ for $H\in L^1$, and \begin{equation} \chi m_G=\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{(-i)^k}{k!}\,m_k\,\widehat{\mc A_kG}\quad\text{uniformly on }\R . \end{equation} If moreover the series $S:=\sum_k\frac{(-i)^k}{k!}\mc M_k\mc A_kG$ converges in $X^\C_\gamma$ (for $1<\gamma<p+2$ this follows from lem:c08_Ak_bound, lem:c08_Mk_bound), then $\mc T_{\rm l}G=S$.
nodes.proof_html: The two transform identities are lem:c08_average_fourier, lem:c08_convolution_fourier; lem:c08_low_fourier_series gives the uniform Fourier sum. Under the additional weighted-space convergence hypothesis, lem:c08_low_series_identification identifies the limit with $\mc T_{\rm l}G$.

nodes.title: Second-derivative formula for $\mc A_kG$ on the negative axis
nodes.statement_html: Let $\gamma>1$, $G\in Y_\gamma$, $k\ge0$. On $(-\infty,0)$, $\mc A_kG\in C^1$ with $(\mc A_kG)'(y)=\int_0^1(1-t^\alpha)^kt^{-1}G'(y/t)dt$, $(\mc A_kG)'$ is locally Lipschitz, and for a.e.\ $y<0$ \[ (\mc A_kG)''(y)=\begin{cases}-\dfrac{G'(y)}{y},&k=0,\\[4pt]-\dfrac{\alpha k}{y}\displaystyle\int_0^1t^{\alpha-1}(1-t^\alpha)^{k-1}G'(y/t)\,dt,&k\ge1.\end{cases} \]
nodes.proof_html:
For $y<0$: $|t^{-1}G'(y/t)|\le\|G\|t^{-1}(t/|y|)^{\gamma+1}$ is integrable in $t$ uniformly for $y$ in compacts of
  $(-\infty,0)$; integrating the difference quotient in $y$ and using Fubini gives the first-derivative formula (continuity
  of the right side: substitute $u=y/t$ and use dominated convergence). Integration by parts in $t$, using
  $t^{-1}G'(y/t)=-\frac ty\p_t[G(y/t)]$ and boundary terms $t(1-t^\alpha)^kG(y/t)|_{t=0}^{t=1}=\mathbf 1_{k=0}G(y)$:
  \[
    y(\mc A_kG)'(y)=B_k(y)-\mathbf 1_{k=0}G(y),\qquad B_k(y):=\int_0^1\bigl[(1-t^\alpha)^k-\alpha kt^\alpha(1-t^\alpha)^{k-1}\bigr]G(y/t)\,dt .
  \]
  $B_k$ is $C^1$ on $(-\infty,0)$ with $B_k'=(\mc A_kG)'-\alpha k\int_0^1t^{\alpha-1}(1-t^\alpha)^{k-1}G'(y/t)dt$ (as before). Hence
  $(\mc A_kG)'=(B_k-\mathbf 1_{k=0}G)/y$ is locally Lipschitz, and differentiating
  $y(\mc A_kG)'=B_k-\mathbf 1_{k=0}G$ gives $(\mc A_kG)'+y(\mc A_kG)''=B_k'-\mathbf 1_{k=0}G'$ a.e., i.e.\ the claim.
  Lean route: fundamental theorem of calculus along $s\mapsto G(s/t)$, integration by parts in $t$ with an $\epsilon$-cutoff near $t=0$, and Lebesgue differentiation for the a.e.\ second-derivative identity.

nodes.title: $\mc A_k:Y_\gamma\to Z_\gamma$
nodes.statement_html: Let $\gamma>1$. There is $C=C(\gamma)$ with $\|\mc A_kG\|_{Z_\gamma}\le C\|G\|_{Y_\gamma}$ for all $k\ge0$, $G\in Y_\gamma$ (in particular $\le C(1+k)\|G\|_{Y_\gamma}$ as in eqn:linear_low_frequency_factor_bounds).
nodes.proof_html: $\mc A_kG$ is continuous (dominated convergence). Since $\ang{y/t}\ge\ang{y}$ for $t\in(0,1]$ and $0\le(1-t^\alpha)^k\le1$: $|\mc A_kG(y)|\le\|G\|\ang{y}^{-\gamma}$. For $y\le-1$, by lem:c08_Ak_formulas and $\ang{y/t}\ge|y|/t$: $|(\mc A_kG)'(y)|\le\|G\|\int_0^1t^{-1}(t/|y|)^{\gamma+1}dt\le\|G\||y|^{-\gamma-1}\le C\|G\|\ang{y}^{-\gamma-1}$; and, using $\alpha k\int_0^1t^{\alpha-1}(1-t^\alpha)^{k-1}dt=1$ and $|G'(y/t)|\le\|G\|\ang{y}^{-\gamma-1}$, $|(\mc A_kG)''(y)|\le\|G\|\ang{y}^{-\gamma-1}/|y|\le C\|G\|\ang{y}^{-\gamma-2}$.

nodes.title: Differentiation of the low-frequency convolution
nodes.statement_html: Let $\frac34<p<1$, $\gamma>1$, $k\ge0$, and $H\in Z_\gamma$. Then $\mc M_kH\in C^2(\R;\C)$, and for $j\in\{0,1,2\}$ and every $y\in\R$, \[ \partial_y^j\mc M_kH(y)=\int_\R H_k^{(j)}(y-z)H(z)\,dz, \] with absolute convergence of each integral. There is $C_\gamma>0$, independent of $H$, with $\|H\|_{L^1}\le C_\gamma\|H\|_{Z_\gamma}$.
nodes.proof_html: The value part of the $Z_\gamma$ norm gives $|H(z)|\le\|H\|_Z\ang z^{-\gamma}$, which is integrable. Each derivative $H_k^{(j)}$, $j\le2$, is continuous and bounded by the kernel lemma. Thus $\|H_k^{(j)}\|_\infty|H(z)|$ is a common majorant independent of $y$. Apply the dominated differentiation theorem twice, and dominated convergence to the second derivative; these statements establish differentiability rather than merely identities for a total derivative.

nodes.title: Global weighted bounds for the low-frequency convolution
nodes.statement_html: Let $\frac34<p<1$ and $1<\gamma<p+2$. There exist $C,Q>0$, depending only on $p,\gamma$ and the fixed cutoff, such that for every $k\ge0$, $H\in Z_\gamma$, $j\in\{0,1,2\}$ and $y\in\R$, \[ |\partial_y^j\mc M_kH(y)|\le C Q^k\|H\|_{Z_\gamma}\ang y^{-\gamma}. \] In particular this controls all positive-half-line $X_\gamma$ weights and the negative weights on $[-2,0]$.
nodes.proof_html: Insert the derivative representation and the bounds $|H_k^{(j)}(y-z)|\le C_1C_2^k\ang{y-z}^{-p-2-j}$ and $|H(z)|\le\|H\|_Z\ang z^{-\gamma}$. Apply weighted convolution with $a=p+2+j>\gamma=b>1$ and take the maximum of the three constants. The extra positive-half-line weights $\ang y^{-j/p}$ are at most one; the negative weights $\ang y^j$ are bounded on $[-2,0]$.

nodes.title: Derivative decay gain on the negative half-line
nodes.statement_html: Let $\frac34<p<1$ and $1<\gamma<p+2$. There exist $C,Q>0$, depending only on $p,\gamma$ and the fixed cutoff, such that for every $k\ge0$, $H\in Z_\gamma$, $j\in\{1,2\}$ and $y\le-2$, \[ |\partial_y^j\mc M_kH(y)|\le C Q^k\|H\|_{Z_\gamma}\ang y^{-\gamma-j}. \] The near/far integrals in the proof and their integrations by parts are absolutely convergent.
nodes.proof_html: In the derivative integral set $\nu_y(z)=\chi(8(y-z)/\ang y)$. On its support, $|y-z|\le\ang y/4$, $z<-1$ and $\ang z$ is comparable to $\ang y$. For the near part integrate by parts $j$ times in $z$: \[ \int\nu_y(z)H_k^{(j)}(y-z)H(z)dz =\int H_k(y-z)\partial_z^j(\nu_yH)(z)dz. \] Compact support inside $(-\infty,-1)$ removes boundary terms; $H\in C^1$ with locally Lipschitz derivative there justifies the second integration by parts using the a.e.\ second derivative. Leibniz and the $Z_\gamma$ weights give $|\partial_z^j(\nu_yH)|\le C\|H\|_Z\ang y^{-\gamma-j}$ a.e.; use $\|H_k\|_1\le C_1'C_2^k$. For the far part $|y-z|\ge\ang y/8$, so the kernel estimate bounds its absolute value by $C C_2^k\ang y^{-p-2-j}\|H\|_1$. The $L^1$ bound in lem:c08_Mk_differentiation and $\gamma<p+2$ give the required power. Add the two contributions. Lean route: an indicator cutoff $|u|\le\ang y/8$ and the vanishing moments of $H_k'$, $H_k''$ (with a second-order Taylor bound for $H$ on the window) replace the integration by parts against a smooth cutoff.

nodes.title: $\mc M_k:Z_\gamma\to X_\gamma$
nodes.statement_html: Let $1<\gamma<p+2$. There is $C=C(p,\gamma,\chi)$ such that for all $k\ge0$ and $H\in Z_\gamma$: $\mc M_kH\in C^2$ and \begin{equation} \|\mc M_kH\|_{X^\C_\gamma}\le C\,C_2^k\,\|H\|_{Z_\gamma}. \end{equation}
nodes.proof_html: The convolution is $C^2$ by lem:c08_Mk_differentiation. Use lem:c08_Mk_global_decay for $y\ge-2$ and for the value term on all of $\R$; lem:c08_Mk_negative_gain supplies the stronger derivative decay for $y\le-2$. Choose the maxima of the geometric bases and constants, sum the three weighted terms on each half-line, and take essential suprema. This proves finiteness of the $X^\C_\gamma$ norm as well as its quantitative bound; $C^2$ regularity gives the required local Lipschitz property of the derivative.

nodes.title: Low-frequency estimate
nodes.statement_html: Let $1<\gamma<p+2$ (this contains every admissible $\gamma$). There is $C_{\rm l}=C_{\rm l}(p,\gamma,\chi)$ such that for every $G\in Y_\gamma$, $\mc T_{\rm l}G$ (def:c08_frequency_split) is a real $C^\infty$ function in $X_\gamma$ with $\|\mc T_{\rm l}G\|_{X_\gamma}\le C_{\rm l}\|G\|_{Y_\gamma}$. No condition $\ell(G)=0$ is needed.
nodes.proof_html: By lem:c08_Ak_bound, lem:c08_Mk_bound, \begin{equation} \|\mc A_k\|_{Y_\gamma\to Z_\gamma}\le C,\qquad\|\mc M_k\|_{Z_\gamma\to X^\C_\gamma}\le CC_2^k, \end{equation} so $\sum_k\frac1{k!}\|\mc M_k\mc A_kG\|_{X^\C_\gamma}\le C e^{C_2}\|G\|_{Y_\gamma}$. The partial sums are $C^2$ and converge with their first two derivatives locally uniformly, so the sum $S$ is $C^2$, $\|S\|_{X^\C_\gamma}\le Ce^{C_2}\|G\|_{Y_\gamma}$ (norm is lower semicontinuous under pointwise convergence of $r,r',r''$), and $S=\mc T_{\rm l}G$ by lem:c08_low_series. Each term $(-i)^k\mc M_k\mc A_kG=((-i)^kH_k)*\mc A_kG$ is real (lem:c08_Hk_kernel), so $S\in X_\gamma$.

nodes.title: Reconstruction from the two frequency pieces
nodes.statement_html: Let $\frac34<p<1$, $\gamma>1$, and $G\in Y_\gamma$. Suppose that $\mc T_{\rm l}G,\mc T_{\rm h}G\in X_\gamma$ and that the high-frequency representative satisfies $\widehat{\mc T_{\rm h}G}=(1-\chi)m_G$ in $\mathcal S'(\R)$. Then \[ \mc T_0G=\mc T_{\rm l}G+\mc T_{\rm h}G,\qquad \widehat{\mc T_0G}=m_G,\qquad \mc T_0G\in X_\gamma, \] and $\|\mc T_0G\|_{X_\gamma}\le \|\mc T_{\rm l}G\|_{X_\gamma}+\|\mc T_{\rm h}G\|_{X_\gamma}$.
nodes.proof_html: Apply prop:linear_low_frequency at $\min\{\gamma,p+1\}\in(1,p+2)$, using the monotone embedding of the weighted spaces, to obtain smoothness of $\mc T_{\rm l}G$ and its defining Fourier identity. By lem:c08_free_ode, $m_G$ is bounded and continuous. The sum of the two representatives is continuous and polynomially bounded and has Fourier transform $m_G$, by linearity tested against Schwartz functions. Fourier uniqueness identifies it with $\mc T_0G$. The $X_\gamma$ regularity and triangle inequality give the remaining conclusions.

nodes.title: Weights
nodes.statement_html: For $\gamma\in\R$, $j\in\{0,1,2\}$ and $y\in\R$ put \[ w_{\gamma,j}(y):=\begin{cases}\ang{y}^{-\gamma+j/p},&y\ge0,\\ \ang{y}^{-\gamma-j},&y<0,\end{cases} \qquad w_E(z):=\begin{cases}\ang{z}^{-1},&z\le0,\\ \ang{z}^{\frac{1-p}{2p}},&z>0.\end{cases} \]

nodes.title: Weights versus the norms of $X_\gamma$, $Y_\gamma$
nodes.statement_html:
Let $\gamma$ be admissible.
  • If $r\in X_\gamma$ then $|r^{(j)}(y)|\le\|r\|_{X_\gamma}w_{\gamma,j}(y)$ for $j=0,1$ and all $y$, and for $j=2$ and a.e.\ $y$. Conversely, if $r:\R\to\R$ is $C^1$ with $r'$ locally Lipschitz and $|r^{(j)}|\le A\,w_{\gamma,j}$ ($j=0,1$ everywhere, $j=2$ a.e.), then $r\in X_\gamma$ and $\|r\|_{X_\gamma}\le 6A$.
  • If $G\in Y_\gamma$ then $|G(y)|\le\|G\|_{Y_\gamma}w_{\gamma,0}(y)$ for all $y$ and $|G'(y)|\le\|G\|_{Y_\gamma}w_{\gamma,1}(y)$ for a.e.\ $y$; in particular $|G'(y)|\le\|G\|_{Y_\gamma}\ang{y}^{-\gamma+1/p}\le\|G\|_{Y_\gamma}$ a.e.
  • There is $C$ with $\|G\|_{L^1}+\|G'\|_{L^1}+\int_\R|G'(z)|\,w_E(z)\,dz\le C\|G\|_{Y_\gamma}$ for all $G\in Y_\gamma$.
  • (Peetre) $\ang{a+b}\le\sqrt2\,\ang{a}\ang{b}$ for $a,b\in\R$; hence $\ang{y-z}^{-s}\le2^{s/2}\ang{y}^{-s}\ang{z}^{s}$ for $s\ge0$.
  • (Shifted derivative, paper eq. eqn:linear\_nonstationary\_shifted\_derivative) There is $C$ such that for $G\in Y_\gamma$, every $y\in\R$ and a.e.\ $z\in\R$: $|G'(y-z)|\le C\|G\|_{Y_\gamma}\ang{z}^{\gamma+1}w_{\gamma,1}(y)$.
  • For every $y,z$: $|G(y-z)|\le 2^{\gamma/2}\|G\|_{Y_\gamma}\ang{y}^{-\gamma}\ang{z}^{\gamma}$.
nodes.proof_html: (1),(2): read off def:X_gamma, def:Y_gamma; for the converse each of the two suprema in $\|r\|_{X_\gamma}$ is $\le3A$. For (2), on $y\le0$ we have $\ang{y}^{-\gamma-1}\le\ang{y}^{-\gamma+1/p}$, and $\gamma>1/p$. (3): $\|G\|_{L^1}+\|G'\|_{L^1}\le C\|G\|$ is lem:c08_L1_embedding; directly: on $z\le0$ the integrands are $\lesssim\ang z^{-\gamma}$, $\ang{z}^{-\gamma-1}$, $\ang{z}^{-\gamma-2}$; on $z\ge0$ they are $\lesssim\ang z^{-\gamma}$, $\ang{z}^{-\gamma+1/p}$, $\ang{z}^{\frac{3-p}{2p}-\gamma}$, integrable since $\gamma>1$, $\gamma-\frac1p>1$ and $\gamma-\frac{3-p}{2p}>1\iff\gamma>\frac{p+3}{2p}$ (the admissibility threshold, used exactly here). (4): $1+(a+b)^2\le1+2a^2+2b^2\le2(1+a^2)(1+b^2)$; apply with $a=y-z$, $b=z$. (5): if $y\ge0$ use (2) and (4) with $s=\gamma-\frac1p\ge0$, then $\ang{z}^{\gamma-1/p}\le\ang{z}^{\gamma+1}$. If $y<0$ and $y-z\le0$: $|G'(y-z)|\le\|G\|\ang{y-z}^{-\gamma-1}$ and (4) with $s=\gamma+1$. If $y<0<y-z$, then $z<y<0$, so $|z|>|y|$, and $|G'(y-z)|\le\|G\|\le\|G\|\ang{z}^{\gamma+1}\ang{y}^{-\gamma-1}$. (6): (2) and (4) with $s=\gamma$.

nodes.title: Positive high-frequency part; paper line 2904
nodes.section: The positive high-frequency part and its kernel
nodes.statement_html: For admissible $\gamma$ and $G\in\sq Y_\gamma$ define the function on $\R$ \[ \widehat{\mc T_+G}(\xi):=\mathbf 1_{\{\xi>0\}}(1-\chi(\xi))\,m_G(\xi), \] and (once lem:c09_tail_formula shows $\widehat{\mc T_+G}\in L^1$) $\mc T_+G(y):=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^\infty\widehat{\mc T_+G}(\xi)e^{iy\xi}\,d\xi$, a bounded continuous complex function.

nodes.title: Tail integrals
nodes.section: The positive high-frequency part and its kernel
nodes.statement_html: For $z\in\R$ and $\xi\ge0$ put $\Psi_z(\eta):=\Phi_0(\eta)-z\eta$ and \[ E_z(\xi):=\lim_{N\to\infty}\int_\xi^Ne^{i\Psi_z(\eta)}\,d\eta . \] For admissible $\gamma$ and $G\in Y_\gamma$ put $F_G(\xi):=\int_\R G'(z)E_z(\xi)\,dz$, $\xi\ge0$.

nodes.title: Basic properties of the tail integrals
nodes.section: The positive high-frequency part and its kernel
nodes.statement_html:
• The limit defining $E_z(\xi)$ exists for all $z\in\R$, $\xi\ge0$; $(z,\xi)\mapsto E_z(\xi)$ is continuous on $\R\times[0,\infty)$; $E_z(\xi)\to0$ as $\xi\to\infty$ for each $z$; and $\partial_\xi E_z(\xi)=-e^{i\Psi_z(\xi)}$.
  • There is $C_E=C_E(p)$ with $|E_z(\xi)|\le C_E\,w_E(z)$ for all $z\in\R$, $\xi\ge0$.
  • For admissible $\gamma$ there is $C$ such that for $G\in Y_\gamma$: $F_G$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)$, $|F_G(\xi)|\le C\|G\|_{Y_\gamma}$, and $F_G(\xi)\to0$ as $\xi\to\infty$.
nodes.proof_html: (1) For $N'>N\ge N_z:=\max\{\xi,(|z|+1)^{1/p}\}$ the phase derivative $\psi(\eta)=\eta^p-z\ge1$ is increasing, and one integration by parts gives $\int_N^{N'}e^{i\Psi_z}=\bigl[\frac{e^{i\Psi_z}}{i\psi}\bigr]_N^{N'}+\int_N^{N'}\frac{\psi'}{i\psi^2}e^{i\Psi_z}$, of modulus $\le3/\psi(N)\to0$: Cauchy criterion. The same estimate is locally uniform in $(z,\xi)$, so the limit is continuous, and $|E_z(\xi)|\le3/\psi(\xi)\to0$. The derivative formula is the fundamental theorem of calculus. (2) lem:appendix_stationary (with its $y$ renamed $z$) gives the bound for $\xi>0$; let $\xi\downarrow0$ using (1). (3) $|G'(z)E_z(\xi)|\le C_E|G'(z)|w_E(z)$, integrable by lem:c09_weight_facts(3); dominated convergence gives continuity and the limit $0$.

nodes.title: Tail formula; the Remark at paper line 2909
nodes.section: The positive high-frequency part and its kernel
nodes.statement_html:
Let $\gamma$ be admissible and $G\in Y_\gamma$. (Items (2),(4) are prop:linear_ell_continuity and lem:c08_T0_tail rewritten with the tail integrals $E_z$; we only need the form with $F_G$.)
  • For $0\le\xi<\Xi$: $\int_\xi^\Xi\eta e^{i\Phi_0(\eta)}\widehat G(\eta)\,d\eta=-i\bigl(F_G(\xi)-F_G(\Xi)\bigr)$.
  • The limit in def:ell exists and $\ell(G)=-iF_G(0)=-i\int_\R G'(z)E_z(0)\,dz$.
  • For $\xi>0$: $m_G(\xi)=\xi^{-2}e^{-i\Phi_0(\xi)}\bigl(\ell(G)+iF_G(\xi)\bigr)$.
  • If $G\in\sq Y_\gamma$, then for $\xi>0$ \[ \widehat{\mc T_+G}(\xi)=i\,(1-\chi(\xi))\,\xi^{-2}e^{-i\Phi_0(\xi)}F_G(\xi) =-(1-\chi(\xi))\frac{e^{-i\Phi_0(\xi)}}{\xi^2}\int_\xi^\infty\eta e^{i\Phi_0(\eta)}\widehat G(\eta)\,d\eta \] (the last integral as $\lim_{\Xi\to\infty}\int_\xi^\Xi$), and $|\widehat{\mc T_+G}(\xi)|\le C\|G\|_{Y_\gamma}\mathbf 1_{\{\xi>1\}}\xi^{-2}$; in particular $\widehat{\mc T_+G}\in L^1(\R)$.
nodes.proof_html: $G\in W^{1,1}(\R)$ by lem:c09_weight_facts(3) and $G(y)\to0$ as $|y|\to\infty$, so $\widehat{G'}(\eta)=i\eta\widehat G(\eta)$, i.e. $\eta\widehat G(\eta)=-i\widehat{G'}(\eta)$. (1): by Fubini on $[\xi,\Xi]\times\R$ ($G'\in L^1$, bounded integrand), $\int_\xi^\Xi\eta e^{i\Phi_0}\widehat G=-i\int_\R G'(z)\int_\xi^\Xi e^{i\Psi_z(\eta)}d\eta\,dz=-i\int G'(z)(E_z(\xi)-E_z(\Xi))dz$. (2): let $\Xi\to\infty$ in (1) with $\xi=0$ and use lem:c09_tail_basic(3). (This is the representation of prop:linear_ell_continuity, since $K(y)=-iE_y(0)$ for the kernel of lem:c08_ell_kernel.) (3): def:T_0 gives $m_G(\xi)=\xi^{-2}e^{-i\Phi_0(\xi)}\int_0^\xi\eta e^{i\Phi_0}\widehat G$, and by (1),(2) $\int_0^\xi=-iF_G(0)+iF_G(\xi)=\ell(G)+iF_G(\xi)$. (4): put $\ell(G)=0$ in (3); the second form is (1) with $\Xi\to\infty$. The bound follows from lem:c09_tail_basic(3) and $1-\chi=0$ on $[0,1]$.

nodes.title: Reality; $\mc T_{\textup{h}}=2\operatorname{Re}\mc T_+$
nodes.section: The positive high-frequency part and its kernel
nodes.statement_html: Let $\gamma$ be admissible and $G\in Y_\gamma$ (real-valued). Then $m_G$ is a bounded continuous function on $\R$ ($|m_G|\le\frac12\|G\|_{L^1}$) with $m_G(-\xi)=\overline{m_G(\xi)}$. If moreover $G\in\sq Y_\gamma$, then $(1-\chi)m_G\in L^1(\R)$, $\mc T_{\textup{h}}G(y)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_\R(1-\chi(\xi))m_G(\xi)e^{iy\xi}d\xi$ is a bounded continuous real function (it represents the distribution $\mc T_{\textup{h}}G$ of def:c08_frequency_split), and $\mc T_{\textup{h}}G=2\operatorname{Re}\mc T_+G$. In particular $\mc T_+G$ is the inverse Fourier transform of $\mathbf 1_{\{\xi>0\}}(1-\chi)m_G$.
nodes.proof_html: (Continuity, the bound and the symmetry are lem:c08_free_ode(1),(2).) The first formula in eqn:linear_free_inverse, $m_G(\xi)=\int_0^1te^{-i(1-t^{p+1})\Phi_0(\xi)}\widehat G(t\xi)dt$ (substitution $\eta=t\xi$ in def:T_0, valid for $\xi\neq0$ of either sign, and taken as the value at $\xi=0$), gives continuity and the bound $|m_G|\le\frac12\sup|\widehat G|\le\frac12\|G\|_{L^1}$. Since $G$ is real, $\widehat G(-\eta)=\overline{\widehat G(\eta)}$, and $\Phi_0$ is odd, so each integrand at $-\xi$ is the conjugate of the one at $\xi$. Integrability of $(1-\chi)m_G$ follows from lem:c09_tail_formula(4) on $\xi>0$ and the symmetry on $\xi<0$. Since $\chi$ is even, $(1-\chi)m_G=\widehat{\mc T_+G}(\xi)+\overline{\widehat{\mc T_+G}(-\xi)}$ a.e., and the inverse Fourier transform of $\overline{\widehat{\mc T_+G}(-\cdot)}$ is $\overline{\mc T_+G}$. Hence $\mc T_{\textup{h}}G=\mc T_+G+\overline{\mc T_+G}=2\operatorname{Re}\mc T_+G$.

nodes.title: Frequency truncation
nodes.section: The positive high-frequency part and its kernel
nodes.statement_html: For $R\ge2$ put $\theta_R(\xi):=\chi(\xi/R)$ and, for admissible $\gamma$, $G\in\sq Y_\gamma$, \[ \mc T_+^RG(y):=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^\infty\theta_R(\xi)\widehat{\mc T_+G}(\xi)e^{iy\xi}\,d\xi,\qquad \mc T_{\textup{h}}^RG:=2\operatorname{Re}\mc T_+^RG . \] For $y\in\R$ put $R_0(y):=\max\{2,\ang{y}^{1/p}\}$.

nodes.title: Kernels $K_{+,j}$; paper line 2920, paper eq.~\texttt{eqn:linear\_positive\_kernel}
nodes.section: The positive high-frequency part and its kernel
nodes.statement_html: For $j\in\{0,1,2\}$, $R\ge2$ define the amplitude ($\xi>0$; set $a_j^R(\xi)=0$ for $\xi\le0$) \[ a_j^R(\xi):=-\frac{i^{j+1}}{2\pi}(\chi(\xi)-1)\,\theta_R(\xi)\,\xi^{j-2} \] and the kernel \[ K_{+,j}^R(y,z):=\int_1^{2R}a_j^R(\xi)\,e^{i(y\xi-\Phi_0(\xi))}\,E_z(\xi)\,d\xi,\qquad y,z\in\R . \] (Formally, with $\theta_R\equiv1$ and the $\eta$-integral inside $E_z$ written out, this is the paper's $K_{+,j}(y,z)=-\frac{i^{j+1}}{2\pi}\int_{1<\xi<\eta}(\chi(\xi)-1)\xi^{j-2}e^{i(\Phi_0(\eta)-\Phi_0(\xi)-z\eta+y\xi)}d\xi\,d\eta$.)

nodes.title: Smoothness after truncating the positive symbol
nodes.section: The positive high-frequency part and its kernel
nodes.statement_html: Let $\frac34<p<1$, let $\gamma$ be admissible, let $G\in\sq Y_\gamma$, and let $R\ge2$. For every integer $j\ge0$ the function $\xi\mapsto\mathbf1_{\{\xi>0\}}(i\xi)^j\theta_R(\xi)\widehat{\mc T_+G}(\xi)$ is in $L^1(\R)$ and vanishes outside $[1,2R]$. The function $\mc T_+^RG$ is $C^\infty(\R;\C)$, and for every $j\ge0$, $y\in\R$, \[ \partial_y^j\mc T_+^RG(y)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_1^{2R} (i\xi)^j\theta_R(\xi)\widehat{\mc T_+G}(\xi)e^{iy\xi}\,d\xi . \] Every integral here is absolutely convergent. For each $j$ there is $C_{p,\gamma,R,j}>0$, independent of $G$ and $y$, such that $|\partial_y^j\mc T_+^RG(y)|\le C_{p,\gamma,R,j}\|G\|_{Y_\gamma}$.
nodes.proof_html: The symbol bound in lem:c09_tail_formula(4), together with $0\le\theta_R\le1$ and its support, gives an integrable majorant $C\|G\|_{Y_\gamma}\xi^{j-2}\mathbf1_{[1,2R]}$ for each order $j$. The same majorant for order $j+1$ controls the difference quotients of the $j$th derivative uniformly in $y$. Apply differentiation under the integral and dominated convergence, then induct on $j$. Integrating the majorant gives the final bound; no estimate uniform in $R$ is asserted here.

nodes.title: An integrable majorant for the truncated kernel
nodes.section: The positive high-frequency part and its kernel
nodes.statement_html: Let $\frac34<p<1$ and $R\ge2$. There is $C_{p,R}>0$, independent of $j,y,z$, such that for $j\in\{0,1,2\}$ and every $y,z\in\R$ the defining $\xi$-integral for $K_{+,j}^R(y,z)$ is absolutely convergent and \[ \int_1^{2R}|a_j^R(\xi)E_z(\xi)|\,d\xi\le C_{p,R}w_E(z),\qquad |K_{+,j}^R(y,z)|\le C_{p,R}w_E(z). \] The kernel $(y,z)\mapsto K_{+,j}^R(y,z)$ is continuous on $\R^2$.
nodes.proof_html: Use $|E_z(\xi)|\le C_Ew_E(z)$ on $[1,2R]$, where $a_j^R$ is continuous and integrable. A valid common constant is $1+C_E\sum_{j=0}^2\int_1^{2R}|a_j^R(\xi)|d\xi$. The exponential has modulus one. Joint continuity follows by dominated convergence on each compact set of $(y,z)$, using continuity of $E_z(\xi)$ and boundedness of $w_E$ on its $z$ projection.

nodes.title: Fubini for the truncated kernel and the input derivative
nodes.section: The positive high-frequency part and its kernel
nodes.statement_html: Let $\frac34<p<1$, let $\gamma$ be admissible, let $G\in Y_\gamma$, $R\ge2$, and $j\in\{0,1,2\}$. For every $y\in\R$ the function \[ (\xi,z)\longmapsto a_j^R(\xi)e^{i(y\xi-\Phi_0(\xi))}E_z(\xi)G'(z) \] is integrable on $[1,2R]\times\R$. Moreover $z\mapsto K_{+,j}^R(y,z)G'(z)$ is integrable and \[ \int_1^{2R}a_j^R(\xi)e^{i(y\xi-\Phi_0(\xi))}F_G(\xi)\,d\xi =\int_\R K_{+,j}^R(y,z)G'(z)\,dz . \] There is $C_{p,\gamma,R}>0$, independent of $G,j,y$, bounding the double integral of the absolute value by $C_{p,\gamma,R}\|G\|_{Y_\gamma}$.
nodes.proof_html: The kernel factors are jointly continuous on $[1,2R]\times\R$ and $G'$ is measurable. Tonelli and lem:c09_kernel_majorant bound the double integral by $C_{p,R}\int|G'(z)|w_E(z)dz$, finite and bounded by lem:c09_weight_facts(3). Fubini now applies to the absolutely integrable product. The inner integrals are precisely $F_G(\xi)$ and $K_{+,j}^R(y,z)$; the kernel majorant separately gives integrability of the latter pairing.

nodes.title: The differentiated truncated integral equals its kernel pairing
nodes.section: The positive high-frequency part and its kernel
nodes.statement_html: Let $\frac34<p<1$, let $\gamma$ be admissible, $G\in\sq Y_\gamma$, and $R\ge2$. For every $j\in\{0,1,2\}$ and $y\in\R$, \[ \partial_y^j\mc T_+^RG(y)=\int_\R K_{+,j}^R(y,z)G'(z)\,dz, \] with an absolutely convergent integral on the right.
nodes.proof_html: Insert the projected tail formula $\widehat{\mc T_+G}=i(1-\chi)\xi^{-2}e^{-i\Phi_0}F_G$ for $\xi>0$ into lem:c09_truncated_smooth. Check the normalization exactly: $(2\pi)^{-1}(i\xi)^j\theta_R\,i(1-\chi)\xi^{-2}=a_j^R$. Then apply lem:c09_kernel_fubini. The integration by parts establishing $\widehat{G'}=i\xi\widehat G$ is already part of lem:c09_tail_formula; it is not assumed anew.

nodes.title: Uniform error of frequency truncation
nodes.section: The positive high-frequency part and its kernel
nodes.statement_html: Let $\frac34<p<1$ and let $\gamma$ be admissible. There is $C_{p,\gamma}>0$, independent of $G,R,y$, such that for every $G\in\sq Y_\gamma$, $R\ge2$ and $y\in\R$, \[ |\mc T_+^RG(y)-\mc T_+G(y)|\le C_{p,\gamma}R^{-1}\|G\|_{Y_\gamma},\qquad |\mc T_{\rm h}^RG(y)-\mc T_{\rm h}G(y)|\le2C_{p,\gamma}R^{-1}\|G\|_{Y_\gamma}. \] In particular both truncations converge uniformly on $\R$ as $R\to\infty$.
nodes.proof_html: Since $\theta_R=1$ on $[0,R]$ and $|1-\theta_R|\le1$, the difference of the two positive-frequency integrals is bounded by $(2\pi)^{-1}C\|G\|_{Y_\gamma}\int_R^\infty\xi^{-2}d\xi$. Absolute convergence justifies subtracting the integrals. The integral is $R^{-1}$ and the estimate is independent of $y$. Use lem:c09_conjugate_symmetry, including its distributional Fourier identity and identification of the continuous representative, to replace $\mc T_{\rm h}G$ by $2\operatorname{Re}\mc T_+G$. Taking real parts gives the second inequality and the uniform limits.

nodes.title: Kernel representation of $\partial_y^j\mc T_+^R$
nodes.section: The positive high-frequency part and its kernel
nodes.statement_html: Let $\gamma$ be admissible, $G\in\sq Y_\gamma$, $R\ge2$. Then $\mc T_+^RG\in C^\infty(\R)$, $|K_{+,j}^R(y,z)|\le C_R\,w_E(z)$, and for $j=0,1,2$ and all $y$ \[ \partial_y^j\mc T_+^RG(y)=\int_\R K_{+,j}^R(y,z)\,G'(z)\,dz\qquad\text{(absolutely convergent).} \] Moreover $\sup_{y\in\R}|\mc T_+^RG(y)-\mc T_+G(y)|\to0$ and $\sup_y|\mc T_{\textup{h}}^RG-\mc T_{\textup{h}}G|\to0$ as $R\to\infty$.
nodes.proof_html: Smoothness is lem:c09_truncated_smooth. The constant $C_R$ and the kernel bound are lem:c09_kernel_majorant; absolute convergence and the pointwise derivative identity are lem:c09_kernel_fubini, lem:c09_truncated_representation. Finally lem:c09_truncation_L1_error gives both uniform limits, with their correct representatives.

nodes.title: Stationary/nonstationary decomposition; paper line 2932
nodes.statement_html:
• (paper eq. eqn:linear\_stationary\_cutoffs) For $y\in\R$, $\xi>0$: $\chi_{\textup{s}}(y,\xi):=\chi\bigl(100(\xi-y^{1/p})/y^{1/p}\bigr)$ if $y>0$, $\chi_{\textup{s}}(y,\xi):=0$ if $y\le0$; $\chi_{\textup{ns}}:=1-\chi_{\textup{s}}$.
  • $a_j^{\textup{s},R}(y,\xi):=\chi_{\textup{s}}(y,\xi)a_j^R(\xi)$, $a_j^{\textup{ns},R}(y,\xi):=\chi_{\textup{ns}}(y,\xi)a_j^R(\xi)$.
  • (paper eq. eqn:linear\_stationary\_kernel\_split) $K_{+,j}^{\textup{s},R}(y,z):=\int_1^{2R}a_j^{\textup{s},R}(y,\xi)e^{i(y\xi-\Phi_0(\xi))}E_z(\xi)d\xi$ and $K_{+,j}^{\textup{ns},R}$ likewise with $a_j^{\textup{ns},R}$; thus $K_{+,j}^R=K_{+,j}^{\textup{s},R}+K_{+,j}^{\textup{ns},R}$.
  • (paper eq. eqn:linear\_stationary\_operators) $\mc T_{+,j}^{\textup{s},R}G(y):=\int K_{+,j}^{\textup{s},R}(y,z)G'(z)dz$, $\mc T_{+,j}^{\textup{ns},R}G(y):=\int K_{+,j}^{\textup{ns},R}(y,z)G'(z)dz$, so that $\partial_y^j\mc T_+^RG=\mc T_{+,j}^{\textup{s},R}G+\mc T_{+,j}^{\textup{ns},R}G$ by lem:c09_kernel_representation.

nodes.title: Cutoff and amplitude bounds
nodes.statement_html:
There are constants $c_*\in(0,1)$ and $C_\ell$ ($\ell\ge0$), depending only on $p,\chi$, such that for all $R\ge2$, $y\in\R$, $\xi>0$, $j\in\{0,1,2\}$:
  • $\chi_{\textup{s}}(y,\xi)\neq0\Rightarrow y>0$ and $|\xi-y^{1/p}|\le y^{1/p}/50$; $\chi_{\textup{s}}(y,\xi)=1$ if $y>0$ and $|\xi-y^{1/p}|\le y^{1/p}/100$.
  • $|\partial_\xi^\ell\chi_{\textup{s}}(y,\xi)|+|\partial_\xi^\ell\chi_{\textup{ns}}(y,\xi)|\le C_\ell\xi^{-\ell}$ for $\ell\ge1$, and $0\le\chi_{\textup{s}},\chi_{\textup{ns}}\le1$; moreover $\int_0^\infty|\partial_\xi\chi_{\textup{ns}}(y,\xi)|d\xi\le C_0$.
  • $a_j^R$ is smooth on $(0,\infty)$, vanishes on $(0,1]$ with all derivatives, is supported in $[1,2R]$, and $|\partial_\xi^\ell a_j^R(\xi)|\le C_\ell\xi^{j-2-\ell}$ (uniformly in $R$); $\int_0^\infty|\partial_\xi[(1-\chi)\theta_R](\xi)|d\xi\le C_0$.
  • If $\chi_{\textup{ns}}(y,\xi)\neq0$ (or $\xi$ is in its support) and $\xi\ge1$ then $|y-\xi^p|\ge c_*(|y|+\xi^p)$; and $|y|+\xi^p\ge2^{-1/2}\ang{y}$ for $\xi\ge1$.
  • If $a_j^{\textup{s},R}(y,\xi)\neq0$ then $y\ge y_*:=(50/51)^p$, $\frac{49}{50}y^{1/p}\le\xi\le\frac{51}{50}y^{1/p}$, and $\ang{y}\le C_0\,y$.
nodes.proof_html:
(1) $\operatorname{supp}\chi\subset[-2,2]$, $\chi=1$ on $[-1,1]$. (2) $\partial_\xi^\ell\chi_{\textup{s}}=(100y^{-1/p})^\ell\chi^{(\ell)}(\cdot)$, supported where
  $\xi\approx y^{1/p}$ by (1); the $L^1$ norm of $\partial_\xi\chi_{\textup{s}}$ is $\|\chi'\|_{L^1}$ (change of variables).
  (3) Product rule; $|\partial^\ell\theta_R|=R^{-\ell}|\chi^{(\ell)}(\xi/R)|\le 2^\ell\|\chi^{(\ell)}\|_\infty\xi^{-\ell}$ on $\operatorname{supp}\theta_R\subset[0,2R]$; $1-\chi$ vanishes
  on $[-1,1]$; $L^1$ norms of derivatives of $\chi$, $\theta_R$ are $R$-independent.
  (4) $y\le0$: $|y-\xi^p|=|y|+\xi^p$. $y>0$, $\xi\ge\frac{101}{100}y^{1/p}$: $\xi^p-y\ge(1-(\frac{100}{101})^p)\xi^p\ge\frac12(1-(\frac{100}{101})^p)(\xi^p+y)$.
  $y>0$, $\xi\le\frac{99}{100}y^{1/p}$: $y-\xi^p\ge(1-0.99^p)y\ge\frac12(1-0.99^p)(y+\xi^p)$. Last claim: $|y|+\xi^p\ge\max(|y|,1)$.
  (5) $a_j^R(\xi)\neq0$ needs $\xi>1$; combine with (1).

nodes.title: Stationary kernel, near case
nodes.statement_html: There is $C$ (depending on $p,\chi$) such that for all $R\ge2$, $j\in\{0,1,2\}$, $y>0$ and $z\ge y/4$: $|K_{+,j}^{\textup{s},R}(y,z)|\le C\ang{y}^{\frac jp-\frac{p+3}{2p}}\ang{z}^{\frac{1-p}{2p}}$.
nodes.proof_html: By lem:c09_cutoff_bounds(5) we may assume $y\ge y_*$ (else the kernel is $0$), so $\ang{y}\approx y$. Apply lem:appendix_triangle with $x_0=y^{1/p}$, $L=y^{1/p}/25$, $I=(x_0-L,x_0+L)$, $a=a_j^{\textup{s},R}(y,\cdot)$ (in $C^\infty_c(I)$ by lem:c09_cutoff_bounds(1)), $\Phi(\xi)=y\xi-\Phi_0(\xi)$, $\Psi=\Psi_z$, $\omega=y-z$ (so $\Phi+\Psi=\omega\xi$), $E=E_z$ (with $E'=-e^{i\Psi}$). Hypotheses: $\Phi'(x_0)=y-x_0^p=0$; on $I$, $\xi\in[\frac{24}{25}x_0,\frac{26}{25}x_0]$, so $|\Phi''|=p\xi^{p-1}\approx\kappa:=y^{(p-1)/p}$ and $|\Phi'''|=p(1-p)\xi^{p-2}\lesssim y^{(p-2)/p}\approx\kappa L^{-1}$; $|\partial^\ell a|\lesssim y^{(j-2)/p}y^{-\ell/p}\approx AL^{-\ell}$ ($\ell\le2$) with $A=y^{(j-2)/p}$, by lem:c09_cutoff_bounds(2),(3); $|E_z|\le M:=C_E\ang{z}^{\frac{1-p}{2p}}$ by lem:c09_tail_basic(2) ($z>0$). Conclusion: $|K^{\textup{s},R}_{+,j}|\lesssim y^{\frac{j-2}p}\bigl(\ang{z}^{\frac{1-p}{2p}}y^{\frac{1-p}{2p}}+y^{\frac{1-p}p}\bigr)$. As $z\ge y/4$, $y^{\frac{1-p}{2p}}\le4^{\frac{1-p}{2p}}\ang{z}^{\frac{1-p}{2p}}$, so both terms are $\lesssim y^{\frac{j-2}p+\frac{1-p}{2p}}\ang{z}^{\frac{1-p}{2p}}$ and $\frac{j-2}{p}+\frac{1-p}{2p}=\frac jp-\frac{p+3}{2p}$.

nodes.title: Asymptotic expansion of the tail in the nonstationary regime
nodes.statement_html: Let $z\in\R$, $\xi_0>0$, $c_1\in(0,1]$ with $\xi_0^p-z\ge c_1(\xi_0^p+|z|)$. Put $\psi(\eta)=\eta^p-z$, $g_0=1/(i\psi)$ and $Dh:=h'/(i\psi)$ on $[\xi_0,\infty)$. Then $\psi(\eta)\ge c_1(\eta^p+|z|)$ for $\eta\ge\xi_0$; for $k,\ell\ge0$ there is $C_{k,\ell}=C_{k,\ell}(p,c_1)$ with \[ |\partial_\eta^\ell D^kg_0(\eta)|\le C_{k,\ell}\,\eta^{-k-\ell}(\eta^p+|z|)^{-k-1},\qquad\eta\ge\xi_0; \] and for every $\xi\ge\xi_0$, $M\ge0$, \[ E_z(\xi)=e^{i\Psi_z(\xi)}\sum_{k=0}^M(-1)^{k+1}D^kg_0(\xi)+(-1)^{M+1}\int_\xi^\infty e^{i\Psi_z(\eta)}\partial_\eta\bigl[D^Mg_0\bigr](\eta)\,d\eta, \] the last integral being absolutely convergent.
nodes.proof_html:
$\psi(\eta)=(\eta^p-\xi_0^p)+(\xi_0^p-z)\ge(\eta^p-\xi_0^p)+c_1(\xi_0^p+|z|)\ge c_1(\eta^p+|z|)$.
  Derivative bounds: $\partial^\ell(1/\psi)$ is a sum of terms $\psi^{-1-r}\prod_{i=1}^r\psi^{(\ell_i)}$ with $\ell_i\ge1$, $\sum\ell_i=\ell$, and
  $|\psi^{(\ell_i)}|\lesssim\eta^{p-\ell_i}\le\eta^{-\ell_i}(\eta^p+|z|)$, so $|\partial^\ell(1/\psi)|\lesssim\eta^{-\ell}(\eta^p+|z|)^{-1}$; then induction on $k$ with the
  Leibniz rule ($D$ costs one derivative and one factor $1/\psi$). Expansion: induction on $M$. For $M=0$, write $e^{i\Psi_z}=g_0\,\partial_\eta e^{i\Psi_z}$ and
  integrate by parts on $[\xi,N]$, $N\to\infty$ (boundary term at $N$ is $O((N^p+|z|)^{-1})\to0$). For the step,
  $\int_\xi^\infty e^{i\Psi_z}\partial(D^Mg_0)=\int_\xi^\infty D^{M+1}g_0\,\partial e^{i\Psi_z}=-D^{M+1}g_0(\xi)e^{i\Psi_z(\xi)}-\int_\xi^\infty\partial(D^{M+1}g_0)e^{i\Psi_z}$.
  Absolute convergence: $|\partial D^Mg_0|\lesssim\eta^{-M-1}(\eta^p+|z|)^{-M-1}\le c\,\eta^{-1-p}$ (as $M\ge0$, $\eta\ge\xi_0>0$) is integrable at $\infty$.

nodes.title: Stationary kernel, far case
nodes.statement_html: For every $M\ge0$ there is $C_M$ (depending on $p,\chi,M$) such that for all $R\ge2$, $j\in\{0,1,2\}$, $y>0$, $z<y/4$: $|K_{+,j}^{\textup{s},R}(y,z)|\le C_M\ang{y}^{-M}(\ang{y}+|z|)^{-M}$.
nodes.proof_html: Assume $y\ge y_*$ (else $K=0$). Let $\xi_0=\frac{49}{50}y^{1/p}$; then $\xi_0^p\ge\frac{49}{50}y$, and $z<y/4$ gives $\xi_0^p-z\ge\frac12(\xi_0^p+|z|)$ (if $z\le0$ trivially; if $0\le z<y/4$, $\xi_0^p-z\ge0.73y$ and $\xi_0^p+|z|\le1.25y$). Fix $N\ge1$ and insert the expansion of lem:c09_tail_expansion (order $N$, $c_1=\frac12$) for $\xi\in\operatorname{supp}a_j^{\textup{s},R}(y,\cdot)\subset[\xi_0,\frac{51}{50}y^{1/p}]$. Since $y\xi-\Phi_0(\xi)+\Psi_z(\xi)=\xi(y-z)$, \[ K_{+,j}^{\textup{s},R}=\sum_{k=0}^N(-1)^{k+1}\!\int a_j^{\textup{s},R}(y,\xi)e^{i\xi(y-z)}D^kg_0(\xi)d\xi +(-1)^{N+1}\!\int a_j^{\textup{s},R}(y,\xi)e^{i(y\xi-\Phi_0(\xi))}\!\int_\xi^\infty e^{i\Psi_z}\partial(D^Ng_0)\,d\eta\,d\xi . \] (paper eq. eqn:linear\_stationary\_boundary\_ibp) $y-z\ge\frac35(y+|z|)\ge c(\ang y+|z|)$. Integrating by parts $N$ times in $\xi$ (compact support, no boundary terms) and using lem:c09_cutoff_bounds(2),(3),(5) and $\xi\approx y^{1/p}$, $\xi^p+|z|\approx y+|z|$ on the support (length $\lesssim y^{1/p}$): the $k$-th term is $\lesssim_N|y-z|^{-N}y^{1/p}y^{(j-2-N-k)/p}(y+|z|)^{-k-1}\lesssim\ang{y}^{(j-1-N-k)/p}(\ang y+|z|)^{-N-k-1}$. (paper eq. eqn:linear\_stationary\_remainder\_bound) $\int_\xi^\infty\eta^{-N-1}(\eta^p+|z|)^{-N-1}d\eta\le N^{-1}\xi^{-N}(\xi^p+|z|)^{-N-1}$, so the last term is $\lesssim_N y^{1/p}y^{(j-2)/p}y^{-N/p}(y+|z|)^{-N-1}\approx\ang{y}^{(j-1-N)/p}(\ang y+|z|)^{-N-1}$. As $j\le2$, choosing $N:=2M+1$ gives $(N+1-j)/p\ge M$ and $N+1\ge M$, whence the claim.

nodes.title: Stationary estimate
nodes.statement_html: Let $c=\frac14$. There is $C$ and, for every $M\ge0$, $C_M$ (depending on $p,\chi$, $M$) such that for all $R\ge2$, $j\in\{0,1,2\}$, $y,z\in\R$: $K_{+,j}^{\textup{s},R}(y,z)=0$ unless $y\ge y_*=(50/51)^p$, and \[ |K_{+,j}^{\textup{s},R}(y,z)|\le\begin{cases}C\ang{y}^{\frac jp-\frac{p+3}{2p}}\ang{z}^{\frac{1-p}{2p}},&z\ge cy,\\ C_M\ang{y}^{-M}(\ang y+|z|)^{-M},&z<cy.\end{cases} \]
nodes.proof_html: Vanishing: lem:c09_cutoff_bounds(5). The two cases are lem:c09_stationary_near, lem:c09_stationary_far.

nodes.title: Nonstationary symbol expansion
nodes.statement_html:
Fix $R\ge2$, $y\in\R$, $j\in\{0,1,2\}$ and put $\Theta_y(\xi):=y\xi-\Phi_0(\xi)$ (so $\Theta_y'=y-\xi^p$ for $\xi>0$). Define on $(0,\infty)$ (paper eq. eqn:linear\_nonstationary\_symbols) \[ m_{j,0}^R(y,\xi):=\frac{a_j^{\textup{ns},R}(y,\xi)}{i(y-\xi^p)},\qquad m_{j,k+1}^R(y,\xi):=-\frac{\partial_\xi m_{j,k}^R(y,\xi)}{i(y-\xi^p)}, \] set to $0$ where $a_j^{\textup{ns},R}(y,\cdot)$ vanishes identically nearby (these are $C^\infty$ functions of $\xi$ supported in $[1,2R]$, since $a_j^{\textup{ns},R}(y,\cdot)$ vanishes on a neighbourhood of the zero $\xi=y^{1/p}$ of $y-\xi^p$). Then for $M\ge1$:
  • for every $\eta\ge1$, $\int_1^\eta a_j^{\textup{ns},R}(y,\xi)e^{i\Theta_y(\xi)}d\xi=e^{i\Theta_y(\eta)}\sum_{k=0}^{M-1}m_{j,k}^R(y,\eta)-\int_1^\eta e^{i\Theta_y(\xi)}\partial_\xi m_{j,M-1}^R(y,\xi)\,d\xi$;
  • for every $z\in\R$, with $K_{\mc R_{j,M}}^R(y,z):=-\int_1^{2R}\partial_\xi m^R_{j,M-1}(y,\xi)e^{i\Theta_y(\xi)}E_z(\xi)\,d\xi$, \[ K_{+,j}^{\textup{ns},R}(y,z)=2\pi\sum_{k=0}^{M-1}\widecheck{m_{j,k}^R(y,\cdot)}(y-z)+K_{\mc R_{j,M}}^R(y,z); \]
  • (paper eq. eqn:linear\_nonstationary\_expansion) for admissible $\gamma$ and $G\in\sq Y_\gamma$, $\mc T_{+,j}^{\textup{ns},R}G(y)=2\pi\sum_{k=0}^{M-1}\bigl[\widecheck{m_{j,k}^R(y,\cdot)}*G'\bigr](y)+\mc R_{j,M}^RG(y)$ with $\mc R^R_{j,M}G(y):=\int K^R_{\mc R_{j,M}}(y,z)G'(z)dz$ (paper eq. eqn:linear\_nonstationary\_remainder\_definition); all integrals absolutely convergent.
nodes.proof_html: (1) Induction on $M$. On $\operatorname{supp}a_j^{\textup{ns},R}$, $a^{\textup{ns}}e^{i\Theta_y}=m_{j,0}^R\partial_\xi e^{i\Theta_y}$; integrate by parts on $[1,\eta]$; the boundary term at $1$ vanishes since all $m_{j,k}^R(y,\cdot)$ vanish on $(0,1]$. Step: $-\int_1^\eta\partial m_{j,M-1}e^{i\Theta_y}=\int_1^\eta m_{j,M}\partial e^{i\Theta_y} =m_{j,M}(\eta)e^{i\Theta_y(\eta)}-\int_1^\eta\partial m_{j,M}e^{i\Theta_y}$. (2) For $N>2R$, by lem:c09_tail_basic(1), $E_z(\xi)=\lim_N\int_\xi^Ne^{i\Psi_z}$ with $|\int_\xi^N e^{i\Psi_z}|\le2C_Ew_E(z)$, so by dominated convergence and Fubini on the bounded triangle $\{1\le\xi\le\eta\le N\}$, $K_{+,j}^{\textup{ns},R}(y,z)=\lim_N\int_1^Ne^{i\Psi_z(\eta)}\int_1^{\eta}a_j^{\textup{ns},R}e^{i\Theta_y}\,d\xi\,d\eta$. Insert (1). Since $\Psi_z(\eta)+\Theta_y(\eta)=\eta(y-z)$, the first part gives $\sum_k\int_1^{2R}m_{j,k}^R(y,\eta)e^{i\eta(y-z)}d\eta=2\pi\sum_k\widecheck{m^R_{j,k}(y,\cdot)}(y-z)$; in the second part swap back (Fubini on the triangle) to get $-\int_1^{2R}\partial_\xi m^R_{j,M-1}e^{i\Theta_y}\int_\xi^Ne^{i\Psi_z}d\eta\,d\xi\to K^R_{\mc R_{j,M}}(y,z)$. (3) Integrate (2) against $G'(z)$: $\widecheck{m^R_{j,k}(y,\cdot)}$ is a Schwartz function (smooth compactly supported symbol) and $|K^R_{\mc R_{j,M}}(y,z)|\le C_Rw_E(z)$, so every term is absolutely integrable (lem:c09_weight_facts(3)). Lean route: (2) is proved by repeated integration by parts in $\xi$ directly against $E_z$ (using $\partial_\xi E_z=-e^{i\Psi_z}$ and $m_{j,k}^R(y,2R)=0$) instead of Fubini on the triangle; (3) by integrating (2) against $G'$.

nodes.title: Symbol-class bounds for $m_{j,k}$
nodes.statement_html: For $j\in\{0,1,2\}$, $k,\ell\ge0$ there is $C_{k,\ell}$ (depending on $p,\chi$) such that for all $R\ge2$, $y\in\R$, $\xi>0$: \[ |\partial_\xi^\ell m_{j,k}^R(y,\xi)|\le C_{k,\ell}\,\xi^{j-2-k-\ell}(|y|+\xi^p)^{-k-1}. \] Moreover $i^{-(j+k)}m_{j,k}^R(y,\xi)\in\R$; $m^R_{j,0}=(i\xi)^jm^R_{0,0}$; and, with $b:=(1-\chi)\chi_{\textup{ns}}(y,\cdot)\theta_R$, \[ m_{2,1}^R=-\frac{i}{2\pi}\Bigl[\frac{\partial_\xi b}{(y-\xi^p)^2}+\frac{p\,b\,\xi^{p-1}}{(y-\xi^p)^3}\Bigr],\qquad \xi m_{1,1}^R=-i\,m_{2,1}^R+\frac{b}{2\pi\,\xi\,(y-\xi^p)^2}. \]
nodes.proof_html: On $\operatorname{supp}\chi_{\textup{ns}}(y,\cdot)\cap[1,\infty)$, $|y-\xi^p|\ge c_*(|y|+\xi^p)$ (lem:c09_cutoff_bounds(4)), and as in the proof of lem:c09_tail_expansion, $|\partial^\ell(y-\xi^p)^{-1}|\lesssim\xi^{-\ell}(|y|+\xi^p)^{-1}$ there. With $|\partial^\ell a_j^{\textup{ns},R}|\lesssim\xi^{j-2-\ell}$ (lem:c09_cutoff_bounds(2),(3)) the case $k=0$ follows from Leibniz; the recursion $m_{j,k+1}=i\,\partial_\xi m_{j,k}\cdot(y-\xi^p)^{-1}$ gains $\xi^{-1}(|y|+\xi^p)^{-1}$. Reality: $m_{j,0}=\frac{i^j}{2\pi}\,b\,\xi^{j-2}(y-\xi^p)^{-1}$ and each step multiplies by $i$ times a real function. The explicit formulas: direct differentiation of $m_{2,0}=-\frac1{2\pi}b(y-\xi^p)^{-1}$ and $m_{1,0}=\frac{i}{2\pi}b\xi^{-1}(y-\xi^p)^{-1}$.

nodes.title: The function $q$
nodes.statement_html:
For $y\in\R$, $R\ge2$, $\xi>0$ put $q^R(y,\xi):=-\frac1{2\pi}\theta_R(\xi)\chi_{\textup{ns}}(y,\xi)(y-\xi^p)^{-1}$ (so $m_{2,0}^R=(1-\chi)q^R$; $q^R$ is real, smooth on $(0,\infty)$, continuous on $[0,\infty)$ if $y\neq0$, and $|q^R(0,\xi)|=\frac1{2\pi}\xi^{-p}$ near $0$). There is $C$ (depending on $p,\chi$) such that
  • for all $R\ge2$ and $\xi>0$: $|q^R|\le C(|y|+\xi^p)^{-1}$ and $|\partial_\xi^\ell q^R|\le C_\ell\xi^{-\ell}(|y|+\xi^p)^{-1}$;
  • if $R\ge R_0(y)$: $|\partial_\xi q^R|\le C\xi^{p-1}(|y|+\xi^p)^{-2}$ and $|\partial_\xi^2q^R|\le C\xi^{p-2}(|y|+\xi^p)^{-2}$ for all $\xi>0$.
nodes.proof_html: (1) as in lem:c09_mjk_bounds (for $\xi<1$ use $\chi_{\textup{ns}}=1$ unless $\xi\approx y^{1/p}$, and lem:c09_cutoff_bounds(4) holds on the support of $\chi_{\textup{ns}}$ for all $\xi>0$ by the same proof). (2) Derivatives falling on $(y-\xi^p)^{-1}$ give $p\xi^{p-1}(y-\xi^p)^{-2}$ and $p(p-1)\xi^{p-2}(y-\xi^p)^{-2}+2p^2\xi^{2p-2}(y-\xi^p)^{-3}$, bounded as claimed. Derivatives falling on $\chi_{\textup{ns}}$ live where $\xi^p\approx y$, where $\xi^{-\ell}(|y|+\xi^p)^{-1}\approx\xi^{p-\ell}(|y|+\xi^p)^{-2}$. Derivatives falling on $\theta_R$ live on $[R,2R]$, where $R\ge R_0(y)$ gives $\xi^p\ge R^p\ge|y|$, so again $\xi^{-\ell}(|y|+\xi^p)^{-1}\le2\xi^{p-\ell}(|y|+\xi^p)^{-2}$.

nodes.title: Leading kernel $m_{2,0}$
nodes.statement_html: For every $L\ge0$ there is $C_L$ such that for all $y\in\R$, $R\ge R_0(y)$, $z\neq0$: \[ \bigl|\operatorname{Re}\widecheck{m_{2,0}^R(y,\cdot)}(z)\bigr|\le C_L\begin{cases}|z|^{p-1},&0<|z|\le\ang{y}^{-1/p},\\ \ang{y}^{-2}|z|^{-p-1}+\ang{y}^{-1},&\ang{y}^{-1/p}<|z|\le1,\\ \ang y^{-1}|z|^{-L},&|z|>1.\end{cases} \]
nodes.proof_html: Write $q=q^R(y,\cdot)$. Since $q$ is real, $2\pi\operatorname{Re}\widecheck{m^R_{2,0}}(z)=\int_0^\infty q\cos(z\xi)d\xi-\int_0^\infty\chi q\cos(z\xi)d\xi$ (both absolutely convergent: compact support, $|q|\lesssim\xi^{-p}$ near $0$). Second term: $\le\int_0^2C(|y|+\xi^p)^{-1}\le C\ang{y}^{-1}$. First bound, $0<|z|\le1$: split at $1/|z|$; $\int_0^{1/|z|}|q|\le C\int_0^{1/|z|}\xi^{-p}\lesssim|z|^{p-1}$; on $[1/|z|,\infty)$ integrate by parts once: $\le|z|^{-1}(|q(1/|z|)|+\int_{1/|z|}^\infty|q'|)\lesssim|z|^{-1}(|z|^{p}+\int_{1/|z|}^\infty\xi^{-p-1})\lesssim|z|^{p-1}$ (lem:c09_q_bounds(1)). Second bound, $|y|\ge1$, $0<|z|\le1$: integrate by parts on $(0,\infty)$ ($q$ is continuous at $0$, $\sin0=0$): $\int q\cos(z\xi)=-z^{-1}\int_0^\infty q'\sin(z\xi)$. On $(0,1/|z|)$ use $|\sin(z\xi)|\le|z|\xi$ and lem:c09_q_bounds(2): $\le|z|^{-1}\cdot|z|\int_0^{1/|z|}C\xi^p|y|^{-2}\lesssim|y|^{-2}|z|^{-p-1}$. On $(1/|z|,\infty)$ integrate by parts again: $\le|z|^{-2}(|q'(1/|z|)|+\int_{1/|z|}^\infty|q''|)\lesssim|z|^{-2}|y|^{-2}(|z|^{1-p}+|z|^{1-p})$. Total $\lesssim|y|^{-2}|z|^{-p-1}$. Combination: in the first region $\ang y^{-1}\le1\le|z|^{p-1}$; in the second region, if $|y|\ge1$ use the second bound ($|y|^{-2}\le2\ang y^{-2}$), and if $|y|<1$ then $|z|>2^{-1/(2p)}$ so $|z|^{p-1}\lesssim1\lesssim\ang{y}^{-2}|z|^{-p-1}$. Third region: choose an integer $N\ge\max\{2,L\}$. $(1-\chi)q$ is smooth, supported in $[1,2R]$ and flat at $1$; integrating by parts $N$ times, $|\widecheck{m^R_{2,0}}(z)|\le\frac{|z|^{-N}}{2\pi}\int_1^\infty|\partial^N((1-\chi)q)|\lesssim|z|^{-N}\int_1^\infty\xi^{-N}(|y|+\xi^p)^{-1}d\xi\lesssim\ang{y}^{-1}|z|^{-N}\le\ang{y}^{-1}|z|^{-L}$ (lem:c09_q_bounds(1), lem:c09_cutoff_bounds(4)). Lean route: one works directly with $(1-\chi)q$ (supported in $[1,2R]$) instead of $q-\chi q$, via $2\pi\operatorname{Re}\widecheck{m^R_{2,0}}(z)=\int_1^{2R+1}(1-\chi)q\cos(z\xi)\,d\xi$.

nodes.title: Leading kernels $m_{1,0}$, $m_{0,0}$
nodes.statement_html: For all $y$, $R\ge2$: $\partial_z\widecheck{m^R_{1,0}(y,\cdot)}=\widecheck{m^R_{2,0}(y,\cdot)}$ and $\partial_z\widecheck{m^R_{0,0}(y,\cdot)}=\widecheck{m^R_{1,0}(y,\cdot)}$. For every $L\ge0$ there is $C_L$ with, for all $y\in\R$, $R\ge R_0(y)$, $z\in\R$: $|\operatorname{Re}\partial_z\widecheck{m^R_{0,0}(y,\cdot)}(z)|\le C_L\ang{y}^{-1}\ang{z}^{-L}$ (paper eq. eqn:linear\_nonstationary\_leading\_kernel\_j0).
nodes.proof_html: $\partial_z\widecheck m=\widecheck{i\xi m}$ (Schwartz symbols) and $m_{j+1,0}=i\xi m_{j,0}$ (lem:c09_mjk_bounds). Since $m_{1,0}$ is purely imaginary, $\operatorname{Re}\widecheck{m_{1,0}}(0)=\frac1{2\pi}\operatorname{Re}\int m_{1,0}=0$, so for $|z|\le1$, $|\operatorname{Re}\widecheck{m_{1,0}}(z)|\le\int_0^{1}|\operatorname{Re}\widecheck{m_{2,0}}(\pm s)|ds \lesssim\int_0^{\ang y^{-1/p}}s^{p-1}ds+\ang{y}^{-2}\int_{\ang y^{-1/p}}^1s^{-p-1}ds+\ang y^{-1}\lesssim\ang{y}^{-1}$ by lem:c09_m20_kernel. For $|z|>1$ choose an integer $N\ge\max\{L,1\}$ and integrate by parts $N$ times in $\widecheck{m_{1,0}}(z)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_1^\infty m_{1,0}e^{iz\xi}$: $\lesssim|z|^{-N}\int_1^\infty\xi^{-1-N}(|y|+\xi^p)^{-1}\lesssim\ang y^{-1}|z|^{-N}$. For $|z|\le1$, $\ang z^{-L}\ge2^{-L/2}$; for $|z|>1$, $|z|^{-N}\le2^{L/2}\ang{z}^{-L}$.

nodes.title: Uniform bound for the sine integral
nodes.statement_html: There is an absolute constant $C_{\mathrm{Si}}$ such that $\bigl|\int_a^b\frac{\sin t}{t}dt\bigr|\le C_{\mathrm{Si}}$ for all $0<a<b$; consequently $\bigl|\int_1^\xi\frac{\sin(z\eta)}{\eta}d\eta\bigr|\le C_{\mathrm{Si}}$ for all $z\in\R$, $\xi\ge1$.
nodes.proof_html:
For $b\le1$ the integrand is bounded by $1$. For $a\ge1$ integrate by parts: $|\int_a^b|\le\frac1a+\frac1b+\int_a^bt^{-2}\le3$. Split otherwise. The second
  claim follows by substituting $t=z\eta$ ($z>0$; odd in $z$; trivial for $z=0$).

nodes.title: Kernels with $k=1$
nodes.statement_html: For every $L\ge0$ there is $C_L$ such that for all $R\ge2$, $y,z\in\R$: \[ \sum_{j=0}^1\bigl|\operatorname{Re}\partial_z\widecheck{m^R_{j,1}(y,\cdot)}(z)\bigr|+\bigl|\operatorname{Re}\widecheck{m^R_{2,1}(y,\cdot)}(z)\bigr|\le C_L\ang{y}^{-2}\ang z^{-L}. \]
nodes.proof_html: Write $\partial_z\widecheck{m_{j,1}}=\widecheck{i\xi m_{j,1}}$. $L^1$ bounds: $\|\xi m_{0,1}\|_{L^1}\lesssim\int_1^\infty\xi^{-2}(|y|+\xi^p)^{-2}\lesssim\ang y^{-2}$; by the formula in lem:c09_mjk_bounds, $\|m_{2,1}\|_{L^1}\lesssim\ang{y}^{-2}\int|\partial_\xi b|+\int_1^\infty\xi^{p-1}(|y|+\xi^p)^{-3}d\xi\lesssim\ang{y}^{-2}$, using lem:c09_cutoff_bounds(2),(3),(4) ($\|\partial_\xi b\|_{L^1}\le C$ uniformly in $y,R$). Hence for $|z|\le1$ the terms with $\xi m_{0,1}$ and $m_{2,1}$ are $\lesssim\ang y^{-2}$.
