nodes.statement_html: For every noninteger $a>0$ there is $C_a>0$ such that for all $z\in\R$, $\eta-\tau_z\eta\in C^a(\R)$ and $N_a(\eta-\tau_z\eta)\le C_a\min\{|z|,1\}$.
nodes.proof_html: For $|z|\le1$ use $\eta(x)-\eta(x-z)=z\int_0^1\eta'(x-tz)dt$ and global translation bounds for $\eta'$. For $|z|>1$ use the triangle inequality and $2N_a(\eta)$. Smooth compact support supplies finiteness of the cutoff norms in both cases.

nodes.title: Quantitative cutoff extension from the interval
nodes.section: Fixed data and global Holder transport
nodes.statement_html: For every noninteger $a>0$ there is $C_a>0$ such that, for every $h\in C^a([-1,1])$, the function $\eta h$, extended by zero outside $[-1,1]$, belongs to $C^a(\R)$ and $N_a(\eta h)\le C_aN_a(h;[-1,1])$. Values of $h$ outside $[-1,1]$ have no effect.
nodes.proof_html: Apply the interval product estimate. The support is separated from the endpoints by $1/8$, so extension by zero preserves the derivatives. For Holder pairs crossing outside the interval, either both derivative values vanish or their distance is at least $1/8$; use the sup bound.

nodes.title: Near-part smoothness without bounds at infinity
nodes.statement_html: Let $0<p<1$ and $w\in C^\infty(\R)$, without global derivative bounds. The function $U(x)=c_p\int\chi(z)(w(x)-w(x-z))|z|^{-1-p}dz$ is smooth. For every $m\in\N$ its derivative is the same absolutely convergent integral with $w$ replaced by $w^{(m)}$. On every compact $x$ interval all differentiated integrands admit a common integrable majorant, using only the local bound for $w^{(m+1)}$ on the interval enlarged by two.
nodes.proof_html:
Write $w^{(m)}(x)-w^{(m)}(x-z)=z\int_0^1w^{(m+1)}(x-tz)dt$.
  The resulting majorant is a constant times $\mathbf1_{|z|\le2}|z|^{-p}$.
  Apply dominated differentiation inductively; the point $z=0$ is assigned value zero.

nodes.title: Far-part smoothness by differentiating the kernel
nodes.statement_html: Let $0<p<1$, and let $w$ be smooth and bounded on $\R$. Put $\kappa_p(z)=(1-\chi(z))|z|^{-1-p}$, with value zero near the origin. Every derivative of $\kappa_p$ is integrable. The far part is \[ c_p\left(w(x)\int\kappa_p-\int\kappa_p(x-z)w(z)dz\right). \] It is smooth, and its convolution term can be differentiated any number of times by differentiating $\kappa_p$. Every such integral converges absolutely, locally uniformly in $x$.
nodes.proof_html: For $|z|\ge2$, the $m$th kernel derivative is bounded by $C_{p,m}|z|^{-1-p-m}$; the remaining region is compact and smooth. Use the smooth-convolution argument c03\_aux\_conv\_smooth, or move that Schauder-free helper upstream. No derivatives of $w$ at infinity enter the convolution bound.

nodes.title: The local right-hand-side norm is finite
nodes.statement_html: For $0<p<1$ and smooth bounded $w$, the singular integral defining $|D|^pw(x)$ converges absolutely for every $x$ and is smooth on $\R$. In particular $|D|^pw\in C^a([-1,1])$ for every noninteger $a>0$. This is a qualitative finiteness assertion; no bound by finitely many global derivatives of $w$ is assumed or claimed.
nodes.proof_html: Split the integral with $\chi$ and add the two smooth functions. Smoothness on a neighborhood of a compact interval implies finiteness of each noninteger Holder norm there.

nodes.title: Cutoff commutator identity and convergence
nodes.statement_html: Let $0<p<1$ and $w$ be smooth and bounded. Then all integrals in the identity \[ |D|^p(\eta w)=\eta|D|^pw+C_{\eta,p}w \] converge absolutely and the equality holds at every point.
nodes.proof_html: Expand the difference of the two fractional kernels after putting them in the same shifted variable. The remaining numerator is $(\eta(x)-\eta(x-z))w(x-z)$, bounded by a constant times $\|w\|_\infty\min(|z|,1)$. Integrability permits splitting the integral.

nodes.title: Global Holder bound for the commutator
nodes.statement_html: For $0<p<1$ and noninteger $a>0$ there is $C_{p,a}>0$ such that every smooth $w\in C^a(\R)$ satisfies $C_{\eta,p}w\in C^a(\R)$ and $N_a(C_{\eta,p}w)\le C_{p,a}N_a(w)$.
nodes.proof_html: The $C^a$ norm of $(\eta-\tau_z\eta)\tau_z w$ is bounded by $C_a\min(|z|,1)N_a(w)$. All required mixed derivatives are measurable. Integrate this majorant against $|z|^{-1-p}$; its scalar integral is $2/(1-p)+2/p$. This is precisely where $p<1$ is used.

nodes.title: Quantitative localized right-hand side
nodes.statement_html: For $0<p<1$ and noninteger $\beta>0$ there is $C_{p,\beta}>0$ such that, for smooth $w\in C^\beta(\R)$, $v=\eta w$ is smooth and compactly supported and $h=|D|^pv$ belongs to $C^\beta(\R)$ with \[ N_\beta(h)\le C_{p,\beta}\bigl(N_\beta(w)+N_\beta(|D|^pw;[-1,1])\bigr), \qquad \|v\|_\infty\le N_\beta(w). \]
nodes.proof_html: The local norm is finite by the first lemma. Apply quantitative cutoff extension to $|D|^pw$ and add the commutator estimate. The fixed cutoff satisfies $0\le\eta\le1$.

nodes.title: Finite dyadic telescoping
nodes.statement_html: For every $n\in\N$ and $\xi\in\R$, \[ \chi(\xi)+\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\varphi(2^{-j}\xi)=\chi(2^{-n}\xi). \] The right side tends to one as $n\to\infty$ and is bounded in absolute value by one.
nodes.proof_html: Telescope the defining difference. For fixed $\xi$, eventually $|2^{-n}\xi|\le1$.

nodes.title: Real Schwartz inverse kernels
nodes.statement_html: For $0<p<1$, the inverse transforms of $q_p$ and $\chi$ are real Schwartz functions. Their Fourier transforms are respectively $q_p$ and $\chi$, in the project's convention. In particular, $K_p$ and every derivative are integrable; for every $m\in\N$ and $a\ge0$, $\int|z|^a|K_p^{(m)}(z)|dz<\infty$.
nodes.proof_html: Bundle smooth compactly supported symbols using HasCompactSupport.toSchwartzMap. Apply Schwartz Fourier inversion with the $2\pi$ normalization bridge. Reality follows from even real symbols. Schwartz decay with an integer weight greater than $a+1$ proves the weighted integrability.

nodes.title: Vanishing polynomial moments
nodes.statement_html: For $0<p<1$ and all integers $r,m\ge0$, the moment integral converges absolutely and \[ \int_\R z^r K_p^{(m)}(z)dz=0. \]
nodes.proof_html: The transform of $K_p^{(m)}$ is $(i\xi)^mq_p(\xi)$, whose derivatives all vanish at zero. Apply the Fourier differentiation formula for Schwartz functions and evaluate there. Record the project's normalization explicitly; the zero conclusion is independent of its nonzero factor.

nodes.title: Exact dyadic scaling and weighted norms
nodes.statement_html: For $0<p<1$, $j,m\in\N$, and $a\ge0$, \[ K_{p,j}^{(m)}(x)=2^{(m+1-p)j}K_p^{(m)}(2^jx),\qquad \widehat K_{p,j}(\xi)=\varphi(2^{-j}\xi)|\xi|^{-p}, \] where the symbol at zero is defined to be zero. Moreover, \[ \int|z|^a|K_{p,j}^{(m)}(z)|dz =2^{(m-p-a)j}\int|z|^a|K_p^{(m)}(z)|dz, \qquad \int z^rK_{p,j}^{(m)}(z)dz=0\quad(r\in\N). \]
nodes.proof_html: Differentiate the scaled kernel and substitute $u=2^jz$ in the integrals. For the Fourier transform, $2^{-pj}q_p(2^{-j}\xi)=\varphi(2^{-j}\xi)|\xi|^{-p}$. This scaling factor is essential to the gain of $p$ derivatives.

nodes.title: Compact-input fractional Fourier bridge
nodes.statement_html: Let $0<p<1$ and $v\in C_c^\infty(\R;\R)$. The function $m(\xi)=|\xi|^p\widehat v(\xi)$ is integrable and $|D|^pv(x)=\widecheck m(x)$ pointwise, with absolute convergence on both sides.
nodes.proof_html: Apply the Schwartz multiplier identity of lem:c03_frac_kernel_formula; it is valid for all $0<p<1$. The Fourier transform of $v$ is Schwartz, so multiplication by $|\xi|^p$ preserves integrability. Use the real-to-complex bridge for the displayed identity.

nodes.title: Dyadic block factorization
nodes.statement_html: For $0<p<1$, $v\in C_c^\infty(\R;\R)$, $h=|D|^pv$, and every $j\in\N$, \[ \Delta_jv(x)=(K_{p,j}*h)(x)\qquad(x\in\R). \] The convolution and the double integral used in this identity are absolutely convergent.
nodes.proof_html: Substitute the inverse-transform expression for $h$. Fubini follows from $\|K_{p,j}\|_1\||\xi|^p\widehat v\|_1<\infty$. The two symbols multiply to $\varphi(2^{-j}\xi)$, also at zero. This proof does not require a general distributional transform theorem for $h$.

nodes.title: Global Holder Taylor remainder
nodes.statement_html: Let $\beta=k+\theta>0$, $k\in\N$, $0<\theta<1$. There is $C_\beta>0$ such that for every $h\in C^\beta(\R)$ and $x,z\in\R$, \[ \left|h(x-z)-\sum_{r=0}^k\frac{h^{(r)}(x)(-z)^r}{r!}\right| \le C_\beta N_\beta(h)|z|^\beta. \]
nodes.proof_html:
For $k=0$ use the Holder inequality. For $k\ge1$, use Taylor's integral formula through
  order $k-1$, subtract the constant $k$th derivative inside its remainder, and use its
  Holder bound. The estimate is global and works for both signs of $z$.

nodes.title: Cancellation estimate for differentiated blocks
nodes.statement_html: For $0<p<1$, noninteger $\beta>0$, and every $m\in\N$, there is $C_{p,\beta,m}>0$ such that for every $h\in C^\beta(\R)$ and $j\in\N$, $K_{p,j}*h$ is smooth, its $m$th derivative is the absolutely convergent convolution $K_{p,j}^{(m)}*h$, and \[ \|\partial^m(K_{p,j}*h)\|_\infty \le C_{p,\beta,m}2^{(m-\beta-p)j}N_\beta(h). \]
nodes.proof_html: Differentiate the Schwartz kernel, using boundedness of $h$ and local translation majorants. Subtract the Taylor polynomial of $h(x-z)$ under the integral; every polynomial term vanishes by the kernel moments. Bound the remainder and use the exact weighted scaling. No additional derivatives of $h$ are required.

nodes.title: Low-frequency bounds from the value norm
nodes.statement_html: For every $m\in\N$ there is $C_m>0$ such that, for every real $v\in C_c^\infty(\R)$, $S_0v=\chi^\vee*v$ is smooth and $\|\partial^mS_0v\|_\infty\le C_m\|v\|_\infty$. Every differentiated convolution is absolutely convergent.
nodes.proof_html: Fubini identifies the inverse-transform definition with convolution. Differentiate the Schwartz kernel and use its derivative $L^1$ norm.

nodes.title: Uniform reconstruction, including differentiated partial sums
nodes.section: Reconstruction of the higher Holder norm
nodes.statement_html: Let $v\in C_c^\infty(\R;\R)$ and $P_nv=S_0v+\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\Delta_jv$. For every integer $m\ge0$, $\partial^mP_nv\to\partial^mv$ uniformly on $\R$ as $n\to\infty$.
nodes.proof_html: The differentiated partial sum is the real inverse transform of $(i\xi)^m\chi(2^{-n}\xi)\widehat v(\xi)$. Dominated convergence in $L^1_\xi$ follows from the Schwartz decay of $\widehat v$. The inverse-transform $L^1\to L^\infty$ bound and Fourier inversion give the conclusion. This compact-input argument avoids building a general theorem on differentiating infinite series.

nodes.title: The scalar dyadic increment estimate
nodes.section: Reconstruction of the higher Holder norm
nodes.statement_html: For every $0<\theta<1$ there is $C_\theta>0$ such that for every $d\ge0$ and $n\in\N$, \[ \sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\min\{2^{-\theta j},d\,2^{(1-\theta)j}\} \le C_\theta d^\theta. \] For every $a>0$, $\sum_{j\ge0}2^{-aj}$ converges, with sum $(1-2^{-a})^{-1}$.
nodes.proof_html:
If $d=0$ the first sum is zero; if $d\ge1$ use the decreasing geometric series.
  For $0<d<1$, choose $J\in\N$ with $2^Jd\le1<2^{J+1}d$.
  Sum the increasing geometric expression for $j\le J$ and the decreasing one for $j>J$.
  Both are bounded by a constant times $d^\theta$, uniformly in the partial-sum cutoff.

nodes.title: Compact-input global Schauder estimate
nodes.section: Reconstruction of the higher Holder norm
nodes.statement_html: Let $0<p<1$, $\beta>0$, and assume $\beta$ and $s=\beta+p$ are nonintegers. There is $C_{p,\beta}>0$ such that, for every real $v\in C_c^\infty(\R)$ with $h=|D|^pv\in C^\beta(\R)$, \[ v\in C^{\beta+p}(\R),\qquad N_{\beta+p}(v)\le C_{p,\beta}\bigl(\|v\|_\infty+N_\beta(h)\bigr). \]
nodes.proof_html: Put $k=\lfloor s\rfloor$, $\theta=s-k$. For $0\le m\le k$, sum the block bounds $2^{(m-s)j}$ and pass to the uniformly reconstructed derivative. For the $k$th derivative increment, each block is bounded by a constant times $N_\beta(h)\min(2^{-\theta j},|x-y|2^{(1-\theta)j})$. Use the scalar increment lemma and pass from finite sums to $v^{(k)}$ by uniform convergence. The low block is controlled by its $k$th and $(k+1)$st derivative bounds, splitting $|x-y|\le1$ from $|x-y|\ge1$. Assemble the finite Holder norm with the norm constructors. The $(k+1)$st derivative block estimate is used only for increments: its infinite series is not claimed to be summable.

nodes.title: Kernel, adjoint cancellation and renormalized potential
nodes.section: The two-dimensional operator and its normalization
nodes.statement_html: Let $E=\R^2$ with the Euclidean norm, and write $(x,y)\in E$ for the point with coordinates $x,y$. For a vector field $Q:E\to E$ put $\operatorname{div}Q=\partial_1Q_1+\partial_2Q_2$. For $z\ne0$ set \[ P_{\alpha,c}(z)=c|z|^{-\alpha},\qquad K_{\alpha,c}(z)=\alpha c\,Jz\,|z|^{-\alpha-2}=-J\nabla P_{\alpha,c}(z), \] and set both kernels to zero at the single point zero. For a vector test function $\Phi:E\to E$ define \[ B^*_{\alpha,c}\Phi(Y)=\int_E K_{\alpha,c}(z)\cdot(\Phi(Y+z)-\Phi(Y))\,dz. \] For a bounded measurable real density $\theta$ define \[ V_{\alpha,c}[\theta](X)=\int_E [P_{\alpha,c}(X-Y)-\mathbf1_{|Y|>1}P_{\alpha,c}(-Y)]\theta(Y)\,dY. \] These are total formulas; the next lemmas establish their analytic meanings. The unsubtracted integral $P*\theta$ is not asserted to converge for an infinite patch.

nodes.title: Canonical and front normalizations
nodes.section: The two-dimensional operator and its normalization
nodes.statement_html: Put \[ A_\alpha=\frac{2^{2-\alpha}\pi\Gamma(1-\alpha/2)}{\Gamma(\alpha/2)},\qquad c_{\rm std}=A_\alpha^{-1},\qquad c_{\rm front}=\operatorname{calpha}(\alpha-1),\qquad \kappa_\alpha=\frac{c_{\rm front}}{c_{\rm std}}. \] The two-dimensional Fourier convention is $\widehat f(\xi)=\int_E f(X)e^{-iX\cdot\xi}dX$, with inverse factor $(2\pi)^{-2}$. The canonical operator $-\nabla^\perp(-\Delta)^{-1+\alpha/2}$ has multiplier $-iJ\xi|\xi|^{\alpha-2}$, given value zero at $\xi=0$. Identification of the real-space operator with this multiplier is a theorem below. The two coefficients are kept distinct; the final application records the corresponding time change.

nodes.title: Euclidean coordinates and radial majorants
nodes.section: The two-dimensional operator and its normalization
nodes.statement_html: Coordinate identification $E\leftrightarrow\R\times\R$ preserves Lebesgue measure, and $|z|^2=z_1^2+z_2^2$. For $r>0$, \[ \int_{|z|<r}|z|^{-\alpha}dz=\frac{2\pi}{2-\alpha}r^{2-\alpha},\qquad \int_{|z|>r}|z|^{-\alpha-1}dz=\frac{2\pi}{\alpha-1}r^{1-\alpha}. \] The displayed nonnegative integrands are integrable on their respective domains. Consequently there is $C_{\alpha,c}>0$ such that for every $\xi\in E$, \[ \int_E|K_{\alpha,c}(z)|\,|e^{-iz\cdot\xi}-1|dz \le C_{\alpha,c}|\xi|^{\alpha-1}, \] with the integral zero when $\xi=0$.
nodes.proof_html:
Use the volume-preserving Euclidean-to-coordinate map and radial integration in dimension two.
  For the last bound split at $r=|\xi|^{-1}$ and use $|e^{-is}-1|\le\min(|s|,2)$.
  The cases $\alpha>1$ and $\alpha<2$ control different ends of the integral.

nodes.title: $L^1$ translation estimate for test fields
nodes.section: The two-dimensional operator and its normalization
nodes.statement_html: For every vector test function $\Phi:E\to E$ and every $z\in E$, \[ \int_E|\Phi(Y+z)-\Phi(Y)|dY \le\min\left(|z|\int_E\|D\Phi(Y)\|dY,\ 2\int_E|\Phi(Y)|dY\right). \] All the displayed integrals are finite.
nodes.proof_html:
Apply segment FTC to $\Phi(Y+tz)$, integrate its norm, and use Fubini and translation invariance.
  The second bound is the triangle inequality. This is a finite-dimensional test-function lemma.

nodes.title: Absolute adjoint pairing
nodes.section: The two-dimensional operator and its normalization
nodes.statement_html: For every vector test $\Phi$, the function $(Y,z)\mapsto K_{\alpha,c}(z)\cdot(\Phi(Y+z)-\Phi(Y))$ is absolutely integrable on $E\times E$. The inner integral defining $B^*\Phi(Y)$ converges absolutely for every $Y$, and \[ \|B^*\Phi\|_{L^1(E)}\le C_{\alpha,c} (\|\Phi\|_{L^1(E)}+\|D\Phi\|_{L^1(E)}). \] Thus $\int\theta B^*\Phi$ is absolutely convergent for every bounded measurable $\theta$.
nodes.proof_html: Use Tonelli for the norm majorant and split $|z|\le1$ from its complement. Pointwise convergence uses the bounded derivative of the test field near zero and its bounded values at infinity.

nodes.title: Test potential and adjoint divergence identity
nodes.section: The two-dimensional operator and its normalization
nodes.statement_html: For a vector test $\Phi$, let $A_\Phi(Y)=\int_E P_{\alpha,c}(X-Y)\Phi(X)dX$. This integral is absolutely convergent, $A_\Phi$ is $C^1$, and \[ B^*\Phi=-\operatorname{div}(J A_\Phi). \] If $\operatorname{supp}\Phi\subset\{|X|\le L\}$, then for $|Y|>2L+1$, $|A_\Phi(Y)|\le C_{\alpha,c}|Y|^{-\alpha}\|\Phi\|_1$. In particular $B^*(\nabla\zeta)=0$ for every scalar test $\zeta$.
nodes.proof_html: Differentiate the compact test factor after shifting variables. Integration by parts in the locally integrable potential kernel gives the adjoint identity; retain the cancellation at zero. For a gradient test, the scalar curl is zero by equality of mixed derivatives. Lean route: $A_\Phi$ is the convolution $P*\Phi$ ($P$ even), differentiated on the compact test factor; the adjoint identity $B^*\Phi(Y)=\int P(z)\operatorname{curl}\Phi(Y+z)dz$ is proved for the regularized kernel $P_\delta=c(|z|^2+\delta^2)^{-\alpha/2}$ by whole-space integration by parts and oddness of $K_\delta$, then $\delta\to0$ by dominated convergence, keeping the cancellation $\Phi(Y+z)-\Phi(Y)$ until the limit.

nodes.title: Absolute convergence of the renormalized potential
nodes.section: The two-dimensional operator and its normalization
nodes.statement_html: For every $R\ge1$ there is $C_{\alpha,c,R}>0$ such that for every bounded measurable $\theta$ with $|\theta|\le M$, $M\ge0$, and every $|X|\le R$, \[ \int_E|P(X-Y)-\mathbf1_{|Y|>1}P(-Y)|\,|\theta(Y)|dY\le C_{\alpha,c,R}M. \] The integral defining $V[\theta]$ is therefore absolutely convergent at every $X$, measurable and locally bounded. Changing the subtraction radius to another positive radius changes it by a finite constant independent of $X$.
nodes.proof_html: On $|Y|>2R+2$, use the mean-value estimate $|P(X-Y)-P(-Y)|\le C_{\alpha,c}R|Y|^{-\alpha-1}$. In the remaining bounded region integrate the translated singular kernel using its radial integral. Measurability follows from parameter integration. The difference of two subtraction choices is an integral over a bounded annulus and contains no $X$.

nodes.title: Renormalized potential and its distributional gradient
nodes.section: The two-dimensional operator and its normalization
nodes.statement_html: For every bounded measurable $\theta$, the defining integral for $V_{\alpha,c}[\theta](X)$ converges absolutely for every $X$ and defines a locally bounded measurable function. For every vector test $\Phi$, \[ \int_E\theta B^*\Phi=-\int_E V_{\alpha,c}[\theta]\,\operatorname{div}(J\Phi). \] Both sides converge absolutely. This is $B_{\alpha,c}\theta=-J\nabla V_{\alpha,c}[\theta]$ in distributions. Replacing the subtraction radius $1$ by another positive radius changes $V$ by a finite constant independent of $X$ and leaves the velocity unchanged.
nodes.proof_html: For $|Y|>2|X|+2$, the subtracted kernel is bounded by $C_{\alpha,c}|X||Y|^{-\alpha-1}$. Near $Y=X$ use local integrability of $|X-Y|^{-\alpha}$. Establish local bounds by integrating the singular kernel, not by taking a pointwise supremum over its moving pole. Integrate by parts in the kernel with a small-radius cutoff; its error is $O(r^{2-\alpha})$. Keep the subtraction until Fubini is justified. Its contribution against $\operatorname{div}(J\Phi)$ then vanishes because the integral of a compactly supported divergence is zero.

nodes.title: Gamma layer representation of the singular kernel
nodes.section: The two-dimensional operator and its normalization
nodes.statement_html: For $z\ne0$, \[ |z|^{-\alpha}=\frac1{\Gamma(\alpha/2)}\int_0^\infty s^{\alpha/2-1}e^{-s|z|^2}ds,\qquad K_{\alpha,c}(z)=\frac{2c}{\Gamma(\alpha/2)}Jz\int_0^\infty s^{\alpha/2}e^{-s|z|^2}ds. \] Both scalar parameter integrals converge absolutely. For each $\xi\in E$, multiplying the second representation by $e^{-iz\cdot\xi}-1$ yields an absolutely integrable double integrand in $(s,z)\in(0,\infty)\times E$.
nodes.proof_html: Substitute $u=s|z|^2$ in the Gamma integral and use $\Gamma(1+\alpha/2)=(\alpha/2)\Gamma(\alpha/2)$. Tonelli on the norm reduces double-integrability to the radial cancellation majorant.

nodes.title: Two-dimensional Gaussian transform and first moment
nodes.section: The two-dimensional operator and its normalization
nodes.statement_html: For every $s>0$ and $\xi\in E$, the following integrals converge absolutely: \[ \int_Ee^{-s|z|^2-i z\cdot\xi}dz=\frac\pi s e^{-|\xi|^2/(4s)},\qquad \int_E z e^{-s|z|^2-i z\cdot\xi}dz =-\frac{i\pi}{2s^2}\xi e^{-|\xi|^2/(4s)},\qquad \int_E z e^{-s|z|^2}dz=0. \] The vector formulas are interpreted componentwise after complexification.
nodes.proof_html:
Apply the inner-product-space Gaussian Fourier integral in dimension two with
  phase coefficient $-i$, or coordinate Fubini and the one-dimensional formula.
  Differentiate in $\xi$ under the integral, with a Gaussian moment majorant, for the first moment.
  Oddness gives the final identity. Keep the $e^{-iz\cdot\xi}$ convention explicit.

nodes.title: Inverse-parameter Gamma integral
nodes.section: The two-dimensional operator and its normalization
nodes.statement_html: For every $a,b>0$, the integrand is integrable on $(0,\infty)$ and \[ \int_0^\infty s^{-1-a}e^{-b/s}ds=b^{-a}\Gamma(a). \]
nodes.proof_html:
Use the decreasing substitution $u=b/s$, including the absolute Jacobian.
  Gamma integrability proves convergence at both endpoints before the change of variables.

nodes.title: Gaussian evaluation of the velocity symbol
nodes.section: The two-dimensional operator and its normalization
nodes.statement_html: For every $\xi\in E$, the vector integral is absolutely convergent and \[ \int_E K_{\alpha,c}(z)(e^{-iz\cdot\xi}-1)dz =-icA_\alpha J\xi|\xi|^{\alpha-2}, \] where the right side is zero at $\xi=0$. In particular $A_\alpha,c_{\rm std},\kappa_\alpha>0$.
nodes.proof_html: Use the Gamma representation $K(z)=\frac{2c}{\Gamma(\alpha/2)}Jz\int_0^\infty s^{\alpha/2}e^{-s|z|^2}ds$. Absolute Fubini follows from the radial cancellation majorant before evaluating the Gaussian. The two-dimensional Gaussian first moment is $\int z e^{-s|z|^2-i z\cdot\xi}dz=-i\pi\xi(2s^2)^{-1}e^{-|\xi|^2/(4s)}$. Substitution $u=|\xi|^2/(4s)$ gives $A_\alpha$. Handle $\xi=0$ separately. Gamma positivity gives $c_{\rm std}>0$; use the already proved positivity of calpha for the ratio.

nodes.title: Identification with the canonical two-dimensional operator
nodes.section: The two-dimensional operator and its normalization
nodes.statement_html: For every real Schwartz function $f$ on $E$, the integral $B_{\alpha,c}f(X)=\int K(z)(f(X-z)-f(X))dz$ converges absolutely, belongs to $L^1(E;E)$, and has Fourier multiplier $-icA_\alpha J\xi|\xi|^{\alpha-2}$, componentwise. Equivalently, $B_{\alpha,c}f=-cA_\alpha\nabla^\perp(-\Delta)^{-1+\alpha/2}f$. For bounded densities the adjoint pairing and renormalized potential give the same distributional extension.
nodes.proof_html: Fourier-transform the absolutely integrable difference kernel using Fubini, or insert Schwartz inversion and the symbol integral. The bound $C|\xi|^{\alpha-1}$ justifies the latter exchange. Differentiation of the inverse transform of $|\xi|^{\alpha-2}\widehat f$ is legitimate by absolute integrability. Duality is meaningful for bounded densities because $B^*\Phi\in L^1$; no divergent unsubtracted potential or undefined product of tempered distributions is used.

nodes.title: Admissible graphs, patches and canonical representatives
nodes.statement_html: Let $I$ be a nonempty open time interval. A graph $F:\R\times I\to\R$ is admissible if it is jointly smooth on $\R\times I$ (no smoothness is required at the endpoints of $I$ or outside $\R\times I$) and for every compact interval $J_0\subset I$ there is $M_{J_0}\ge0$ with $|F_x(x,t)|\le M_{J_0}$ for all $x\in\R,t\in J_0$. No global bound on $F$, $F_{xx}$ or time derivatives at spatial infinity is assumed. Put $\gamma_t(s)=(s,F(s,t))$, $\tau_t(s)=(1,F_x(s,t))$, $\Omega_t=\{(x,y):y<F(x,t)\}$, and $\theta_F=\mathbf1_{\Omega_t}$. Define, for $X\notin\Gamma_t=\gamma_t(\R)$, \[ U_{\alpha,c}[F](X,t)=-c\int_\R\tau_t(s)|X-\gamma_t(s)|^{-\alpha}ds, \] and give $U$ value zero on $\Gamma_t$. This candidate boundary representation is not assumed to satisfy the two-dimensional velocity law; that is proved in sec:c13_velocity_law. Define separately \[ W_{\alpha,c}[F](x,t)=c\int_\R [F_x(x,t)-F_x(s,t)]|\gamma_t(x)-\gamma_t(s)|^{-\alpha}ds. \] The graph normal is $(-F_x,1)/\sqrt{1+F_x^2}$; $W$ is its normal velocity multiplied by $\sqrt{1+F_x^2}$. It is not the value of the arbitrarily extended vector field on the graph.

nodes.title: Measurability, null graphs and a distance bound
nodes.statement_html: Each patch is measurable, each graph has two-dimensional measure zero, and the spacetime graph has three-dimensional measure zero. For a fixed-time slope bound $|F_x|\le M$, let $h=s-x$ and $\delta=y-F(x,t)$. Then \[ h^2+\delta^2\le2(1+M^2)\bigl(h^2+(y-F(s,t))^2\bigr). \] The same constants work on a compact time interval with its common slope bound.
nodes.proof_html:
Openness of the subgraph follows from continuity; Fubini makes each vertical graph section a
  null singleton. Use $|F(s,t)-F(x,t)|\le M|h|$ and the squared triangle inequality.

nodes.title: Finite graph-domain flux formula
nodes.statement_html: Let $R>0$, $F\in C^1(\R)$, $H>0$ with $-H<F(s)$ for $|s|\le R$, and $Q:E\to E$ be $C^1$ on a neighborhood of the closed domain $D=\{(s,y):|s|<R,-H<y<F(s)\}$. Then \[ \begin{split} \int_D\operatorname{div}Q ={}&\int_{-R}^{R}(Q_2-F'Q_1)(s,F(s))ds-\int_{-R}^{R}Q_2(s,-H)ds\\ &+\int_{-H}^{F(R)}Q_1(R,y)dy-\int_{-H}^{F(-R)}Q_1(-R,y)dy . \end{split} \] Every integral is absolutely convergent.
nodes.proof_html:
Coordinate Fubini and vertical FTC give the $Q_2$ terms.
  Differentiate $s\mapsto\int_{-H}^{F(s)}Q_1(s,y)dy$, then use one-dimensional FTC.
  This is the graph-specific substitute for a general Gauss theorem.
  Lean route: for the $x$-derivative term substitute $y=(F(s)+H)\tau-H$, which maps the domain to the
  rectangle $[-R,R]\times[0,1]$, then use Fubini there and FTC in $s$ and in $\tau$.

nodes.title: Flux formula for an unbounded subgraph and a compact test field
nodes.statement_html: For a $C^1$ graph with bounded slope and a compactly supported $C^1$ vector field $Q$, \[ \int_{y<F(x)}\operatorname{div}Q(X)dX =\int_\R(Q_2-F'Q_1)(x,F(x))dx, \] with absolute convergence.
nodes.proof_html: Use $H_R=|F(0)|+(M+1)R+1$. Once $R$ is large enough, the artificial sides lie outside the support of $Q$. Pass to the limit in the compactly supported volume integral.

nodes.title: Off-graph velocity convergence and size
nodes.section: The candidate velocity as an actual function
nodes.statement_html: For $|F_x|\le M$ the contour integral for $U(X,t)$ converges absolutely at every $X\notin\Gamma_t$. There is $C_{\alpha,c,M}>0$, independent of $F,X$, such that \[ |U((x,y),t)|\le C_{\alpha,c,M}|y-F(x,t)|^{1-\alpha}\quad(y\ne F(x,t)). \]
nodes.proof_html:
Bound $|\tau|$ by $\sqrt{1+M^2}$ and compare the denominator with
  $h^2+\delta^2$, using $|F(s,t)-F(x,t)|\le M|s-x|$ directly. The one-dimensional integral of $(h^2+\delta^2)^{-\alpha/2}$
  scales as $|\delta|^{1-\alpha}$ and converges because $\alpha>1$.

nodes.title: Local integrability and joint contour-test Fubini
nodes.section: The candidate velocity as an actual function
nodes.statement_html: For an admissible graph, $U$ is jointly measurable and locally integrable on $E\times I$. For a compact spatial set $Q$ and compact time interval $J_0\subset I$, $\int_{J_0}\int_Q|U|<\infty$. For every compactly supported spatial test $\Phi$, the integrand $|\tau_t(s)||X-\gamma_t(s)|^{-\alpha}|\Phi(X)|$ is integrable in $(s,X)$; its bound is uniform in $t\in J_0$ for tests supported in a fixed compact set with bounded sup norm.
nodes.proof_html: Integrate $|y-F(x,t)|^{1-\alpha}$ over bounded vertical intervals; the bound is uniform in the center $F(x,t)$ since $1-\alpha>-1$. For joint contour-test integrability, use Tonelli: bounded $s$ uses local two-dimensional integrability of $|X-\gamma(s)|^{-\alpha}$; large $|s|$ uses horizontal separation and the integrable tail $|s|^{-\alpha}$. Lean route: the vertical estimate and the graph nullness are proved directly in coordinates (Tonelli in lintegral); joint measurability on $E\times I$ uses a piecewise modification, since $F$ is not controlled for $t\notin I$. Do not replace this Tonelli argument by a pointwise integral assigned zero on the singular graph.

nodes.title: Spatial smoothness and divergence-free velocity
nodes.section: The candidate velocity as an actual function
nodes.statement_html: For each fixed time, $U$ is spatially $C^1$ on $E\setminus\Gamma_t$ and $\operatorname{div}_X U=0$ there. Its first spatial derivatives are jointly continuous in $(X,t)$ off the spacetime graph. No time differentiability of $U$ is claimed from the present hypotheses.
nodes.proof_html: On off-graph compact subsets the vertical gap is bounded away from zero and the global slope is bounded uniformly in time. The kernel and its first spatial derivative have tails bounded by $C|s|^{-\alpha}$ and $C|s|^{-\alpha-1}$, respectively. For divergence, use $\operatorname{div}U=c\int\partial_s|X-\gamma_t(s)|^{-\alpha}ds$. FTC on $[-R,R]$ and horizontal separation make both endpoint terms vanish.

nodes.title: Artificial-boundary errors vanish
nodes.section: Identification of the candidate with the two-dimensional velocity law
nodes.statement_html: Fix a time and $|F'|\le M$. Put $H_R=|F(0)|+(M+1)R+1$ and $D_R=\{|x|<R,-H_R<y<F(x)\}$. For every vector test $\Phi$, the sum of the three artificial-boundary contributions in the finite graph flux formula for $Q=J A_\Phi$ has modulus at most $C_{\alpha,c,M,F(0),\Phi}R^{1-\alpha}$ for all sufficiently large $R$. The constant and lower threshold for $R$ are chosen independently of $R$.
nodes.proof_html:
Each artificial side is at distance at least $R/2$ from the test support once $R$ is large.
  Its length is at most $C_{M,F(0)}R$. Multiply this length by the $R^{-\alpha}$ potential bound.
  Lean route: that far-field bound, $|A_\Phi(Y)|\le|c|2^\alpha|Y|^{-\alpha}\|\Phi\|_1$ for
  $|Y|\ge2L$, is proved directly from $|X-Y|\ge|Y|/2$ on the test support, without citing the earlier lemmas.
  The exponent $1-\alpha<0$ is essential here.

nodes.title: Bulk-to-contour velocity identity
nodes.section: Identification of the candidate with the two-dimensional velocity law
nodes.statement_html: For a fixed smooth bounded-slope graph, every vector test $\Phi$ satisfies \[ \int_E\theta_F(Y)B^*\Phi(Y)dY =-\int_\R A_\Phi(\gamma(s))\cdot\tau(s)ds =\int_E U[F](X)\cdot\Phi(X)dX. \] All integrals are absolutely convergent. Hence the candidate contour velocity is a locally integrable representative of the independently defined two-dimensional operator $B_{\alpha,c}\theta_F$.
nodes.proof_html: Apply the finite flux formula to $J A_\Phi$ on $D_R$ and use $B^*\Phi=-\operatorname{div}(JA_\Phi)$. On the graph, $n\,ds=(-F',1)ds=J\tau\,ds$, so $(JA_\Phi)\cdot n\,ds=A_\Phi\cdot\tau\,ds$. The outer minus sign gives the negative contour velocity. The artificial sides vanish by the preceding lemma; dominated convergence applies to $\theta_{D_R}B^*\Phi$, which is dominated by $|B^*\Phi|\in L^1$. The graph is null, so the value of $U$ on it is irrelevant. Joint contour-test Fubini gives the second equality.

nodes.title: Bulk principal values agree with the weak velocity
nodes.section: Identification of the candidate with the two-dimensional velocity law
nodes.statement_html: Set $u_\varepsilon(X)=\int_{|z|>\varepsilon}K(z)\theta_F(X-z)dz$ for $\varepsilon>0$. Each integral is absolutely convergent. Off the graph, the limit as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ exists and equals the absolutely convergent desingularized integral $\int K(z)(\theta_F(X-z)-\theta_F(X))dz$. The functions $u_\varepsilon$ converge in $L^1_{\rm loc}(E)$ to $U[F]$; the desingularized expression and $U[F]$ therefore agree a.e. No boundary vector principal value is asserted.
nodes.proof_html: Oddness gives $\int_{|z|>\varepsilon}K(z)dz=0$. Off the graph the density is constant in a ball of radius comparable to the vertical gap, so the desingularized integrand vanishes there. Uniformly in $\varepsilon$, its norm is bounded by $C|y-F(x)|^{1-\alpha}$, an $L^1_{\rm loc}$ majorant: it is bounded by a multiple of the contour majorant $\int|\tau||X-\gamma(s)|^{-\alpha}ds$, which is locally integrable by joint contour-test Fubini. The limit represents $B\theta_F$ by the adjoint pairing and thus equals $U$ a.e. Use the locally-integrable test-function uniqueness theorem, not an unproved pointwise trace claim.

nodes.title: Normal-speed convergence and continuity
nodes.statement_html: The integral defining $W[F](x,t)$ converges absolutely and $W$ is continuous on $\R\times I$. For $|x|\le R$, $t\in J_0\Subset I$, a bound for the integrand in the variable $h=s-x$ is \[ c L_{R,J_0}|h|^{1-\alpha}\mathbf1_{0<|h|\le1} +2c M_{J_0}|h|^{-\alpha}\mathbf1_{|h|>1}, \] where $L_{R,J_0}$ bounds $|F_{xx}|$ on $[-R-1,R+1]\times J_0$.
nodes.proof_html:
Use the mean-value bound for the numerator near $s=x$ and the global slope bound in the tail.
  The denominator is at least $|s-x|^\alpha$. Shift to $h=s-x$ before dominated convergence.

nodes.title: Two-sided vertical normal trace with an error estimate
nodes.statement_html: For $d\ne0$ put $W_d(x,t)=U_2(x,F(x,t)+d,t)-F_x(x,t)U_1(x,F(x,t)+d,t)$. For every $R>0$, $J_0\Subset I$ there is $C=C(\alpha,c,R,J_0,F)>0$ such that \[ \sup_{|x|\le R,\,t\in J_0}|W_d(x,t)-W(x,t)|\le C|d|^{2-\alpha} \quad(0<|d|\le1). \] Thus both vertical normal traces exist and agree with $W$.
nodes.proof_html: Combine the two velocity components inside their absolutely convergent off-graph integrals. The resulting numerator is $c(F_x(x,t)-F_x(x+h,t))$. Split $|h|$ into $(0,|d|)$, $(|d|,1)$ and $(1,\infty)$. Use the near majorant in the first part and the kernel derivative bound $|\partial_d(h^2+(F(x,t)+d-F(x+h,t))^2)^{-\alpha/2}|\le C_\alpha|h|^{-\alpha-1}$ in the other two. The bounds involve only the same compact-time slope and local curvature constants. Lean route: the convergence of the limit integral $W$ is re-derived from the same pointwise majorant, after the substitution $h=|d|r$, so the separate continuity lemma for $W$ is not needed here.

nodes.title: Flat-graph sign and trace check
nodes.statement_html: For $F=0$ and $d\ne0$, \[ U(x,d)=-c\,C_\alpha|d|^{1-\alpha}(1,0),\qquad C_\alpha=\int_\R(1+s^2)^{-\alpha/2}ds\in(0,\infty),\qquad W=0. \] In particular the tangential velocity diverges in magnitude at the boundary while its normal component is zero. Assigning any values to $U$ on the null graph leaves its weak equations unchanged.
nodes.proof_html:
Substitute $s=x+|d|r$ in the velocity integral. Positivity and tail integrability give $C_\alpha>0$.
  Use nullness of the graph to justify representative independence.

nodes.title: Weak patch system with coefficient $c$
nodes.section: Transport and equivalence with the front equation
nodes.statement_html: A scalar (respectively vector) spacetime test on $E\times I$ is a smooth compactly supported function $E\times\R\to\R$ (respectively $E\times\R\to E$) whose support lies in $E\times I$. A bounded measurable density $\theta:E\times I\to\R$ and a measurable $u\in L^1_{\rm loc}(E\times I;E)$ obey the coefficient-$c$ velocity law if, for every vector spacetime test $\Phi$, \[ \int_I\!\int_E u(X,t)\cdot\Phi(X,t)dXdt =\int_I\!\int_E\theta(Y,t)B^*_{\alpha,c}(\Phi(\cdot,t))(Y)dYdt. \] They solve the weak patch system if also, for every scalar spacetime test $\zeta$, \[ \int_I\!\int_E\theta(X,t) [\partial_t\zeta(X,t)+u(X,t)\cdot\nabla_X\zeta(X,t)]dXdt=0. \] All pairings must be absolutely integrable. For $\theta=\theta_F$ boundedness is automatic. With $c=c_{\rm std}$ this is the canonical gSQG operator, as identified in sec:c13_operator. The product $\theta u$ is formed only after obtaining the locally integrable velocity representative.

nodes.title: Spacetime velocity law and uniqueness of the representative
nodes.section: Transport and equivalence with the front equation
nodes.statement_html: For every admissible $F$, the representative $U[F]$ satisfies the coefficient-$c$ velocity law on $E\times I$. Every other locally integrable velocity satisfying that law for $\theta_F$ equals $U[F]$ a.e. in spacetime. Such velocities are divergence-free distributionally in space.
nodes.proof_html: Integrate the spatial identity in time; compact-time slope bounds and test-function seminorms justify Fubini. Apply locally-integrable test-function uniqueness componentwise to the difference. For divergence use gradient tests and $B^*(\nabla\zeta)=0$.

nodes.title: Spatial weak flux across the actual graph
nodes.section: Transport and equivalence with the front equation
nodes.statement_html: For every fixed $t\in I$ and scalar spatial test $\zeta$, \[ \int_{\Omega_t}U(X,t)\cdot\nabla\zeta(X)dX =\int_\R W(x,t)\zeta(x,F(x,t))dx. \] Both integrals are absolutely convergent, with estimates uniform on compact time intervals for tests with a common compact support and bounded first derivatives.
nodes.proof_html: First integrate over $y<F(x,t)-d$, $d>0$. To apply the compact-field formula, multiply $U\zeta$ by a smooth function of the vertical gap that equals one for gap at least $d$ and zero for gap at most $d/2$. This field is $C^1$ across the excluded original graph. On the truncated domain its divergence is $U\cdot\nabla\zeta$. Pass $d\downarrow0$: local integrability controls the volume term, and the cancelled normal trace controls the boundary term, with continuity of $W$ for the dominated boundary limit. Never pass to separate vector boundary traces.

nodes.title: Time derivative of the moving-patch pairing
nodes.section: Transport and equivalence with the front equation
nodes.statement_html: For every scalar spacetime test $\zeta$, \[ \int_I\!\int_E\theta_F\partial_t\zeta =-\int_I\!\int_\R F_t(x,t)\zeta(x,F(x,t),t)dxdt, \] with absolute convergence.
nodes.proof_html:
Write the spatial pairing as $\int dx\int_{-H}^{F(x,t)}\zeta(x,y,t)dy$, with $H$ below
  the vertical test support and below $F$ on its compact horizontal/time projection.
  Differentiate by endpoint FTC and parameter differentiation. Integrate the resulting total
  time derivative over the compact test support; its endpoint terms vanish.
  Lean route: translate $y=F(x,t)+s$ and set $Z(x,s,t)=\zeta(x,F(x,t)+s,t)$, so that
  $\partial_t\zeta(x,F+s,t)=\partial_tZ-F_t\partial_sZ$; then Fubini and FTC on $s\le0$ and in $t$,
  with no differentiation under the integral sign.

nodes.title: Lifting tests from the graph
nodes.section: Transport and equivalence with the front equation
nodes.statement_html: For every scalar test $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\R\times I)$ there is a scalar spacetime test $\zeta\in C_c^\infty(E\times I)$ satisfying $\zeta(x,F(x,t),t)=\psi(x,t)$. Consequently a continuous $r:\R\times I\to\R$ whose integral against all these traces is zero must vanish pointwise.
nodes.proof_html:
Choose a fixed smooth compactly supported $\eta$ with $\eta(0)=1$ and set
  $\zeta(x,y,t)=\psi(x,t)\eta(y-F(x,t))$. The function $F$ is bounded on the compact
  support of $\psi$, making the lifted support compact. Its time support stays inside $I$,
  so extension by zero outside $I$ is smooth. Finish by test-function uniqueness
  and continuity on the open domain.

nodes.title: Two-dimensional patch equation is equivalent to the graph equation
nodes.section: Transport and equivalence with the front equation
nodes.statement_html: Let $F$ be admissible. Then $(\theta_F,U_{\alpha,c}[F])$ solves the coefficient-$c$ weak patch system if and only if \[ F_t(x,t)=c\int_\R \frac{F_x(x,t)-F_x(s,t)}{((x-s)^2+(F(x,t)-F(s,t))^2)^{\alpha/2}}ds \quad(x\in\R,t\in I). \] The same equivalence holds with any locally integrable $u$ satisfying the velocity law, interpreted up to a.e. equality. Every front integral is absolutely convergent.
nodes.proof_html: The transport pairing equals $\int(W-F_t)\zeta(x,F,t)dxdt$. One direction follows by substitution; in the other use lifted tests and continuity of $W-F_t$. A.e. equality of velocities preserves all transport pairings because $\theta_F$ is bounded.

nodes.title: Local time continuity and the initial-value formulation
nodes.section: Transport and equivalence with the front equation
nodes.statement_html: For $R>0$ and $s,t\in I$, \[ \int_{[-R,R]^2}|\theta_F(X,t)-\theta_F(X,s)|dX \le\int_{-R}^R|F(x,t)-F(x,s)|dx. \] Thus $t\mapsto\theta_F(t)$ is continuous into $L^1_{\rm loc}(E)$. If the equivalent equations above hold and $t_0<t_1$ both lie in $I$, let $\zeta$ be smooth on a neighborhood of $E\times[t_0,t_1]$, have a common compact spatial support there, and vanish for $t$ sufficiently close to $t_1$. It may be nonzero at $t_0$. Then \[ \int_{t_0}^{t_1}\!\int_E\theta_F(\partial_t\zeta+U\cdot\nabla\zeta) +\int_E\theta_F(X,t_0)\zeta(X,t_0)dX=0. \] For an initial endpoint outside $I$, this last assertion requires additionally a locally uniform graph limit and a common global slope bound on a one-sided time neighborhood; it is not implied by interior compact-time bounds alone.
nodes.proof_html: Integrate the difference of two half-line indicators on vertical slices. Uniform continuity of $F$ on compact horizontal/time sets gives the local time trace. For the initial-value identity use only the weak transport equation, tested with $\chi_h(t)\zeta$ for a time cutoff $\chi_h$ rising from $0$ at $t_0$ to $1$ at $t_0+h$, together with the $L^1_{\rm loc}$ continuity just proved. Retain the lower endpoint term in the time pairing identity; its sign is positive in the weak formula. Initial-value tests are restrictions of smooth ambient functions, not globally smooth functions required to vanish before $t_0$; that latter restriction would force the initial term to be zero. For the stated endpoint extension, start at $t_0+h$ and use the uniform-slope integrability estimate and the $L^1_{\rm loc}$ density trace as $h\downarrow0$. Lean route: for that endpoint case, the velocity bound and the common slope bound give integrability of $U$ on $K\times(t_0,t_1]$; the limit $F_0$ is continuous, and the $L^1_{\rm loc}$ density limit comes from the slice estimate above applied to the glued graph equal to $F_0$ at $t_0$ and to $F$ for $t>t_0$.

nodes.title: Uniform slope for the self-similar family
nodes.section: Transfer of the front theorem to the canonical patch system
nodes.statement_html: For every profile supplied by thm:main, the graph $F_{\epsilon,T}$ is admissible on $(-\infty,T)$ and satisfies $|F_x(x,t)|\le\sqrt\epsilon(C+1)$ for all $x,t<T$, with the profile-bound constant $C$. No global curvature bound is required.
nodes.proof_html: The two profile estimates imply $|f'|\le C+1$. Differentiate the ansatz to obtain $F_x=\sqrt\epsilon f'(x/L(t))$. Joint smoothness is already part of the main theorem. Local curvature bounds follow on spacetime compacts lying strictly below $T$.

nodes.title: Exact time normalization
nodes.section: Transfer of the front theorem to the canonical patch system
nodes.statement_html: Let $p=\alpha-1$, $\kappa=\kappa_\alpha>0$ and let an admissible $F$ solve the normalized front equation on $I$. Then $G(x,t)=F(x,t/\kappa)$, on $\{t:t/\kappa\in I\}$, is admissible and satisfies the coefficient-$c_{\rm std}$ graph equation. If $I=(-\infty,T/\kappa)$, the new interval is $(-\infty,T)$. For the self-similar ansatz its physical scale is \[ L_{\rm std}(t)=(\alpha(T-t)/\kappa)^{1/\alpha}. \]
nodes.proof_html: The literal normalized graph equation has coefficient $c_{\rm front}$. Time differentiation contributes $1/\kappa=c_{\rm std}/c_{\rm front}$. The ansatz with normalized blow-up time $T/\kappa$ gives the displayed scale. Positivity of $\kappa$ follows directly from positivity of the Gamma factors in $A_\alpha$ and of calpha. Preserve the density jump equal to one; do not absorb the coefficient by silently changing the patch strength.

nodes.title: Canonical two-dimensional patches forming a corner
nodes.section: Transfer of the front theorem to the canonical patch system
nodes.statement_html: Let $\alpha\in(7/4,2)$ and $p=\alpha-1$. There exist $\epsilon_0,C>0$, depending only on $\alpha$, such that for every $0<\epsilon<\epsilon_0$ there is a profile $f_\epsilon$ satisfying all profile estimates of thm:main with constant $C$ and the following property. For every $T>0$, define \[ G(x,t)=\sqrt\epsilon L_{\rm std}(t)f_\epsilon(x/L_{\rm std}(t)),\qquad \theta(X,t)=\mathbf1_{X_2<G(X_1,t)},\qquad u=U_{\alpha,c_{\rm std}}[G]. \] Then on $E\times(-\infty,T)$ the pair is a weak solution of \[ \partial_t\theta+\operatorname{div}(\theta u)=0,\qquad u=-\nabla^\perp(-\Delta)^{-1+\alpha/2}\theta, \] with the canonical normalization defined above and with the initial trace at $t=0$. The interface is smooth for $t<T$ and $\|G(\cdot,t)-\sqrt\epsilon x_-\|_\infty\le C\sqrt\epsilon(T-t)^{1/\alpha}$. For each such $\epsilon$ there is $b_\epsilon>0$, independent of $T$ and $\delta$, such that for every $T,\delta>0$ there is $t_\delta<T$ with $\sup_{|x|<\delta}|\partial_x^2G(x,t)|\ge b_\epsilon(T-t)^{-1/\alpha}$ whenever $t_\delta<t<T$. Moreover, with $\theta_*(X)=\mathbf1_{X_2<\sqrt\epsilon(X_1)_-}$, $\theta(t)\to\theta_*$ in $L^1_{\rm loc}(E)$ as $t\uparrow T$. This is an infinite-area patch result; no global $L^1$ assumption on $\theta$ is made.
nodes.proof_html: Apply the completed front theorem at normalized time $T/\kappa$ and use the equivalence theorem with coefficient $c_{\rm std}$. The initial time zero is interior to the time interval. Corner convergence acquires the fixed factor $\kappa^{-1/\alpha}$ and the curvature lower bound the fixed factor $\kappa^{1/\alpha}$; positivity preserves both claims. On $[-R,R]^2$, the density error is at most $2R$ times the uniform graph-height error. No classical vector velocity at the interface or continuation beyond the corner time is claimed.
